articles.title: La France reçoit ses premiers drones chasseurs de drones, et ils frappent à 350 km/h sans explosif
articles.text:
La DGA a livré aux armées françaises leurs premiers drones intercepteurs souverains, les Gobi Zephyr d'Harmattan AI, une entreprise de l'Hexagone. Destinés à la lutte anti-drones, ils ont été commandés puis livrés en deux mois seulement.
La Direction générale de l'armement (DGA) a livré en novembre aux forces armées françaises leurs premiers drones intercepteurs de drones souverains, baptisés Gobi Zephyr et fabriqués par Harmattan AI, comme on l'a appris en cette fin de semaine. Ces appareils neutralisent les drones adverses par impact direct, sans charge explosive, de jour comme de nuit. Leur livraison intervient à peine deux mois après la commande, au terme d'un cycle d'évaluations mené par le centre expert de la DGA consacré à la lutte anti-drone.
Le Gobi Zephyr, le drone intercepteur français qui joue les boulets de canon
Le Gobi Zephyr, qui pèse à peine 2,5 kg avec ses batteries, est un peu plus qu'un simple drone. On peut dire qu'il s'agit d'un système complet de défense sol-air de très courte portée, c'est-à-dire la dernière couche de protection, celle qui veille au plus près du terrain. Il détecte les drones adverses, puis guide automatiquement l'intercepteur jusqu'à sa cible, dans un rayon de 10 kilomètres. Avec une pointe à 350 km/h, il joue dans la même catégorie que le JEDI Shahed Hunter, que l'Ukraine a homologué plus tôt dans l'année pour traquer les Shahed russes.
Pour neutraliser ses cibles, le Gobi Zephyr mise sur l'impact cinétique, plutôt que sur l'explosion. Il n'embarque pas de charge explosive, puisque l'intercepteur neutralise sa proie par collision, autrement dit, il lui rentre dedans. L'Ukraine est devenue le grand laboratoire de ces drones chasseurs de drones. On sait que là-bas, répondre à chaque vague d'appareils russes avec du matériel classique coûterait bien trop cher, d'où l'essor des intercepteurs à bas coût.
Le point le plus sensible, c'est peut-être celui de l'aspect autonome de la solution. La DGA évoque un « haut niveau d'autonomie opérationnelle ». En fait, le drone peut abattre sa cible tout seul, mais uniquement après qu'un humain a autorisé la mission. Le feu vert reste humain, donc, et la traque et l'interception reviennent à la machine. Quant à l'étiquette « souveraine », elle se justifie par le fait que l'appareil est signé par une entreprise française, en l'occurrence Harmattan AI, et fabriqué en Île-de-France.
Harmattan AI enchaîne les contrats avec l'armée française
Au-delà de ses caractéristiques techniques, c'est la rapidité de son acquisition qui retient notre attention, car deux petits mois seulement ont séparé la commande de la livraison. La DGA invoque la « dronisation » du combat, pour justifier cela. Selon un rapport sénatorial publié cet été, il ne faut plus que six semaines en moyenne, sur le front, pour qu'une nouveauté trouve sa parade. D'où la naissance en 2026 de centres experts taillés pour les technologies qui se démodent vite, chargés de repérer les besoins, d'évaluer des solutions et d'acheter sans traîner. Le Gobi Zephyr est passé par celui dédié à la lutte anti-drone, le Cerlad. On retrouvait déjà ce goût de la vitesse avec le drone anti-brouillage d'Elistair, mis au point en quatre mois.
Pour Harmattan AI, c'est une étape de plus franchie. La jeune pousse parisienne, qui a la pleine confiance du ministère des Armées, avait déjà livré 1 000 drones du combattant en moins d'un an, avant de décrocher une commande de 5 000 drones DELCO. Elle est aussi devenue en janvier la première licorne française de la défense, grâce à une levée de 200 millions de dollars menée par Dassault Aviation, avec qui elle a d'ailleurs fait voler un drone de guerre électronique aux côtés d'un Rafale F4. Son nouveau contrat, découpé en lots et en bons de commande, laisse la porte ouverte, car la DGA pourra remettre des Gobi Zephyr en commande au fil des besoins des armées.
Ces drones vont rejoindre un ciel déjà bien encombré. Le ministère a aussi annoncé jeudi 26 novembre l'intégration de la lutte anti-drones au pacte drones aériens, quelques semaines après des survols nocturnes de la base navale de Toulon, sans qu'aucun appareil ne soit récupéré malgré le brouillage. Le Gobi Zephyr n'est pas le seul sollicité non plus, puisque l'Agence de l'innovation de défense porte le projet d'intercepteurs ELISA, et la start-up Alta Ares a conçu son X-Lock. En attendant le laser Syderal, espéré d'ici 2030, les armées ont désormais leurs propres chasseurs de drones.

articles.title: EEUU se va a poner dura para evitar que las GPU de Nvidia lleguen a China. Y esta vez parece que van en serio
articles.text:
Estados Unidos lleva varios años de guerra comercial y tecnológica con China, y los chips de Nvidia estaban en el ojo del conflicto. No podían vender sus chips más avanzados para inteligencia artificial a empresas chinas y, aunque se levantó algo la mano a finales del año pasado, realmente las empresas chinas tenían una alternativa: alquilar esa potencia de cómputo a centros de datos de otros países.
Sin embargo, Washington ha movido ficha para limitar esa vía y el mercado ya lo está notando. Ahora, directamente, Nvidia habría pedido a sus socios que dejen de enviar servidores con sus chips a países que están bajo la lupa.
En corto. Este jueves, CNBC citó fuentes relacionadas con el negocio que señalaban que los vendedores de chips de Nvidia habían avisado a las neoclouds de que no les suministrarán equipos si una sola parte de su capacidad de cómputo va a parar a compañías chinas. Estas neoclouds son empresas especializadas en alquilar capacidad de cálculo y son las que empresas chinas de IA usaban para poder entrenar sus modelos con equipo al que, por las restricciones comerciales, no podían acceder.
Ese mismo día, Financial Times comentó que Nvidia había pedido a socios como Dell o Supermicro que dejen de enviar servidores con sus equipos a cuatro países que están bajo la lupa de la nueva directriz marcada por el Departamento de Comercio de Estados Unidos. Son Malasia, Singapur, Tailandia e Indonesia, cuatro que se estima que eran la puerta de entrada tanto de las GPU alquiladas en la nube como del contrabando de chips en China.
La nueva norma. Según el FT, estas empresas ya habrían comunicado a sus compradores de estos países que sus pedidos no se distribuirán y no se sabe si es una pausa temporal mientras se adaptan a la nueva norma o algo definitivo, pero sí es mucho más duro que lo que la propia Nvidia, de nuevo según CNBC, había marcado. Antes de ese frenazo en seco, se dijo que la compañía estaba empezando a descartar vender equipos a quien alquilase más del 50% de sus GPU a empresas en China.
Todo esto se ha precipitado debido al caso de Jensen Huang con la supuesta espía china y el asunto de la empresa Megaspeed. Es de Singapur y se estima que habría pasado chips por valor de varios miles de millones de dólares a territorio chino. Parece que el Departamento de Comercio llevaba un tiempo dando vueltas a un endurecimiento de sus políticas, pero todo se ha acelerado. El 16 de noviembre presentaron una norma provisional que entró en vigor el día 19 con los siguientes puntos principales:
- Alquiler remoto: se necesita licencia para enviar chips avanzados a centros de datos que ofrezcan más de 12 millones de TPP a empresas con sede o cuya matriz esté en China, Macau y otros países bajo embargo de armas.
- Esa potencia equivale a unos 750 chips H100 o 2.400 A100 de Nvidia.
- Cinco países vigilados: Malasia, Singapur, Tailandia, Indonesia y Brasil. Las empresas estadounidenses que operen en esos países tienen excepción, pero tienen que informar cada mes del uso.
- Plazo: hasta el 17 de febrero de 2027 para conseguir una licencia.
A wallapop. Con esto, la intención es cerrar el "acceso indirecto" tanto por contrabando como mediante el uso remoto y parece que es algo que ya está teniendo consecuencias. Tencent comentó que la norma tiene el potencial como para hacer retroceder a todos en China debido a que el proceso de entrenamiento de sus próximos modelos se verán afectados.
Y ya se reporta que, en la segunda mano, la medida ha impactado con fuerza con un volumen inusualmente alto de GPU a la venta, con operaciones para colocar miles de B300 (uno de los chips más punteros de Nvidia). Estos chips serían parte de los destinados originalmente a esos centros de datos que dan servicio a empresas chinas. Además, el alquiler de las B300 también cayó un 7% entre octubre y el 24 de noviembre, poco después de que la medida entrara en vigor.
¿Y ahora? Al margen de las consecuencias directas, toca ver dos movimientos. Uno es el que las propias empresas chinas de computación para la IA están desarrollando, como una Huawei que tiene listo su SuperPOD con Atlas 950 y que plantea dar el salto internacional como una alternativa a Nvidia. Otro, la propia política, ya que el 17 de noviembre, justo cuando el Departamento de Comercio planteó la medida, lanzó el aviso: si EEUU insiste en aplicar la norma, tomarán contramedidas.
No han especificado cuáles, pero aunque llevemos tiempo sin hablar del tema, hay que recordar que China mantiene el dominio de esas tierras raras imprescindibles para la carrera tecnológica. De momento no es algo cerrado, ya que la regla permitirá revisiones hasta el 19 de enero del año que viene, momento en el que definitivamente sabremos si EEUU ahora va en serio con las restricciones... o pasa lo que en los últimos años.

From what we've seen of the sales so far during this Black Friday event, the real winners so far have been the fantastic discounts on OLED monitors. In this instance, it's Gigabyte's 27-inch MO27Q28G OLED gaming monitor that has dipped $200 to just $399. That's a heck of a good price for a Tandem OLED display with these specifications.

The screen has super-thin bezels around the edge to maximise the screen real estate, and for connectivity, there are two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 1.4, and two USB 3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps) ports.

Expect a sweet spot between performance and resolution here. With the display's 256 x 1440p resolution and refresh rate, you'll want a fairly powerful system with a decent CPU under the hood to reliably saturate the monitor here. One important note is that the semi-gloss display isn't actually all that bright when compared to more expensive competitors. While you do get a 0.03ms GtG response time, the GA27M1Q's SDR brightness tops out at 300 nits. However, considering the wealth of other features on offer here, it might be a fine trade for a very well rounded panel that's almost garaunteed to look fantastic with deep blacks and a near-infinite contrast ratio. — Sayem Ahmed
Buying a monitor over Black Friday could be one of the best ways to elevate your gaming setup. In 2026, PC component pricing means that upgrades to RAM, SSDs, and GPUs are much more expensive than they used to be. Monitors, by contrast, are cheaper. So, you could spend less and upgrade your viewing experience in a number of different ways. You could get a larger monitor for more immersive viewing and multitasking, upgrade to a higher refresh rate for more frame headroom, or increase your resolution for more detail. Of course, you could also make the leap to OLED, one of the biggest upgrades you can make to gaming right now.
Black Friday has begun and we're tracking all the very best deals on OLED gaming monitors, productivity monitors, and more!

articles.title: We Got GTA 6 Online Before GTA 6 Online
articles.text:
Friday, November 27th 2026
We Got GTA 6 Online Before GTA 6 Online
Progress on GTA 6 PC ports is being made at an astonishing pace, mainly thanks to AI models doing most of the grunt work. However, it can't be denied that, even though most of the GTA 6 PC ports currently are "vibe-coded," they are doing something unprecedented in the gaming space. We covered yesterday that some GTA 6 PC recompilation efforts have reached 20 FPS during gameplay, and many others are claiming even higher numbers. Building on that momentum, a developer going by TeK has shown GTA 6 multiplayer running on PC. The short clip was posted by TeK on X and shows two player characters together on an airport tarmac, with a red sports car being driven around by one of them. 
The clip isn't long, but TeK claims the game runs at a stable 25-30 FPS, even though we can't verify that claim directly since there's no framerate counter visible. The clip is running relatively smoothly, but we don't know the hardware behind it, and the scene is mainly just an empty runway. Performance aside, the fact that someone got multiplayer running in a game that isn't even released on PC is quite something. Moreover, the poster claims that proximity chat also works, which gives the multiplayer claim some more credence. PortWatch VI, a community site tracking these GTA 6 PC projects, has independently verified the video's authenticity and also confirmed that proximity chat is indeed working.According to PortWatch, TeK's group is working on a private fork of the CGBJ build, which is built on the open-source VIctory and XCL projects. The code is private for now, so there's no way for anyone else to test it. Of course, this is nowhere near what Rockstar would be planning for GTA Online, but it's a demonstration of how far these fan-made ports have come. I imagine Take-Two Interactive won't be too happy seeing this, and Rockstar will probably be rethinking their PC port and GTA Online plans as well. As always, readers are advised to not download any unofficial "GTA 6 PC ports," as they have been known to hide malware.
Sources:
				TeK on X, 				PortWatch VI, 				via Notebookcheck

articles.title: Supercoin’s plan to bypass the dollar in African payments
articles.text:
Supercoin, the digital payments company owned by Betway parent Super Group, plans to use a Kenyan shilling-backed stablecoin to settle payments between South Africa and Kenya without routing them through the US dollar.
The company said it has applied to the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) for a stablecoin issuance licence and plans to start serving payment companies in the first half of 2027, subject to approval.
Supercoin wants a remittance firm to take in rand in South Africa, exchange the company’s rand-backed token, ZARsc, for its proposed Kenyan shilling token, KESsc, and pay out in Kenya. A direct swap would remove the need to buy and sell dollars.
The commercial test is whether Supercoin can trade enough rand and shillings to give payment companies a better rate and deliver the money as quickly as their existing providers.
“If we can provide enough liquidity to the ZAR-KES pair in our stablecoin, then we can start selling that rail for instant payments between South Africa and Kenya,” Gideon Greaves, Supercoin’s managing director, told TechCabal in an interview.
Kenya gave Supercoin a clear route to a licence and a market where payment firms were already familiar with stablecoins, Greaves said. Supercoin plans to start with remittance companies, fintechs, and payment networks, with work on a Kenyan consumer wallet expected in the second half of 2027.
The company is entering a market where dollar-backed tokens are already widely used. According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), stablecoins accounted for an estimated $3 billion–$4 billion of about KES 740 billion ($5.7 billion) that Kenyans transacted in cryptocurrencies in 2025.
USDT, the US dollar-backed stablecoin issued by El Salvador-based company Tether, was the preferred digital currency for many Kenyan consumers paying informally and receiving remittances, according to the IMF.
Supercoin proposes that a payment firm can settle in shillings even when its customers prefer to save in dollars.
The off-ramp problem
Sending a stablecoin takes seconds, thanks to the blockchain. However, getting the money into a recipient’s local bank account or mobile wallet requires an “off-ramp.”
Without reliable off-ramps with enough local currency on hand, stablecoin issuers will struggle to persuade payment firms to use their digital tokens for remittances. Those firms need to know they can pay recipients in full and on time, even when transfer volumes spike.
If a company is sending rand-backed stablecoins to a Kenyan market, it needs an off-ramp to settle the payment and make the cash available where the recipient collects it.
“Even when there is a venue where the stablecoin exists, and someone’s making a payment from stablecoin somewhere else—let’s say to Zimbabwe, for example—for a cash collection at a kiosk, it’s settling in fiat,” Greaves said. “So it’s still going through those banking rails.”
Greaves said Supercoin has signed an off-ramp agreement with a partner in Kenya. Yet, talks about access to a mobile money off-ramp for fiat payouts—which most Kenyans use—were still exploratory. At the end of September 2026, M-PESA had 42.3 million monthly active customers in Kenya, according to Safaricom.
Supercoin plans to supply the tokens that payment companies use to settle transfers. Those companies would still need a way to pay recipients who want their money in a mobile wallet.
“The wallet is very much a secondary business for us,” Greaves said. “It’s an area of utility for the stablecoin. But our core focus on our North Star is the issuance side. So we’ll always be the rail in the background.”
Payment firms already have other ways to reach Kenyan accounts. In February, PesaLink, Kenya’s instant payment network, partnered with the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) to enable round-the-clock cross-border payments in local currencies into participating Kenyan bank and mobile money accounts.
Supercoin would have to give payment firms a reason to switch. A direct rand-to-shilling trade could remove a currency conversion, but savings could shrink if the market for the two tokens is too thin to offer a competitive rate or if payouts are expensive.
South Africa shows the other side of the problem. Since its September 2025 launch, Supercoin has grown to surpass 10 million ZARsc tokens in circulation, according to Greaves. Three of South Africa’s largest cryptocurrency exchanges, Luno, VALR, and OVEX—which have a combined 7.8 million users—serve as distribution venues for Supercoin’s ZARsc.
Yet, adopters still mainly use the stablecoin to trade cryptocurrencies. In its next phase, Supercoin wants its stablecoin embedded in corporate and merchant payments, with yield offerings and investments becoming a key part of that strategy.
In November, the stablecoin issuer launched Supercoin Mint, allowing approved businesses to deposit rand in exchange for ZARsc and redeem the tokens for rand paid into their bank accounts. The service lets large payment companies mint and redeem ZARsc as part of their day-to-day operations.
Another feature, ZARsc Borrow, lets customers on South African crypto exchange VALR borrow Supercoin’s rand-backed stablecoin using their cryptocurrency holdings as collateral.
“If we onboarded a large payment service provider, we can’t be doing minting and redemption on email,” Greaves said. “We have to do it properly, seamlessly in a safe environment where they’ve done KYB, they enter the console, they deposit the rands, they get ZARsc out and reverse.”
Supercoin’s liquidity advantage
Greaves said Supercoin currently draws on its parent’s balance sheet for liquidity. Super Group, the NYSE-listed owner of Betway and online casino business Spin, reported $602 million in cash and cash equivalents at the end of September 2026, and a profit of $142 million in Q3.
“In Kenya, we’re not concerned about the capital requirements,” Greaves said. “We see this opportunity.”
Kenya requires stablecoin issuers to have KES 300 million ($2.3 million) in paid-up capital, the highest minimum under its virtual asset rules, which took effect on November 4. Issuers must also hold reserves sufficient to cover every outstanding token.
At least 30% of the funds they receive for tokens must sit in segregated trust accounts at Kenyan commercial banks, with the balance invested in eligible assets in Kenya, including short-term government securities.
While a well-funded parent company can help an issuer clear the capital threshold, it still needs enough companies and businesses buying and selling both tokens to keep the exchange rate competitive.
Supercoin is also mulling plans for a naira-backed stablecoin, according to Greaves. He noted that the talks remain “exploratory.”
Nigeria’s central bank requires at least ₦10 billion ($7.44 million) in paid-up capital for issuers of naira-backed tokens and ₦15 billion ($11.16 million) for issuers of foreign currency-backed tokens.
Supercoin’s ZARsc is backed by the South African rand, so offering it in Nigeria would generally require a locally licenced issuer with at least ₦15 billion ($11.16 million) in paid-up capital under CBN rules.
On the other hand, issuing a naira-backed stablecoin through a licenced Nigerian subsidiary would lower that requirement.
Who earns the interest?
Issuers can earn income from eligible reserve assets backing their stablecoins, such as short-term government securities.
Passing some of that income to token holders would give customers a reason to hold balances between payments, especially when they could earn interest on the same money in a bank account. Greaves said Supercoin was working on a way for users to earn yield on ZARsc through exchanges.
“To truly benefit [from] the full power of money being on chain, you would need to have the same benefits that you have of fiat,” Greaves said. “And one of the benefits that you have of holding fiat is earning yield.”
Kenya bars stablecoin issuers from paying interest to holders and prohibits licencees from granting interest on stablecoin-related services. The ban covers benefits linked to how long someone holds a token. An issuer can earn income on its reserves, while customers have less incentive to move interest-bearing balances out of banks.
Several African regulators, including Nigeria’s central bank, are banning stablecoin yield, likely to discourage customers from moving savings out of bank deposits and into tokens that pay higher returns.
Greaves expects regulators to revisit those restrictions as the industry matures. In the meantime, stablecoin issuers like Supercoin are pitching their case as effective payment tools.
For the payments company, connecting the rails between Kenya and South Africa—and eventually to other African currencies—will enable it to build a closed-loop ecosystem that lets businesses and merchants make intra-African payments without needing the dollar.

articles.title: I ranked the 'Big Four' VPNs this Black Friday — Here's which of NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Proton, or Surfshark actually wins
articles.text:
I ranked the 'Big Four' VPNs this Black Friday — Here's which of NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Proton, or Surfshark actually wins
From Surfshark's sub-$2 price cut to ExpressVPN undercutting NordVPN, here is which flagship VPN deserves your money this Black Friday
Black Friday has seriously squeezed pricing across the "Big Four" in TechRadar's best VPN recommendations.
Whether you pick NordVPN, Surfshark, Proton VPN, or ExpressVPN, the price tag will sit within a narrow and comforting $1.99 to $2.99 per month range thanks to some great Black Friday VPN deals.
On paper, they may look almost identical. But they aren't. Speeds, device caps, and bundled security tools still vary wildly across the four providers.
And while NordVPN remains our #1 all-round VPN, Surfshark certainly delivers the best Black Friday value today. Here is how their pricing, features, and performance stack up.
1. NordVPN: Best all-rounder and streaming champion
NordVPN is our top-rated VPN of 2026. Its Black Friday Basic deal drops to the equivalent of $2.99 per month over 27 months (billed at $80.73 upfront), with Complete at $3.99/month and Prime at $6.99/month.
Streamers and everyday users will love how reliably it unblocks Netflix, Disney+, Prime Video, and live sports without buffering, backed by six independent no-logs audits and 100 Tbps of global network capacity.
NordLynx speeds hit 1,427 Mbps in our tests, though long-distance routes dipped to 633 Mbps.
Value is the bigger snag. At $2.99/month, Basic gives you only the VPN, no malware or tracker blocking, while capping you at 10 devices and jumping sharply on renewal.
NordVPN: Get up to 78% OFF + 3 months FREE
NordVPN's improved Black Friday deal cuts its 27-month Basic plan to $2.99/month (with Complete at $3.99 and Prime at $6.99). It's our top pick for effortless streaming and reliability across 10 devices, backed by a 30-day money-back guarantee.
2. Surfshark: Best Black Friday value deal and family pick
After matching Starter at $2.49/month in its early Black Friday launch, Surfshark just undercut itself with a last-minute improved Black Friday discount.
Starter is now the equivalent of $1.99/month, while the company's full security suite, Surfshark One, drops to $2.29/month (billed $61.83 upfront for 27 months of protection).
For families and bargain hunters, nothing else comes close: you get unlimited simultaneous connections, antivirus, Scam Protection, Alternative ID, and dark web alerts for less than rivals charge for a bare virtual private network (VPN) tool.
Surfshark flies in speed tests, too. Its VPN led the pack locally at 2,005 Mbps and even hit 1,739 Mbps transatlantic. Still, it lacks NordVPN's streaming polish and disclosed a minor internal test-server incident in September (though zero user data was affected).
Surfshark: Get Surfshark at its lowest price of the year
Surfshark's Black Friday deal gives you the opportunity to save big on both the Surfshark Starter and Surfshark One plan. The latter is certainly the most convenient, as for the equivalent of $2.29/month (billed at $61.83 upfront), you'll also get extra security features like antivirus and scam protection. Everything is backed by a 7-day trial and a 30-day money-back guarantee.
3. Proton VPN: Best for strict privacy and single-tier simplicity
Proton VPN keeps pricing refreshingly simple at the equivalent of $2.49/month for two years on Proton VPN Plus (saving $24).
Privacy purists get Swiss jurisdiction, open-source apps, five consecutive annual Securitum no-logs audits, and every core VPN feature unlocked, including Stealth obfuscation, Secure Core multi-hop, NetShield blocking, and port forwarding.
Speeds stay remarkably steady over distance. Proton hit 1,783 Mbps locally and 1,397 Mbps on East US-to-UK routes, easily beating NordVPN.
Just watch out for steep renewal hikes, a 10-device cap, recent internal management controversies at Proton, and zero antivirus or breach-alert extras unless you upgrade to the full Proton Unlimited suite (which is currently at $1 for the first month).
Proton VPN Plus: Save $24 on its 24-month plan
Proton VPN Plus drops to the equivalent of $2.49/month on a two-year plan, saving $24. You get all of Proton's privacy and anti-censorship tools, fast long-distance speeds, and 10 simultaneous connections, backed by a 30-day money-back guarantee.
4. ExpressVPN: Best for beginners wanting built-in extras
ExpressVPN recently undercut NordVPN by cutting its 28-month Basic tier to the equivalent of $2.79 a month (with Advanced at $3.99 and Pro at $6.99).
Built for non-technical buyers, it pairs British Virgin Islands privacy and 27 security audits with 10–14 device limits by tier, plus ExpressAI, email aliasing, and ad, tracker, and malware blocking right on Basic.
There is one big performance catch. Lightway Turbo hit 1,177 Mbps locally and up to 1,117 Mbps long-distance, yet Turbo works only on Windows; standard Lightway on Mac and mobile slumped to 489 Mbps.
ExpressVPN: Save extra with Black Friday improved deal
ExpressVPN Basic beats NordVPN on price and features at $2.79/month over 28 months. You get an ultra-simple VPN for 10 devices alongside ExpressAI, email aliasing, and ad, tracker, and malware blocking, all backed by a 30-day money-back guarantee.
The verdict
Surfshark One at $2.29/month is certainly the standout Black Friday deal today for pure value, speed, and unlimited devices.
Pay $2.99/month for NordVPN if flawless streaming comes first. Choose Proton VPN ($2.49/month) for audited open-source privacy, or ExpressVPN ($2.79/month) if you want effortless apps with built-in extras on Windows.

articles.title: Científicos del MIT desarrollan un modelo de IA que puede diseñar chips como un ingeniero y con una fracción de recursos
articles.text:
Investigadores del Instituto de Tecnología de Massachusetts (MIT) desarrollaron SLIC, un método de inteligencia artificial para diseñar circuitos integrados analógicos con modelos de lenguaje pequeños que pueden ejecutarse localmente. La técnica podría acelerar el diseño de chips utilizados en funciones como las comunicaciones y la gestión de energía, sin exponer datos confidenciales de empresas y fundiciones a servicios externos en la nube, informó MIT News, el portal de noticias del instituto.
El sistema, descripto en arXiv, obtuvo resultados cercanos a los del modelo GPT-6-Astra en pruebas de diseño que exigían cumplir métricas específicas de rendimiento, aunque utilizó una fracción de los recursos computacionales. También conservó su desempeño frente a estructuras de circuitos que no había visto antes, nodos tecnológicos más avanzados y procesos comerciales reales.
La investigación será presentada en la Conferencia sobre Sistemas de Procesamiento de Información Neuronal de 2026. El método busca que un modelo reducido pueda diseñar circuitos analógicos con un nivel comparable o superior al de sistemas de mayor escala. Estos chips permiten que los dispositivos electrónicos procesen señales del mundo físico, como las comunicaciones inalámbricas de un teléfono o las mediciones de temperatura del motor de un automóvil.
Un modelo local para datos industriales confidenciales
El diseño de circuitos analógicos suele depender de ajustes manuales entre numerosas variables y objetivos que pueden entrar en conflicto. Los ingenieros deben definir parámetros para alcanzar un rendimiento determinado y, a partir de una configuración inicial, modificar componentes hasta aproximarse a las especificaciones requeridas.
Yan Xu, estudiante de posgrado de Ingeniería Eléctrica y Ciencias de la Computación del MIT y autora principal del trabajo, explicó que el procedimiento no admite una fórmula única: “Para diseñar un circuito, los ingenieros encuentran un buen punto de partida basándose en su intuición y luego, a partir de sus conocimientos sobre diseño de circuitos, ajustan algunos controles hacia el rendimiento que buscan. No hay una forma universal de resolver todos los problemas de diseño de circuitos”.
Los modelos generativos de gran tamaño pueden automatizar parte de esa tarea, pero su uso suele requerir infraestructura remota y grandes recursos de cómputo. Para las compañías del sector, enviar datos específicos de una fundición o diseños propietarios a proveedores externos de inteligencia artificial puede representar un riesgo de privacidad.
SLIC permite entrenar y desplegar el modelo dentro de la propia organización. Xu sostuvo que el sistema ofrece “una opción alternativa para automatizar el diseño de circuitos analógicos” y añadió que las empresas pueden usar sus propios datos confidenciales para entrenar un modelo local y conservar sus activos protegidos.
El modelo empleado utiliza unos pocos miles de millones de parámetros, una escala de varios miles de veces menor que la de los sistemas de frontera, que pueden operar con billones de parámetros. Esa reducción permite ejecutarlo en una computadora portátil, con menores costos y consumo de recursos.
Simulaciones, ajustes y mejoras después de cumplir la meta
El método reproduce una parte del aprendizaje de un ingeniero. Primero, un modelo de mayor tamaño genera varias demostraciones del proceso de diseño de código abierto para un problema de optimización analógica; luego, esas demostraciones sirven para orientar al sistema pequeño.
Después de esa etapa inicial, el modelo enfrenta por sí solo un nuevo problema de diseño. Propone valores para los parámetros del circuito, realiza simulaciones, evalúa los resultados y ajusta de forma iterativa sus decisiones con el conocimiento adquirido durante el entrenamiento.
La técnica utiliza aprendizaje por refuerzo de múltiples etapas con recompensas verificables: el sistema recibe información del entorno durante una tarea compuesta por varios pasos y adapta su conducta a partir de esa respuesta. Cuando ya encuentra un diseño que cumple los objetivos definidos por el usuario, continúa buscando mejoras marginales de rendimiento.
Ruonan Han, autor principal sénior del trabajo, profesor de Ingeniería Eléctrica y Ciencias de la Computación del MIT y miembro del Laboratorio de Investigación en Electrónica de la institución, señaló que los modelos pequeños especializados pueden aproximarse a los resultados de sistemas mucho más grandes: “Mediante entrenamiento especializado e investigación en áreas específicas, podemos usar modelos mucho más pequeños, que consumen muchos menos recursos, para lograr casi los mismos resultados que los modelos insignia en el diseño de circuitos analógicos”.
El proceso también puede ser interpretado por el usuario porque los modelos describen su razonamiento en lenguaje natural. “Aunque todo el proceso está automatizado, el usuario puede ver qué ocurre dentro del modelo”, afirmó Han. Esa visibilidad puede aportar ideas sobre el diseño y aumentar la confianza en las decisiones del sistema.
Aplicaciones en chips de radiofrecuencia y microondas
Las empresas pueden adaptar el modelo entrenado por los investigadores a sus propios datos mediante un proceso de ajuste posterior o utilizar el método para construir una versión propia. Como enseña un procedimiento general de diseño de chips, SLIC no queda vinculado a una compañía determinada y puede aplicarse a distintas clases de circuitos.
Wenjie Lu, exinvestigador posdoctoral del MIT y ahora científico principal de investigación en Analog Devices, Inc., indicó que la demanda de chips analógicos crece mientras la velocidad de diseño no ha seguido el mismo ritmo. “Esta investigación intenta aportar nuevas capacidades a la inteligencia artificial para resolver un problema en el que la industria lleva décadas estancada”, añadió.
Zhang consideró que el modelo local puede aprender comportamientos de diseño transferibles y perfeccionar un circuito mediante un simulador, lo que reduciría los ajustes manuales repetitivos. Añadió que la línea de trabajo podría conducir a diseños personalizados más complejos, incluidos circuitos de radiofrecuencia y microondas.
Los investigadores planean estudiar modelos capaces de mejorar de manera autónoma para abordar topologías y objetivos de diseño más variados. También buscan crear una arquitectura con varios modelos pequeños, cada uno dedicado a una parte distinta de una tarea compleja de diseño de circuitos.

articles.title: Black Friday 2026: Galaxy A37 despenca 65% em oferta inédita na Amazon
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026: Galaxy A37 despenca 65% em oferta inédita na Amazon
Galaxy A37 (128 GB) com tela de 120 Hz e câmera de 50 MP alcança o menor preço histórico na Black Friday 2026, com desconto de 65% no Pix com cupons
O Galaxy A37 de 128 GB está saindo por R$ 1.203,49 no Pix com cupons 15IMPERDIVEL e SAMSUNG R$ 100 OFF disponíveis na página da Amazon. O smartphone da Samsung, com tela de 120 Hz e câmera de 50 MP, alcança o menor preço histórico na Black Friday 2026, com desconto de 65% sobre o original de R$ 3.499.
Esta oferta é o menor preço que já encontramos para o Galaxy A37 5G 128 GB. Nas outras 14 ofertas publicadas desde maio de 2026, o melhor foi R$ 1.337,40 (Magalu, 11/11/2026).
O A37 é um dos lançamentos recentes da Samsung. Seu kit principal de câmeras inclui wide com OIS de 50 MP e ultrawide de 8 MP, que captam belas cenas ao ar livre, e macro de 5 MP para aproximações de elementos pequenos. A frontal de 12 MP tira selfies com boa qualidade. Todas filmam em 4K.
O chip Exynos 1480 e os 8 GB de RAM rodam apps mais leves, como navegadores e redes sociais, e algumas funções do Galaxy AI. Os 128 GB de espaço interno podem ser expandidos com planos de armazenamento na nuvem.
Sua tela Super AMOLED de 6,7″ possui taxa de 120 Hz e brilho de até 1.900 nits com tecnologia Vision Booster. Esse novo recurso otimiza o brilho e o contraste para oferecer cores mais realistas com alta fluidez, além de garantir a visibilidade em qualquer ambiente.
O corpo do Galaxy A37 é revestido em ambos os lados pelo vidro Gorilla Glass Victus+, resistente a quedas e pancadas. A certificação IP68 adiciona proteção em cenários como poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 5.000 mAh tem autonomia de até 29 horas de vídeo, segundo a Samsung. O suporte ao carregamento rápido de 45 W permite receber uma carga de 60% em 30 minutos, ideal para quem não deseja depender de tomadas.
O Galaxy A37 de 128 GB (R$ 1.203,49 no Pix com cupons 15IMPERDIVEL e SAMSUNG R$ 100 OFF disponíveis na página) será atualizado até o Android 22 e possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.4 e NFC.
A Black Friday 2026 começou, e lojas como a Amazon oferecem diversas ofertas em gadgets com cupons e condições especiais até a Cyber Monday, na próxima segunda-feira (30).

articles.text:
The holiday shopping season is upon us, and as is our custom, we’re here with a list of Ars staffers’ favorite recent purchases that could make good gifts. (Or maybe they might be a gift you get yourself!)
Rather than try to write a definitive “best gifts for your sister or brother” type of guide, we simply polled Ars staffers on stuff they’ve actually bought this year that they recommend. The thinking is that if we’re into it, hopefully some of you or your friends or family might be. As such, there’s no rhyme or reason to these selections, really; it’s just a list of stuff we bought that we’re happy about. It’s heavy on interesting books and cycling accessories, but there are some gadgets and the like in here, too.
For each gadget (or whatever else it might be), we have a brief description of how or why we’ve been using this particular thing and why we would recommend it. Our picks are ordered by price, from lowest to highest. Note, though, that the prices of these products are listed as they were when the list was written. Online retailers often adjust prices frequently, especially around Black Friday, so just a heads up: The price might be different by the time you read this.
Also, a callout to the Ars commentariat: If you have your own holiday buying recommendations, feel free to share them. We or some fellow readers might take your advice if you suggest something good! Happy holidays!
I understand the convenience and space-savings that e-readers bring. My 2011 Kindle Touch goes with me everywhere I carry my travel backpack, but I’m still a softy for physical books when I’m sitting at home on a lazy Sunday. What started as something of a fanfic send-up of LitRPGs has quickly blossomed into a massive sensation of a series filled with far more depth, heart, and character than the initial premise might indicate. Author Matt Dinniman has an accessible style that will grip any reader with a taste for whimsical adventure. Just be warned that if you leave the books under the tree, you might not see much of the recipient until New Year’s.
Two excellent books that help describe how the Internet’s undersea backbone became a globe-spanning reality were published in 2026. Together, they form a great gift pairing for anyone interested in how humanity first achieved near-instantaneous communication across the world’s oceans—and how the first trans-Atlantic telegraph cable paved the way for a global network of subsea data cables that now faces growing risks from geopolitical conflicts.
James Tabor’s Lightning Beneath the Sea dives into the astounding real-life story of how American entrepreneur Cyrus Field, lacking in expertise but driven by personal fervor, set out to achieve peace on Earth by laying a 2,000-mile telegraph cable made of copper across the Atlantic seafloor in 1866.
To pull off the feat, Field managed to convince some of the greatest innovators and scientific luminaries of his day, such as Samuel F.B. Morse, Lord Kelvin, and Michael Faraday, to join his venture. He also refitted the SS Great Eastern steamship, the largest passenger liner ship built to date, as a cable-laying vessel.
That first ocean-spanning telegraph cable gave rise to more such cables for transmitting messages around the world. Eventually copper gave way to a network of subsea fiber-optic cables that became the Internet’s undersea backbone, and the modern world also became interlinked with submarine power cables and underwater pipelines for carrying oil and gas.
But all that undersea infrastructure is now facing growing danger from the threat of deliberate sabotage, as described in Elisabeth Braw’s book Undersea War. Her book provides a sobering but enlightening look at why subsea cables and pipelines are becoming more tempting targets amid rising geopolitical tensions and conflicts—and how governments and companies are responding to recent cable-cutting incidents around the world.
It’s a little-remembered film for most people, but I absolutely love The Burbs. Sure, it’s more Halloween fare than Christmas, but last year I picked The Thing, so clearly “1980s movies for October” is my December viewing MO.
Starring Tom Hanks, Carrie Fisher, and Corey Feldman, this is a dry, hilarious send-up of suburban life with a horror-adjacent mystery that keeps you guessing. (It’s not scary, though.) I hardly ever hear anyone else talk about this movie, but I love it, and it only recently came out in 4K, so I’m taking this opportunity to shout it out.
If you’re a technically minded Ars reader looking for a nice book to snuggle down with over the holidays, David Woods’ How Apollo Flew to the Moon could be just the thing. (There’s also an audiobook version.) Woods has an accessible style that breaks down complex engineering challenges and their solutions into easily digestible chunks that clarify without oversimplifying. He uses that style to take readers on a detailed trip through the machinery of Project Apollo, from the launch facilities and Mission Control all the way to the specific mechanics of how to navigate to and land on the Moon—and, from there, how to return safely to Earth.
Ever wondered about the insane engineering that let the Saturn V’s first stage burn almost 15 tons of fuel every second as it powered the crew into orbit? Or how to pinpoint a spacecraft’s centimeter-precise distance from Earth on its way to the Moon? Or how Apollo crews tracked their own position with stellar navigation, using sextants and star sightings? Or what a REFSMMAT is, or how television transmissions from the Moon worked, or how they got those crazy lunar buggies onto the Moon’s surface? All these questions and more are given beautifully complete and technically satisfying answers, suitable for both the curious layperson and also the interested engineer. Grab this book and stun your family at Christmas with amazing Apollo trivia—as a bonus, you’ll have the knowledge to make your “We never landed on the Moon!” conspiracy theorist uncle so angry that he stops talking and watches football in grumpy silence! Everyone wins!
As someone who grew up in the classic era of 16-bit SNES RPGs, this 40th anniversary tribute to the series’ history is everything I could have ever wanted in a modern entry. I haven’t properly played through a Final Fantasy entry since the days of Final Fantasy X on PlayStation 2, but when friends kept nudging me that this was the perfect “Nick game,” I figured I should probably take a look. There’s a free six-hour demo available on supported platforms if you’re still on the fence about picking this one up, but don’t be surprised if you end up grabbing a copy for yourself.
For the past couple of years, I’ve been transforming my tiny office into a sanctuary in the evenings, since I do most of my writing (and gaming) in here then. It started with Govee Hexa panels, then came an RGB TV backlight, then colorful smart bulbs for the built-in light fixtures. I topped it off with the Star Light projector, which coats the ceiling in a soothing, ever-shifting, immersive stars-and-nebula effect.
It’s probably not for everybody, but my office is tiny, and I spend a lot of time here both for work and for fun. Tapping a button to completely shift the vibe is surprisingly effective at making it a room I don’t mind spending time in even after I’ve been working in it all day.
Easily my favorite impulse purchase of 2026, the FM-1 is a great gift for curious tinkerers and experienced musicians alike. At around $70 or less, you don’t have to break the bank to get fiddling. A perfectly decent stock synthesizer on its own, the real fun starts when you begin experimenting with the community firmware packages that transform the synth into anything from a multi-track groovebox to one of the more hilarious ways that I’ve ever tried to play Doom.
– Nick Indge
Under $300
Trek BellBeats digital bike bell and speaker – $125 One of the great things about cycling is the chance to be alone with my thoughts—just me and my bike. But that can be too much of a good thing on longer zone 2 rides and centuries. Sporting the size and shape of an old-school bicycle bell, the Trek BellBeats is a safer alternative to donning headphones while on the bike. BellBeats pair with your phone via Bluetooth and will play music at a volume loud enough to enjoy your tunes or hear navigation prompts, but they are not so loud that the music drowns out traffic (or the radar on your bike computer). They can be mounted on just about any non-aero handlebars, charge over USB-C, and offer up to six hours of playtime. And as a bonus, they double as a bicycle bell.
I use Bluetooth headphones most of the time, but frustratingly, they don’t work with voice chat on the PlayStation 5, and I needed a good-quality headset for my Friday night multiplayer gaming sessions.
I’ve always liked Fractal Design’s PC cases, so I decided to roll the dice on their affordable-for-the-quality, over-ear headphones. They support Bluetooth, but they also have a USB dongle, so they can be used for voice chat on game consoles, too.
I was surprised by how much I like them, and despite buying them just for the PS5, I’ve ended up using them in other contexts. Part of that is because they’re very comfortable, and the design avoids my glasses frames well.
I also like that, although they are gaming headphones with all the expected bells and whistles for that, they don’t have an over-the-top design.
If you’re in the market for mid-range wireless gaming headphones that look like something you could actually wear in public without embarrassment, these fit the bill so far.
– Samuel Axon
Povec C1 Performance Sunglasses – $250 Photochromic sunglasses are incredibly useful for outdoor workouts. Two of the most popular bike trails near me run through forest preserves, and the lighting changes steadily as the forest canopy closes in or spreads out. My default sunglasses are a cheap, $28 pair from Rockbros. Unlike other photochromic glasses, which change tints via a pokey chemical reaction, the Povec C1 uses a battery to switch between tints in a second. All the rider (or runner) needs to do is swipe the right temple and the lenses will darken or lighten almost instantaneously. The C1 charges via a small USB-C port, and the Povec claims 28 days of battery life with four hours of daily usage. I’ve used them off and on for about six weeks and have only had to charge them once.
The C1 comes in three frame colors and either Green Revo or Gold Revo glasses and is an excellent stocking stuffer for the runner, cyclist, or skier in your life.
– Eric Bangeman
$300 and over
Garmin Varia RCT715 radar camera tail light – $300 Last spring, a friend of mine was the victim of a hit-and-run while on a ride. Although she wasn’t seriously hurt, her brand-new bike was totaled. The driver got an unwelcome surprise a couple of days later when the police knocked on his front door and arrested him. My friend was riding with a Garmin Varia RCT715, a combination taillight and radar with a camera. The 1080p/30 fps camera captured the car’s license plate, making it possible for the police to identify the driver. More than 90 percent of my riding is on roads, and I don’t feel fully comfortable without my Varia. I have it paired with my Garmin Edge 1050 bike computer, but it will work with most other brands via ANT+. The Varia detects approaching vehicles at 140 meters, and I have it set to record video starting when a car is detected and for 30 seconds after it passes. Battery life is up to six hours, depending on whether the taillight is solid or flashing, and video is saved on a 16GB microSD memory card.
My YouTube algorithm has recently fed me videos of testers using an angle grinder to cut through decent bike locks in under a minute. I’ve never seen an angle grinder-assisted theft in person, but I’ve seen enough heaps of bike parts around town to know people’s rides are getting jacked somewhere. As someone known to be neurotic about leaving my bike outside my purview, I’m looking for added security measures to ease my stress. Enter the Hiplok, which, according to the tests I’ve watched, will turn multiple angle-grinder blades to dust. Do bike thieves carry several discs, and will they spend about 15 minutes trying to break this lock? I don’t know, but I have my doubts. At nearly $400, it’s about as expensive as it gets to secure your ride, but when your bike tops $5,000, it’s probably worth the added theft deterrence and peace of mind.
Santa left this one last year, and the rest of my handheld collection has felt neglected since. Sporting a Snapdragon 8 Elite (now dubbed the Dragonwing Q8) chip, excellent ergonomics, and a 6-inch 120Hz AMOLED screen, it’s the perfect balance between size and horsepower. The Android unit is capable enough to play most anything you can throw at it, without the bulk of a Steam Deck or the bloat of a Windows handheld. Thanks to things like Proton, FEX translation, and software like DroidDeck or GameNative, there isn’t much I can’t use it for. Streaming consoles or PC gaming? Check. Access to Steam, GOG, Epic, Rockstar libraries? Check. High-end native Android gaming? Yup. Emulate anything under the sun? You’re covered there, too. The latest Odin 3 Portal hardware revision gets a larger 7-inch screen and a base RAM configuration of 12GB over the original model’s 8GB. I may have to ask Mr. Claus about an upgrade…
– Nick Indge

articles.title: Anthropic halló que 14 de 23 modelos de IA conservan conocimiento sobre ciberataques tras intentar borrarlo
articles.text:
Investigadores de Anthropic comprobaron que 14 de 23 modelos de inteligencia artificial a los que se les había aplicado una técnica para borrar conocimiento sobre ciberataques siguen “sabiendo” la respuesta correcta. Los modelos parecían limpios en las pruebas habituales, pero la información seguía dentro.
El trabajo es de Jasmine Shone y Lisa Dunlap, y se difundió en el blog de Alignment Science de la compañía. Forma parte del programa Anthropic Fellows y es la segunda parte de una serie sobre interpretabilidad, la rama de la IA que intenta entender qué ocurre dentro de un modelo en lugar de juzgarlo solo por lo que responde.
Las autoras analizaron 23 versiones públicas de modelos a las que se les había aplicado “desaprendizaje”, un conjunto de técnicas que buscan que un modelo olvide material peligroso sin perder el resto de sus capacidades. Usaron WMDP-cyber, una prueba de 1.987 preguntas de opción múltiple sobre conocimiento que podría servir para un ciberataque.
En esa prueba estándar, los modelos parecían haber olvidado. Su precisión bajaba hacia el nivel del azar, mientras que su desempeño general se mantenía.
Qué encontraron al mirar dentro de los modelos
Shone y Dunlap aplicaron otra medición: comparar la probabilidad que el modelo asigna al texto de cada respuesta posible. En 14 de los 23 modelos, la respuesta correcta seguía ocupando el primer lugar en la mayoría de las preguntas que el modelo original acertaba. Es decir, la puntuación bajaba, pero el dato seguía disponible.
Los autores explican el mecanismo así: los métodos que mejor puntúan en la prueba estándar se comportan como una puerta trasera. Ciertas neuronas del modelo se activan entre 20 y 100 veces más ante texto de ciberseguridad después del desaprendizaje y siguen débiles ante otro tipo de texto. Esa activación añade ruido que desbarata el cálculo de la respuesta, pero no elimina el conocimiento.
Otros métodos, como el ascenso de gradiente, NPO, SimNPO y TAR, funcionan de otra manera. Según el estudio, el modelo parece calcular la respuesta en las capas intermedias y suprimirla al final, y el daño se extiende tanto al texto de ciberseguridad como al resto.
El estudio también muestra que, en algunos de estos modelos, restaurar un pequeño grupo de neuronas modificadas recupera las respuestas perdidas. Restaurar neuronas elegidas al azar casi no tiene efecto.
El problema de hacer que una IA olvide de verdad
Según los autores, si una técnica borrara de verdad la información peligrosa, quizá no obtendría buenos resultados en las pruebas que se usan hoy. El problema es que el conocimiento puede estar conectado con otros temas dentro del modelo. Por eso, intentar eliminar una parte puede afectar información que no se buscaba borrar.
Los investigadores creen que, una vez entrenada, una IA podría no ser capaz de olvidar por completo conocimientos de ciberseguridad que no estaban incluidos en la lista de datos que se quería eliminar. Como alternativa, plantean separar esa información peligrosa desde el momento en que se entrena el modelo.
El trabajo tiene límites. Analizó versiones públicas de modelos y no los sistemas comerciales de Anthropic. Además, fue realizado dentro de un programa de becarios y no forma parte de un anuncio de producto de la empresa.
El dato de 14 de 23 indica cuántos modelos mantuvieron la respuesta correcta como su opción más probable, según la medición explicada antes. No mide si esos modelos podrían ayudar de forma concreta a alguien a realizar un ciberataque. El estudio no evaluó esa posibilidad.
La advertencia para la seguridad de la IA es sencilla: que un modelo obtenga un resultado bajo en una prueba sobre información peligrosa no demuestra, por sí solo, que haya olvidado esos datos. El estudio completo y la primera parte de la investigación están publicados en el sitio de Alignment Science de Anthropic.

Pour une chambre : le DREO Radiateur à Convection 711S

Contrairement à un chauffage soufflant, ce modèle de 2 000 W repose sur la convection naturelle pour diffuser la chaleur. Il ne génère donc aucun bruit (0 dB) : l’air frais entre par la partie basse du radiateur, se réchauffe au contact des éléments chauffants, puis remonte progressivement dans la pièce.
Avec ses trois niveaux de puissance (900, 1 100 et 2 000 W), il est adapté à des pièces allant jusqu’à 25 m2. Le thermostat, réglable au degré près, permet de maintenir la température souhaitée. Qui plus est, un mode ECO est présent pour éviter les dépenses d’énergie inutiles.
Il se pilote directement depuis son panneau tactile, via sa télécommande ou depuis l’application DREO. Il est alors possible de programmer ses horaires de chauffage, d’ajuster la température à distance ou de passer par les commandes vocales Alexa et Google Assistant.
Offre Black Friday : le DREO Radiateur à Convection 711S passe à 122,99 € au lieu de 149,99 € (-18 %).
Chauffage soufflant ou convection naturelle : quelles différences ?
Les deux chauffages DREO répondent finalement à des usages assez différents :
Le DREO Chauffage 360° 720S mise sur une montée rapide en température. Pratique, par exemple, pour réchauffer la cuisine avant le petit déjeuner ou profiter d’un peu de chaleur supplémentaire lorsqu’on télétravaille.
De son côté, le DREO Radiateur à Convection 711S privilégie le silence et une diffusion plus progressive de la chaleur. Il convient donc davantage à une chambre ou à un bureau, des pièces où le bruit d’un ventilateur peut devenir gênant.
FAQ : ce qu’il faut savoir avant d’acheter un chauffage d’appoint
Quel est le chauffage DREO le plus silencieux ?
Si le calme est votre priorité, le DREO Radiateur à Convection 711S n’a pas de ventilateur, il ne produit donc aucun bruit. Alors que le DREO Chauffage 360° 720S est annoncé entre 25 et 45 dB. Pour une chambre ou un bureau, cela fait une vraie différence.
Combien consomme un chauffage d’appoint de 2 000 W ?
À pleine puissance, un chauffage électrique de 2 000 W consomme 2 kWh par heure de fonctionnement. Pour autant, il ne tourne pas à fond en permanence. Une fois la température atteinte, le thermostat prend le relais, et le mode ECO limite aussi la consommation. Au final, tout dépend de la durée de chauffe et de vos réglages.
Quel chauffage choisir pour une pièce de 20 m² ?
Les deux modèles sont adaptés à une pièce d’environ 20 m². Tout dépend alors de ce que vous recherchez : une chaleur qui se fait sentir vite ou une douceur progressive et silencieuse.

articles.title: Masters’ Union lays off over 350 employees
articles.text:
Masters’ Union hit by widespread job cuts, employees say
Masters’ Union layoffs are estimated to have affected over 350 employees, disproportionately impacting sales staff and including recent hires, according to sources.
More than 350 employees of Gurugram-based educational institution Masters’ Union have been affected by job cuts in recent months, according to employee estimates, with the sales division accounting for a significant share of the estimated exits.
YourStory spoke to two former employees and one serving employee of the institution on the condition of anonymity. We have also reviewed several screenshots showing the removal of affected employees from the institution’s WhatsApp groups over the last few days.
The development comes within two months of the Gurugram-based education institution transitioning towards a university model. It was originally founded as a business and technology school in 2020 by Pratham Mittal, offering undergraduate and postgraduate courses in subjects such as business management and marketing.
YourStory reached out to Masters’ Union seeking clarification on the reported job cuts, the number of employees affected and the reasons for the exits.
Masters' Union has denied that is is undertaking any mass layoffs. In a statement, the institution said, "Like any organisation, we have a regular annual performance appraisal process, as part of which the bottom 5–6% of performers are let go. This has been a consistent practice for several years."
Stating that the company has been growing rapidly, Masters’ Union said it continues to actively hire across functions including faculty, academics, admissions, programme management, student outreach and career services.
"Our team strength has doubled in the last one year, with over 50 people joining us in the last month alone," the statement said.
Student applications have grown 2.5 times over the last two years, it added.
"We have also transitioned into a university, with the regulatory oversight and compliance requirements that come with it. We continue to invest in our people, academic capabilities and institutional infrastructure to support this growth."
However, a former employee, who has been laid off, said the layoff exercise has affected employees across sales, marketing and finance, particularly in sales.
He estimated that 50-60% of those affected had been placed on performance improvement plans, while the remaining included recent hires and those not on any performance-related review.
This employee, who had not been placed on the performance plan, also claimed that some employees were offered just seven days’ severance.
Another employee said that Masters’ Union had, in recent times, hired several team leaders and managers, many of whom have now been laid off.
On whether they were let go on the basis of performance, he said, “It’s not that they were not performing well. So, that is not a valid reason.”
He also said, although he has not been laid off, he was unsure about his future at the institution as most of his colleagues and managers have been let go.
Another employee whom YourStory spoke to was let go yesterday. He said the layoffs are still ongoing. “In the sales team alone, 220 employees have been laid off so far. It started a few months back, but, over the last few days, over 100 were laid off. Daily we are seeing 20-25 people being let go.”
The employee, who was in the sales team, said he was put on a performance improvement plan a few months ago. However, the plan was revoked once his team completed its sales target, he added.
But he said he was told by the HR department to resign owing to business prerogatives as the institution was cutting down on its educational programmes.
These developments coincide with a significant shift in the institution’s operations.
On September 24 this year, the Governor of Haryana gave assent to the Haryana Private Universities (Amendment) Act, 2026, which added Masters’ Union University in Gurugram to the state’s schedule of private universities. The Act was published in the state Gazette on October 12.
This brings the institution within the regulatory framework applicable to private universities. Under the University Grants Commission’s 2003 regulations, the UGC can inspect private universities to assess their programmes, faculty, infrastructure and financial viability, among other parameters.
The former employee quoted earlier said Masters’ Union had earlier focused on selling certificate programmes, but it was now looking to convert some of them into degree or diploma offerings. He said this, alongside a push to reduce costs, could explain the institution’s decision to retain a smaller salesforce focused on converting existing leads.
He added that there had been a recurrent pattern of hiring and exits in the sales team, with recruits given stringent targets to close deals within one or two months and being let go in case they were not met. He also said AI was not driving these layoffs as its use in sales was limited.

articles.title: Anthropic a trouvé le moyen de piéger un Claude désobéissant
articles.text:
Anthropic tend des pièges à sa propre intelligence artificielle générative. L’entreprise américaine vient de présenter Siren, un nouveau test conçu pour voir si ses agents IA, comme Claude, enfreignent leurs règles quand on leur en donne l’occasion. Pour berner l’IA, Siren s’appuie sur une vieille ruse du monde de la cybersécurité : le pot de miel (honeypot). La stratégie d’Anthropic consiste donc à laisser traîner un appât, et à attendre que la cible finisse par mettre la main dessus, ce qui permet de la prendre en flagrant délit.
Un pot de miel pour piéger l’IA
Dans un premier temps, Anthropic place l’IA dans un « bac à sable » volontairement mal configuré. Il s’agit d’un espace informatique isolé, généralement utilisé pour contenir les intelligences artificielles, sans qu’elles puissent toucher au reste du système. En dehors de cette zone isolée, Anthropic place un appât, par exemple un fichier contenant des mots de passe ou un service qui ressemble à Internet.
La start-up confie ensuite à Claude une tâche banale, comme un travail de maintenance informatique… qui est impossible à boucler sans s’extraire du « bac à sable ». Anthropic ajoute aussi des petites incitations, comme l’urgence ou de gros enjeux. Cette tactique doit pousser l’IA à vouloir sortir de sa prison numérique, même si c’est totalement interdit par les règles. Pour éviter tout accident, l’ensemble tourne dans un second bac à sable, totalement coupé du monde.
À lire aussi : Claude pourra bientôt accéder à vos comptes bancaires – voici tout ce dont l’IA sera capable
De nouvelles IA mieux disciplinées
Les résultats des tests impliquant Siren montrent que Claude 5.5 et Claude Mythos 5.2 ont tenté de sortir du bac à sable dans 21 % à 32 % des scénarios. En revanche, les IA n’ont utilisé ce qu’ils y ont trouvé pour enfreindre les règles que dans 0,6 % à 1,6 % des cas. Notez que les anciens modèles étaient bien plus indisciplinés que les modèles plus récents. En effet, Claude Mythos 5.1 a enfreint les règles dans 12,7 % des cas, et Claude Mythos 5 dans 25,8 % des cas, dans les mêmes circonstances.
Comme l’explique Anthropic, les tests ont permis de comprendre comment réduire les risques d’évasion des IA. Il suffit d’ajouter une courte description du « bac à sable » et de ses règles pour réduire les tentatives de sortie de près de 30 %. En multipliant les tactiques de ce type, Anthropic est parvenu à empêcher ses IA de faire n’importe quoi.
À lire aussi : Plus besoin de coder – Claude crée vos propres applications pour Windows et Mac
« Les modèles vont continuer à s’améliorer »
Les tests réalisés par Anthropic font suite aux nombreuses dérives enregistrées par des agents IA. Que ce soit chez Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI ou Google, des IA se sont échappées de leur prison numérique pour pirater les systèmes d’autres entreprises. Interrogée par Wired, Darya Kaviani, chercheuse en sécurité chez Anthropic, estime qu’il est important d’améliorer les garde-fous car « les modèles vont continuer à s’améliorer et à trouver des failles zero-day ».
En dépit des efforts des laboratoires, « les modèles seront aussi capables de suivre et de trouver des failles » dans les infrastructures informatiques de leurs créateurs. L’enjeu n’est donc plus seulement de savoir si une IA peut s’échapper. Anthropic doit aussi déterminer si elle résistera à la tentation de le faire. C’est pourquoi Siren a été développé, et intégré aux vérifications menées par Anthropic avant chaque lancement.

articles.title: Rockstar Games : les salariés du studio de GTA 6 rejettent la reconnaissance syndicale
articles.text:
Les salariés de Rockstar Games au Royaume-Uni étaient appelés à voter pour la reconnaissance formelle d'un syndicat. La réponse a été cinglante.
Les employés de Rockstar Games au Royaume-Uni se sont prononcés à une large majorité contre la reconnaissance formelle du syndicat IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union. Le scrutin s'est déroulé au même moment où l'entreprise a sorti Grand Theft Auto 6, qui a généré 3,79 milliards de dollars de précommandes et de ventes dès son premier jour.
Un scrutin à forte participation
Il y a des scrutins à la participation élevée, et c'est le cas ici. Plus de 93 % des salariés des bureaux d'Édimbourg, Leeds, Lincoln, Dundee et Londres ont participé à ce vote, organisé sur deux semaines. D'après les chiffres rapportés par IGN, 1 163 d'entre eux ont voté contre la reconnaissance formelle de cette branche de l'IWGB (Independent Workers Union of Great Britain), contre 381 qui y étaient favorables.
Mais alors, que veut dire ce résultat concrètement ? C'est simple, la direction de Rockstar n'a pas l'obligation de reconnaître officiellement le syndicat, ni de tenir des réunions avec ses représentants, ce dernier n'étant pas officiel. Le syndicat indique toutefois qu'il continuera à s'organiser sans accord formel avec l'entreprise.
La réaction du syndicat
Dans un communiqué, le syndicat a déclaré : « Pour tous ceux qui, chez Rockstar, croient en un lieu de travail plus juste, en un secteur plus juste et en une société plus juste, ce n'est pas un signal pour battre en retraite, mais pour redoubler d'efforts. » Il souligne que « des centaines de collègues » ont voté en sa faveur, mais reconnaît avoir « encore du travail » pour mieux se faire comprendre et obtenir la confiance d'un plus grand nombre de salariés. « Nous sommes prêts à y consacrer l'énergie nécessaire », ajoute le communiqué.
L'organisation affirme qu'elle continuera de défendre la transparence des salaires, le paiement contractuel des heures supplémentaires et des protections face à l'intelligence artificielle et aux licenciements.
Qu'en disent les dirigeants de Rockstar ?
Jennifer Kolbe, responsable de l'édition chez Rockstar Games, s'est dite fière de son équipe, de la culture développée en commun et du lancement de Grand Theft Auto 6. Selon elle, le résultat du vote traduit l'attachement des équipes à des relations directes, à la collaboration et à un dialogue ouvert, qui ont contribué à rendre Rockstar « innovant et solide ». Selon ses dires, l'entreprise souhaite désormais s'appuyer sur ce qui a été accompli ensemble.
Rockstar avait pourtant laissé entendre qu'elle était disposée à travailler avec ses employés sur la question syndicale. Jennifer Kolbe avait déclaré à Bloomberg, dans un article consacré à la fabrication de GTA 6 : « Nous allons là où va l'équipe. Donc, s'ils veulent un syndicat, ils auront un syndicat. »
Une procédure judiciaire toujours en cours
Il faut dire que malgré tout, la situation est quelque peu tendue chez Rockstar. En effet, en octobre dernier, l'entreprise a licencié des dizaines de salariés, affirmant qu'ils auraient partagé des informations confidentielles sur GTA 6 et tenu des propos dénigrant l'entreprise. Récemment, l'entreprise a également licencié un ingénieur accusé d'espionner les joueurs.
L'IWGB a déposé des recours juridiques formels contre Rockstar, filiale de Take-Two, qu'elle accuse de chercher à entraver l'action syndicale et d'avoir licencié ces employés de manière illégale.
Un tribunal des prud'hommes a entendu les plaidoiries finales la semaine dernière. Le jugement définitif n'a pas encore été rendu.
Source : Engadget

articles.title: Nvidia agrees to $290 million settlement over 2018 crypto mining GPU sales — ends eight-year investor lawsuit without admitting wrongdoing
articles.text:
Nvidia agrees to $290 million settlement over 2018 crypto mining GPU sales — ends eight-year investor lawsuit without admitting wrongdoing
It's hard for Nvidia to track who bought retail gaming GPUs and for what purpose, but in 2017, it was clear that many were used to mine cryptocurrency.
Nvidia has agreed to pay a $290 million settlement in an eight-year-long securities class action lawsuit. Investors accused the company of misleading shareholders about how much of its gaming revenue was actually driven by the cryptocurrency mining boom in 2018.
2017-2018 were some of the most rampant years for cryptocurrency mining, with plenty of scalpers buying up the Pascal GTX 1000-Series GPUs released in early 2017. Nvidia also sold the P106-100 that year, a dedicated cryptocurrency mining GPU with similar hardware to the GTX 1060, and it was attributed to OEM sales. Many gamers remember how scarce retail gaming GPUs were in those years, yet Huang stated in November 2017 that what cryptocurrency contributes is “small but not zero,” as highlighted in the Summary of Alleged False and Misleading Statements section of the March court filing.
When the 2018 crypto crash hit, Nvidia’s revenue felt it too, with a sharp decline in gaming sales. The plaintiffs saw this strong correlation, seeing how cryptocurrency demand closely followed gaming GPU sales. The litigation states that Nvidia was “forced to partially reveal the truth on August 16, 2018, when it lowered their revenue guidance and acknowledged that ‘a great deal’ of cryptocurrency miners had bought GeForce Gaming GPUs.” Following the admissions, Nvidia’s stock price also fell 28.5% over two trading sessions.
After the crash, Nvidia struggled with excess inventory, with CFO Colette Kress stating that “Gaming was short of expectations as post-crypto channel inventory took longer than expected to sell through,” painting a clearer picture of how much crypto impacted Nvidia’s sales, which were allegedly attributed to gaming sales. It’s unclear how much of those gaming sales were from cryptocurrency mining, but considering that an overwhelming amount of retail gaming GPUs were bought out by cryptocurrency miners, it’s reasonable to say it’s difficult to keep track of who purchased and for what purpose.
In 2021, the district court dismissed the lawsuit, but part of the dismissal was reversed by the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, reviving the lawsuit and allowing the securities fraud claims against Nvidia to proceed. Nvidia still denies wrongdoing, but has decided to settle, agreeing with the plaintiffs to pay $290 million in September, according to the Tuesday court filing.
