articles.title: Spelunkr.tv: TV-Sender aus Videos des Internet Archive
articles.text:
Diese Webseite verwandelt das Internet Archive in einen TV-Sender
Eine Billion Webseiten, 56 Millionen Texte und 15 Millionen Videos: Die Nonprofit-Organisation Internet Archive sammelt seit 1996 kulturelle Artefakte in digitaler Form. Doch wer soll das alles sehen? Und wie kann man verborgene Schätze dieses Archivs entdecken?
Spelunkr.tv: „Wie Kabelfernsehen, nur seltsamer“
Eine Person hat eine Website gestartet, die Videos aus dem Internet Archive in Form eines TV-Networks zugänglich macht. Spelunkr.tv heißt die Seite. „Wie Kabelfernsehen, nur seltsamer“, beschreibt der anonyme Macher sein Projekt.
„Monsterfilme. Lehrfilme. Krimis. Zeichentrickfilme, die älter sind als deine Großeltern“, verspricht Spelunkr auf der About-Seite. Auch der Inhalt einer VHS-Kassette, die „irgendjemand an einem Samstagmorgen im Jahr 1989 vom TV-Programm aufgezeichnet hat“, kann dabei sein. Inklusive der damaligen Werbung.
Nostalgie fürs klassische Fernsehen ohne tausend Optionen
Eigentlich unterscheidet sich Spelunkr.tv also gar nicht groß vom klassischen Fernsehen. Dies räumt der Macher der Seite auch ein. „Wir haben es nicht erfunden“, heißt es über das gute alte TV. Und: „Wir vermissen es“.
Spelunkr.tv bedient also die Nostalgie nach einer Zeit, die für viele einfacher war. Zumindest was die Mediennutzung betrifft. Eine Sehnsucht nach einer Zeit, in der man sich einfach vor den Fernseher gesetzt und durch die Kanäle gezappt hat. Ohne den Druck, wie bei Youtube oder Netflix aus einem gigantischen Angebot wählen zu müssen.
TV-Guide für 38 Kanäle
Eine Wahl hat man bei Spelunkr.tv aber doch. Die User:innen können aus 38 Kanälen ihren Favoriten aussuchen. In einem rudimentären TV-Guide wird angezeigt, was in den nächsten Stunden auf den jeweiligen Sendern läuft. Ganz orientierungslos ist man auf der Seite also nicht.
Jeder Sender hat ein liebevoll im pixeligen Retro-Stil der 90er-Jahre gestaltetes Icon. Dazu gibt es für jeden Kanal eine kurze Beschreibung, was die Zuschauer:innen hier erwartet.
MTV, Bob Ross und Instruktionen für die Apokalypse
Unter den 38 Sendern ist etwa „Saturday Morning“. Er soll mit Sendungen aus dem Disney Channel das Gefühl erwecken, an einem Samstagmorgen mit einer Schüssel Froot Loops in der Hand Cartoons zu schauen.
Bei „Radio-Active TV“ kann man sich stattdessen ins MTV-Programm von 1990 zoomen. „Happy Trees“ zeigt rund um die Uhr alle Folgen von „The Joy of Painting“ mit dem wuschelhaarigen Kult-Maler Bob Ross.
Neben Kanälen für klassische Genres wie Krimi, Horror und Western gibt es auch Kuriositäten. „Fallout Shelter“ sendet Filme, in denen die Regierung erklärt, wie man sich im Falle einer nuklearen Katastrophe verhalten soll.

articles.title: Tamer Bahgat is betting on social commerce in Nigeria
articles.text:
For nearly two decades, Tamer Bahgat built a career in international finance, moving between New York, London, Dubai, and Singapore. He worked as a finance and private equity lawyer, became a partner at London Magic Circle firms, and previously worked as a banker at Goldman Sachs. Three years ago, he left that career behind to build a technology company in Nigeria.
The idea for the venture had taken shape about 14 years earlier during his exposure to Asia’s technology industry. Bahgat told TechCabal in November that he became interested in how tech companies in the region were building digital ecosystems that brought different services together. He said he believed the model could be adapted for African markets, where growing digital adoption presented an opportunity to rethink how people accessed everyday services.
“When I experienced what they were doing in technology, how they were building it, what their future looked like, and compared it to what we were seeing in the Western world, I came to the conclusion that, given the infrastructure we have across the continent, given its size, its regulators, its culture, its people, a tried and tested model in that shape should be really where the inspiration comes from, and not so much the Western cultures,” he told TechCabal.
That thinking led to the founding of we.yan, a digital ecosystem that brings communication, commerce, and financial services onto a single platform. Launched in June, the startup combines a messaging service, a bank-linked wallet, and a social marketplace that allows users to chat, send money, shop, and manage their finances.
Bahgat told TechCabal that Nigeria was a deliberate starting point for we.yan. Besides being born in northern Nigeria and growing up in Jos, Bahgat believed the country’s young population and familiarity with technology platforms made it a suitable market for the idea.
DataReportal’s Digital 2026 report estimated that Nigeria had 109 million internet users in October 2025, representing 45.5% of its population. The country also had 47.8 million social media user identities, up by 12 million from 2024.
“We also felt that given the social fintech that our ecosystem sits on, there’s no better place than Nigeria that you can be able to combine social, artistic, and financial experiences in one platform, and that’s why Nigeria,” he said.
A chat app with a marketplace and a wallet
we.yan’s product is built around three core pillars that reinforce its premise that users should not have to jump between multiple apps for routine digital tasks. A shopper who spots a vendor on Instagram might move to WhatsApp to negotiate a purchase, transfer money through a banking app, and arrange delivery through a separate logistics provider. Bahgat views this fragmentation as a friction point a unified platform can solve.
“It’s what we would call digital fragmentation,” he said. “Just to make a simple transaction that should take minutes and be seamless and secure, you’ve now utilised five or six different platforms with a whole suite of different experiences.”
we.yan’s product begins with communication. Bahgat said the company built its own messaging stack, allowing users to exchange text messages, voice notes, photos, videos, and locally created stickers. One of its patented features lets users attach money to media and send it directly inside conversations. Users can also request payments or set up group wallets.
“Everything starts with a chat. Transactions start with a chat. Your personal, professional life and engagements start with a chat. And so the chat is at its core,” Bahgat said.
we.yan’s financial services layer includes personal and business wallets, bank transfers, airtime and utility payments, and investment access. we.yan partnered with Kuda, a Nigerian digital bank, for its underlying banking rails. According to Bahgat, the standard wallet carries a daily spending limit of ₦1 million, while users can upgrade to a tier-three wallet with a ₦5 million daily limit after completing further know-your-customer (KYC) verification. The platform also supports transfers to people who are not yet registered on we.yan, holding funds in escrow until the recipient completes KYC and claims them.
Its commerce offering enables merchants to set up digital storefronts, upload catalogues, manage inventory, and receive orders. Buyers chatting on the app can discover products directly inside the ecosystem. Bahgat likened the storefront experience to Shopify, the e-commerce platform that allows businesses to build and run online stores. we.yan says it has also integrated logistics partners, including Courier Plus, to handle fulfilment.
Escrow sits at the centre of how we.yan aims to build trust between buyers and sellers. Bahgat said the company developed an escrow mechanism to protect both sides, releasing payment to the merchant only after the logistics provider confirms delivery. Buyers can also request returns in-app, subject to the merchant’s stated return policy and product type.
Under the hood
Bahgat said we.yan has three main revenue streams, starting with merchant transaction fees and tiered subscriptions. According to Bahgat, higher subscription tiers are slated to offer multi-currency wallets alongside artificial intelligence (AI) tools for inventory management and customer engagement.
we.yan said its second revenue stream will come from cross-border payments and remittances. The company plans to leverage its network and partnerships to move money across markets and charge fees for those transfers. It also intends to partner with commercial banks that can draw on data generated inside the ecosystem to underwrite credit for consumers and businesses.
“One of the things that’s quite unique to we.yan is: because it’s a closed ecosystem, we can see things that typically a bank or a lot of other tech companies cannot,” Bahgat said. “And because the money and the products both originate within our ecosystem—because we have an escrow infrastructure, because we have security rails, and because we have a way that we actually address risk over and above what’s publicly available through different credit scoring models.”
The credit partnerships are not expected to launch until 2027, though Bahgat sees them becoming a major pillar of the business.
we.yan was among the fintechs selected to participate in the Dangote Refinery Initial Public Offering (IPO) that closed in October. Bahgat said the company partnered with Kuda for the digital banking component and Chapel Hill Denham for brokerage access to allow retail investors to register and access the share offer.
Since launching in June, we.yan reported between 100,000 and 120,000 users, roughly 1,200 to 1,300 registered merchants, and more than ₦550 million in processed transactions. we.yan’s ambitions reach beyond Nigeria: positioning itself as pan-African infrastructure, the company aims to connect merchants with buyers across African markets and the diaspora.

articles.title: Teclado gamer Logitech: qual modelo comprar em 2026?

Em dúvida sobre qual teclado Logitech comprar para jogos? Veja a seleção com modelos em diversas faixas de preço para gamers casuais ou profissionais
Escolher um teclado gamer Logitech em 2026 exige observar o tipo de switch, o formato compacto ou completo e o tipo de conexão sem fio ou com fio. A linha Logitech G reúne modelos voltados ao competitivo, setups minimalistas e uso misto no dia a dia.
Neste guia, você encontra análises objetivas dos principais teclados mecânicos e de membrana da marca disponíveis no mercado. Comparamos recursos de resposta rápida, ergonomia e custo-benefício para ajudar na sua decisão.
Conteúdo gerado por IA ✨
Este conteúdo foi gerado com auxílio de inteligência artificial e revisado por especialistas do Tecnoblog.
O Logitech G915 X TKL Lightspeed entrega respostas imediatas em partidas rápidas com construção ultrafina sem teclado numérico. O formato compacto libera espaço amplo para movimentar o mouse em jogos de tiro, enquanto a altura reduzida favorece o posicionamento natural dos pulsos.
Na prática, o modelo traz switches mecânicos GL de baixo perfil com ponto de atuação de 1,3 mm, pensados para elevar o ritmo de ações por minuto. Ele soma conectividade tripla (Lightspeed sem fio, Bluetooth e USB-C com fio), teclas double-shot em PBT, placa superior em alumínio escovado e mapeamento avançado com o recurso KEYCONTROL.
Para quem busca o topo de linha sem fio da marca com perfil baixo e acabamento reforçado, é uma opção direta e versátil. O uso simultâneo durante o carregamento via cabo evita interrupções em sessões longas.
O Logitech G915 TKL Lightspeed oferece mobilidade e resposta sem atrasos perceptíveis em uma estrutura metálica compacta. A ausência do bloco numérico facilita setups com menos área livre e torna o transporte mais prático para eventos ou mudanças de bancada.
A ficha técnica destaca a transmissão sem fio Lightspeed de 1 ms, corpo com estrutura em liga de alumínio e base reforçada, roda de volume dedicada e teclas de mídia de toque suave. Também permite operar conectado via USB para carregar a bateria enquanto você continua jogando.
Ainda que tenha sido sucedido pela geração G915 X em recursos mais recentes, o G915 TKL permanece relevante quando surge com preço competitivo. É indicado para quem quer um teclado sem fio de perfil baixo e visual sóbrio sem abrir mão de controles de mídia físicos.
O Logitech G515 TKL Lightspeed combina digitação silenciosa e conforto em um corpo fino voltado a jogos e trabalho. Seu design tenkeyless de 22 mm de altura reduz o cansaço e abre espaço na mesa para gestos largos de mira.
Por dentro, o modelo reúne switches mecânicos GL de perfil baixo pré-lubrificados de fábrica (com opções tátil ou linear e atuação a 1,3 mm), teclas PBT de dupla moldagem e camadas internas com redução de ruído. A conectividade tripla traz Lightspeed de 1 ms, Bluetooth, uso com fio USB e pareamento 2:1 para compartilhar receptor com mouse compatível, além de bateria de até 36 horas e suporte ao KEYCONTROL.
Ele funciona como um meio-termo inteligente dentro da linha sem fio de baixo perfil da Logitech G. Entrega boa parte da experiência moderna de customização e acústica mais contida com proposta mais acessível que o G915 X TKL.
O Logitech G Pro prioriza portabilidade e precisão direta para quem joga títulos competitivos com foco em desempenho. O formato compacto sem teclado numérico e o cabo removível facilitam levar o periférico em mochilas para campeonatos ou encontros presenciais.
O teclado utiliza switches mecânicos GX Clicky com feedback tátil e sonoro marcante, além de 12 teclas F programáveis via G HUB e memória integrada para perfis de iluminação. O cabo destacável conta com encaixe de três pinos para manter a conexão firme durante partidas intensas.
Trata-se de um modelo com fio focado no essencial competitivo, sem distrações extras na carcaça. Vale a atenção apenas ao conector micro USB removível e à preferência por switches com clique audível antes da compra.
O Logitech G713 aposta em conforto prolongado e estética clara para setups que valorizam visual e ergonomia. O apoio para pulsos macio incluso e o formato TKL ajudam a manter as mãos relaxadas em maratonas de jogo ou digitação.
Na parte técnica, o modelo traz conexão USB-C com fio destacável, controles de mídia dedicados, iluminação RGB Lightsync por tecla e no perímetro, além de opções de switches mecânicos GX (tátil, linear ou clicky). Integrante da linha Aurora, ele também aceita keycaps e placas superiores intercambiáveis vendidas separadamente para mudar o visual.
É uma escolha indicada para quem prefere conexão com fio estável, apoio acolchoado de série e forte apelo estético. Atende bem tanto a quem joga quanto a quem passa horas digitando textos.
O Logitech G413 SE entrega durabilidade e simplicidade para quem quer um teclado mecânico direto ao ponto. O layout completo com bloco numérico atende bem quem alterna entre jogos e planilhas ou digitação frequente sem depender de atalhos.
Ele conta com switches mecânicos táteis, keycaps em PBT resistentes ao desgaste e ao brilho, iluminação em LED branco e anti-ghosting com sobreposição de 6 teclas. A proposta dispensa RGB colorido e recursos extras para focar na resistência estrutural e no funcionamento plug-and-play.
É indicado para quem busca um mecânico sóbrio e resistente sem gastar tanto quanto nos modelos sem fio. Quem precisa de mais espaço livre para o mouse em FPS pode avaliar também a variante TKL SE.
O Logitech G213 foca em conforto diário, baixo nível de ruído e resistência a imprevistos na mesa para uso casual ou misto. O descanso para as mãos integrado e o teclado numérico completo tornam o periférico prático para rotinas de estudo, trabalho e lazer.
Em vez de switches mecânicos tradicionais, adota teclas Tactile Mech-Dome de membrana com acionamento mais suave e silencioso, teclas de mídia dedicadas, iluminação RGB Lightsync em zonas e resistência a derramamentos de líquidos testada para até 60 ml. A presença do layout ABNT2 em versões nacionais facilita a digitação em português com acentuação nativa.
É uma alternativa coerente para quem não faz questão de switch mecânico e prefere silêncio, apoio integrado e preço mais contido. Funciona bem como primeiro teclado gamer ou para quem divide o PC com outras tarefas.
Comece definindo o espaço disponível na mesa e os gêneros de jogo que você mais joga. Modelos TKL liberam área para o mouse, enquanto teclados full-size mantêm o bloco numérico útil para produtividade e planilhas.
Em seguida, avalie a conexão (sem fio Lightspeed ou cabo USB), a altura das teclas (perfil baixo ou tradicional) e o tipo de resposta do switch (linear, tátil ou clicky). Também vale conferir o layout das teclas (ABNT2 ou padrão internacional) e a presença de controles de mídia dedicados.
Lightspeed é a tecnologia de conexão sem fio de 2,4 GHz da Logitech G desenvolvida para entregar baixa latência e estabilidade de sinal em jogos. Na prática, ela busca aproximar a resposta sem fio da experiência de um cabo USB, evitando atrasos perceptíveis em comandos rápidos.
O melhor teclado custo-benefício depende do seu orçamento e do tipo de uso: o G515 TKL Lightspeed se destaca entre os sem fio modernos de baixo perfil, enquanto o G413 SE atende quem busca um mecânico durável mais acessível e o G213 serve a quem quer gastar menos com foco em silêncio e conforto. Avalie o preço promocional no momento da compra e se você precisa de conexão sem fio ou se o cabo resolve bem o seu setup.
O Logitech G Hub centraliza a configuração de efeitos de iluminação RGB Lightsync, perfis por jogo, macros e atalhos das teclas. Em modelos compatíveis com o recurso KEYCONTROL, o software também permite criar camadas e atribuir múltiplas funções por tecla.
Teclados mecânicos costumam oferecer resposta mais consistente, durabilidade elevada dos switches e variedade de sensações (linear, tátil ou clicky) para jogos mais exigentes. Teclados de membrana, como o G213 com teclas Mech-Dome, entregam toque mais silencioso e preço menor, sendo suficientes para jogos casuais e uso misto.
A sigla TKL significa Tenkeyless, ou seja, um teclado sem o bloco numérico à direita. Remover essas teclas reduz a largura total do periférico, dando mais espaço para o movimento do mouse e deixando a mesa mais organizada.
Os teclados da linha Logitech G são compatíveis com Windows e macOS, variando conforme o modelo e o software de configuração. Em consoles como PS5 e Xbox, a conexão USB ou sem fio básica pode funcionar em jogos que aceitam teclado nativamente, mas recursos avançados como macros e perfis completos do G Hub dependem do computador e do suporte de cada jogo.

articles.title: Volvo’s big batteries: We drive its updated 2028 plug-in hybrids
articles.text:
COPENHAGEN, Denmark—If we lived in the world that Volvo’s product planners expected back when the current XC90 debuted in 2015, both it and the smaller but related XC60 (which arrived in 2017) might have been the last of their kind as everything went electric. As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in the critically important US market. At the same time, Europe and China are electrifying, which seems like an argument against spending resources on developing all-new replacements for models that might not have an eight-year lifespan in most markets.
So instead, Volvo has given the XC60 and XC90 another lifecycle refresh. The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. And that’s no bad thing—both were, and remain, handsome shapes that are popular with Volvo’s customer base.
Instead, the Swedish automaker’s attention has been on bringing the technology up to date for model year 2028 standards. Which means a much bigger battery for the PHEVs, with sufficient capacity for a couple of days of daily driving for most of us before needing to be recharged. There’s also new, modern infotainment and interiors that are now even nicer to spend time in than before.
The weather was nowhere near this pleasant on the day we drove across this bridge. This is the XC60.
Volvo Cars
The weather was nowhere near this pleasant on the day we drove across this bridge. This is the XC60.
Volvo Cars
It wasn’t even this nice, just lashing rain. This is the XC90.
Volvo Cars
It wasn’t even this nice, just lashing rain. This is the XC90.
Volvo Cars
The weather was nowhere near this pleasant on the day we drove across this bridge. This is the XC60.
Volvo Cars
It wasn’t even this nice, just lashing rain. This is the XC90.
Volvo Cars
We first saw the revamped 2028 XC60 (and learned about its technical details and those of the XC90) in September, but with the cars going into production now and due to reach the first US customers in the first quarter of next year, we got the opportunity to spend some seat time with the updated cars.
Charge!
Both the midsize XC60 and three-row XC90 use the same PHEV powertrain. Under the hood, there’s a 2.0 L four-cylinder direct-injection gasoline engine that generates 247 hp (184 kW) and 226 lb-ft (306 Nm) together with a 70 hp (50 kW), 122 ft-lb (165 Nm) electric motor, both of which drive the front wheels. At the rear axle there’s a second electric motor, with an output of 174 hp (130 kW) and 228 lb-ft (309 Nm). Combined output for the hybrid system is 455 hp (339 kW) and 560 lb-ft (759 Nm).
There’s also a much bigger battery, with a net capacity of 37.9 kWh (41.2 kWh gross). If you set the car’s mode to Pure, which relies solely on the rear electric motor for propulsion, that translates to an EPA range estimate of 78 miles (126 km) for the XC60 and 73 miles (116 km) for the larger, draggier XC90. Which is significant—when the average driver drives fewer than 30 miles a day, it means these PHEVs carry enough electrons for a couple of days of tailpipe-emissions-free driving before it needs to be plugged in again or the engine to fire up.
There are new matrix LED headlights but still with the Thor’s Hammer DRL.
Credit:
Volvo Cars
There are new matrix LED headlights but still with the Thor’s Hammer DRL.
Credit:
Volvo Cars
When it is time to plug it back in, expect it to take about four hours with a level 2 charger of at least 16 A, or 27 hours if you’re limited to 120 V. In Hybrid mode, where you get the benefit of both electric motors and the gas engine, Volvo expects a combined efficiency of 67 mpge in the XC60, and 61 mpge for the XC90.
Even if the gas engine is running and you’re in Hybrid or Power mode (which keeps the engine on all the time), you can drive these Volvos as if they were EVs with one-pedal driving: just move the transmission from D to B. The Volvos are always using their electric motors to slow the car before the friction brakes intervene, and in B you get the same amount of lift-off regen regardless of mode. For city traffic, it’s very effective. (In Pure, although only the rear motor deploys energy, both front and rear motors regen brake.)
In power mode, with all 455 hp unleashed, you can chirp the wheels on a wet day, but these model year 2028 cars are about one large male human heavier than the outgoing model year, both of which were already pretty heavy. So don’t expect performance-car performance. The XC60 is the sweeter to drive on a winding road, but both are entirely at home cruising on a highway or creeping along in a city, which is where cars like these spend the vast majority of their time. There’s more road intrusion into the cabin of the XC60—the larger Volvo rides on air suspension that does a much better job of filtering that out.
The XC90 is a more cosseting experience.
Credit:
Volvo
The XC90 is a more cosseting experience.
Credit:
Volvo
A first-drive event like this isn’t the best place to get a good read on real-world efficiency. We usually have to share cars with other journalists, and there’s limited time to drive on roads that may not be representative—too sinuous, or not enough traffic, for example. We need to try all the different drive modes and see how cars respond to different inputs. And it’s rare you’ll spend the entire day with one car, finishing at the same point you started.
That said, I can’t give you a definite read on range and efficiency for these two plug-ins. But my unscientific estimate is that my drive partner and I, in an XC60, drove about 60 km in a mix of city driving and higher speeds on the way to Malmo in Sweden, which is on the other side of a gigantic bridge, and we used about half the battery pack to do so. (Volvo asked us to put the PHEVs in Hold or Charge mode at 50 percent to leave some state of charge for whoever drove the cars after lunch.)
Thus, there was little charge left in the XC90 when it was my turn to drive the final stint back into Copenhagen. Since I wasn’t worried about combined efficiency, I ran the car in Charge mode for about 20 min, regenerating the battery from an indicated 10 km to an indicated 21 km, then switched to Pure once we reached the city, with about 16 km to go.
The rear lights are new.
Credit:
Volvo Cars
The rear lights are new.
Credit:
Volvo Cars
Massage time
Volvo already had a reputation for great automotive interiors, and with this refresh, it has pushed things forward a little. There’s a new wood finish, new textiles, and new backlighting. The resemblance between the two interiors from the front seat is now quite strong, particularly since the test cars Volvo brought to Denmark wore identical color schemes inside.
Our final 1.6 km to the hotel took more than 30 minutes to negotiate thanks to a reception for very important people that apparently took place next to the hotel. Most of this jam was on one street, with our destination in sight, but the frustration was in part ameliorated by Volvo’s secret weapon: its seat massage function.
Lots of other OEMs offer massaging front seats, which inflate and deflate the internal air bladder to massage your shoulders, back, and sometimes butt. But none massage you with quite the firmness of a Volvo seat. And they have the power to distract you from terrible in-car situations, as I discovered when stuck in a V90 Cross Country with Nigel the Cat, whose way of remonstrating with me about his trip to the feline ophthalmologist was to scream at high volume until he ran out of breath, at which point he’d pant for a few minutes, then start again. The seat in that car is the only reason we both made it home safely. And so, in Copenhagen, I set the seat to pulse and did some box breathing.
The upgraded XC60 interior.
Volvo Cars
The upgraded XC60 interior.
Volvo Cars
Here’s the XC90.
Volvo Cars
Here’s the XC90.
Volvo Cars
New wood and textile for the dash.
Volvo Cars
New wood and textile for the dash.
Volvo Cars
Here’s the XC90.
Volvo Cars
New wood and textile for the dash.
Volvo Cars
As well as new interior materials, you’ll also notice a new infotainment screen in both cars. Gone are the old 9-inch displays, replaced by a new 11.2-inch touchscreen that stands a little proud of the dash rather than recessed into it. Just this one upgrade alone really lifts both interiors; the old, small screen was showing its age. Most Ars readers will recoil at the news that Gemini has replaced the previous Google Assistant, but at least the voice-recognition capabilities are improved. Gemini will still struggle with some commands—I asked it to tell me my current efficiency, which it failed at, but it’s rather good at looking stuff up on the Internet while I drive.
There are also some updated advanced driver-assistance systems, like a warning if cyclists approach your opening door, and an updated 360-degree parking view. But there’s no point-to-point assist like Mercedes is introducing, or a hands-free “level 2+” system like Super Cruise; Volvo’s experience with the EX90 may have left it a little gun-shy.
With a battery big enough for daily driving and a more modern interior experience, there’s a lot to like about both the 2029 XC60 and XC90. However, we still don’t know how much they’ll cost when they go on sale in Q1 next year. With twice the battery capacity, it’s reasonable to expect a slight price rise, but without knowing how much, it’s hard to say whether it’s a good deal or not.
Jonathan is the Automotive Editor at Ars Technica. He has a BSc and PhD in Pharmacology. In 2014 he decided to indulge his lifelong passion for the car by leaving the National Human Genome Research Institute and launching Ars Technica's automotive coverage. He lives in Washington, DC.

articles.title: Why Everybody Loves a Good Drought is a must-read book
articles.text:
Why Everybody Loves a Good Drought is a must-read book
Discover why Palagummi Sainath's Everybody Loves a Good Drought remains essential reading on rural poverty, inequality and India's development challenges.
What does poverty look like beyond the statistics, government reports and economic discussions?
What happens when development projects promise progress but leave the poorest communities struggling to access basic necessities? These are some of the difficult questions explored in Everybody Loves a Good Drought: Stories from India's Poorest Districts by Palagummi Sainath.
First published in 1996, this landmark work of investigative journalism examines rural poverty, inequality and the realities of development in India.
Through deeply researched reportage and stories from some of the country's poorest districts, Sainath brings attention to communities that often remain overlooked in mainstream discussions.
Rather than presenting poverty through numbers alone, the book focuses on the people living through it. It explores their everyday struggles with healthcare, education, displacement, debt and government policies.
5 Reasons why Everybody Loves a Good Drought deserves a place on your reading list
1. It shows the human face of poverty
Poverty is often discussed through statistics, income levels and economic indicators. However, these numbers rarely capture the everyday experiences of people struggling to access food, healthcare, education and other necessities.
In Everybody Loves a Good Drought, Sainath moves beyond these figures to document the lives of India's rural communities. Through his reporting, readers encounter people whose circumstances reveal the difficulties of living in regions affected by economic hardship and inadequate public services.
The book explores how poverty influences nearly every aspect of life, from children's education to access to medical treatment and opportunities for employment.
By focusing on individual experiences, Sainath makes an important point: poverty is not simply an economic condition but a reality that shapes people's choices, opportunities and futures.
2. It questions what development really means
Development is generally associated with better infrastructure, economic growth, government schemes and improved living standards. But what happens when the benefits of development fail to reach the people who need them most?
This is one of the central questions explored throughout the book.
Sainath investigates how development initiatives and government programmes sometimes fail to address the actual needs of rural communities. He highlights the gap between official promises and the experiences of people living in the affected regions.
The book also examines displacement caused by development projects, showing how communities can lose their homes, livelihoods and connections to their surroundings in the name of progress.
It encourages readers to question whether development can truly be considered successful when its benefits are unevenly distributed.
3. It exposes the gaps in India's rural healthcare and education
Access to healthcare and education plays a significant role in determining the opportunities available to individuals and communities. Yet, for many rural families, these basic services can remain difficult to access.
Sainath dedicates considerable attention to the challenges surrounding rural healthcare and education.
The book documents issues such as inadequate medical facilities, preventable illnesses, shortages of resources and the difficulties faced by children trying to access meaningful education.
It also explores the distance between government policies and the conditions experienced by ordinary people.
These accounts highlight how a lack of essential services can reinforce cycles of poverty, making it harder for future generations to improve their circumstances.
4. It reveals how poverty and inequality are connected to power
One of the book's most important themes is the relationship between poverty, political power and economic inequality.
Sainath examines how local power structures, corruption, debt and exploitation affect vulnerable communities. He explores the circumstances of people who depend on landlords, moneylenders, contractors and government institutions for their livelihoods.
The book also questions why development resources and public assistance do not always reach their intended beneficiaries.
By examining these interconnected problems, Sainath shows that poverty cannot be understood simply as a lack of money. It is also connected to unequal access to resources, opportunities and decision-making power.
This perspective makes the book particularly relevant to readers interested in understanding the deeper causes of social and economic inequality.
5. It demonstrates why ground-level journalism matters
Perhaps the most important reason to read Everybody Loves a Good Drought is its approach to journalism.
Instead of relying entirely on official statements and government reports, Sainath travels to rural communities, meets people and documents their experiences firsthand.
His reporting brings attention to individuals and communities that are often missing from mainstream news coverage. Their stories reveal the realities behind policies, development programmes and economic decisions.
The book also raises questions about the responsibility of the media to report on issues affecting marginalised communities.
For aspiring journalists, writers and readers interested in public affairs, it offers an important example of how patient, field-based reporting can uncover stories that deserve wider attention.
About the Author: Palagummi Sainath
Palagummi Sainath is an Indian journalist, author and rural affairs expert known for his extensive reporting on poverty, inequality and rural communities.
He previously served as the Rural Affairs Editor of The Hindu, where he spent years reporting on the challenges faced by people across rural India.
In 2007, he received the Ramon Magsaysay Award for Journalism, Literature and Creative Communication Arts in recognition of his contribution to journalism.
In 2014, Sainath founded the People's Archive of Rural India (PARI), an independent multimedia platform documenting the lives, livelihoods and challenges of rural communities across the country.
His work has consistently focused on bringing the experiences of underrepresented communities into public conversations.
Final thoughts
Everybody Loves a Good Drought is more than a book about rural poverty. It is an examination of the systems, policies and inequalities that shape the lives of millions of people.
Through detailed reporting and human stories, Palagummi Sainath challenges readers to look beyond economic statistics and question what development means for those who remain at the margins.
Although the book was first published in 1996, its central concerns about poverty, governance, healthcare, education and inequality continue to make it an important work of Indian journalism.
For anyone interested in understanding rural India, social justice, public policy or investigative journalism, this book is an essential addition to their reading list.

articles.title: Rachat de SFR : des centaines de magasins franchisés portent plainte contre l’opérateur
articles.text:
SFR compte environ 543 points de vente en France. Parmi eux, 293 sont des boutiques appartenant à l’opérateur et 250 sont des magasins franchisés. Depuis l’annonce du rachat de SFR par le consortium composé d’Orange, Bouygues Telecom et Free, nous savons que seules 120 des 293 boutiques appartenant à SFR pourraient être reprises, menaçant ainsi près de 1 000 emplois. Mais que va-t-il se passer pour les 250 magasins franchisés, et leurs 1 500 salariés ? Justement, comme le rapporte Le Figaro, l’ADIES, l’Association des distributeurs indépendants de l’enseigne SFR, a annoncé avoir assigné l’opérateur au carré rouge en justice pour faire entendre sa voix.
L’association représentant les franchisés de SFR attaque l’opérateur en justice
L’ADIES, l’association qui représente les magasins franchisés de SFR, a annoncé avoir assigné SFR devant le Tribunal des activités économiques de Paris. La raison ? L’association estime que l’annonce du rachat de SFR a causé beaucoup de tort aux magasins franchisés de l’enseigne. En effet, les clients se seraient détournés de cet opérateur dont la fin est d’ores et déjà annoncée. Des boutiques franchisées se seraient ainsi retrouvées en grandes difficultés financières, entraînant dans certains cas des fermetures et des liquidations judiciaires.
Par ailleurs, le consortium composé d’Orange, Bouygues Telecom et Free a assuré qu’il garantira l’emploi des 8 000 salariés de SFR jusqu’en 2029, mais ce plan temporaire de sauvegarde de l’emploi exclut les employés franchisés. Pour rappel, les boutiques franchisées de SFR n’appartiennent pas à SFR. Ces dernières peuvent vendre les produits et les services de l’opérateur, mais les boutiques en elles-mêmes, ainsi que leurs employés, sont sous le contrôle d’un entrepreneur indépendant.
Les franchisés de SFR réclament des compensations
À travers cette action en justice, l’ADIES réclame deux choses. Premièrement, l’association demande à ce que les contrats qui lient les franchisés à SFR soient rééquilibrés afin de tenir compte de la situation créée par le rachat de l’opérateur. Deuxièmement, l’ADIES réclame une indemnisation de la part de SFR pour les préjudices que les franchisés estiment avoir subis à la suite de l’annonce du rachat.
Les membres du bureau de l’association précisent toutefois : « Nous ne sommes pas opposés à la vente de SFR. Mais notre réseau représente près de la moitié des magasins de l’enseigne et ne peut pas être la variable d’ajustement de cette opération ». L’ADIES affirme avoir tenté de dialoguer avec SFR pendant plus d’un an, sans succès, avant de porter l’affaire devant le Tribunal des activités économiques de Paris. Une audience est d’ores et déjà prévue le 10 décembre prochain.

articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : L'ordinateur Portable Apple MacBook Neo 256 Go à 699,00 €
Actuellement noté 3/5 par notre rédaction, l'ordinateur portable Apple MacBook Neo s'appuie sur un fonctionnement silencieux et un écran bien calibré pour assurer les tâches bureautiques du quotidien. Le Black Friday 2026 fait descendre son prix à 699,00 € chez Amazon, soit une baisse d'environ 9 % et 72,40 € d'économie.
L'Apple MacBook Neo est un ultraportable pensé pour la bureautique simple et pour découvrir l'univers macOS sans viser les tarifs habituels de la marque. Construit autour de la puce Apple A18 Pro, cet ordinateur portable mise sur un format compact et un fonctionnement silencieux. Il s'est distingué lors de son passage dans notre labo par la précision de son affichage et la qualité de ses finitions.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le MacBook Neo descend à 699,00 € chez Amazon, soit environ 9 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (771,40 €). Cela représente une économie de 72,40 €.
Écran fidèle et silence complet au quotidien
Cet ordinateur portable se destine avant tout au traitement de texte, à la navigation web et aux tâches courantes. Comme détaillé dans notre test complet, sa dalle IPS de 13 pouces affiche une excellente justesse avec un delta E mesuré à 1,1, garantissant des couleurs fidèles sans dérive visible à l'œil nu. Sa luminosité maximale atteint 516 cd/m², ce qui assure une bonne lisibilité en intérieur bien éclairé.
Son système de refroidissement passif élimine tout bruit mécanique en fonctionnement. Actuellement noté 3/5 par nos services, l'appareil s'appuie également sur un duo clavier et pavé tactile confortable pour de longues sessions de saisie. Côté endurance, la batterie a résisté pendant 482 minutes lors de nos protocoles de mesure, assurant une journée de cours ou de travail sans chargeur.
Apple MacBook Neo
Points forts
- Construction de qualité.
- Dalle 13 pouces bien calibrée.
- Excellent combo clavier et pavé tactile.
- Silence.
- Autonomie honorable.
Points faibles
- Performances théoriques faiblardes.
- Dalle brillante.
- Aucune évolutivité.
- Connectique limitée et antédiluvienne.
- Pas de wifi 7.
Des concessions marquées sur la connectique et la puissance
Pour atteindre ce positionnement tarifaire, la marque a limité la mémoire vive à 8 Go et le stockage interne à 256 Go, sans aucune possibilité d'évolution matérielle par la suite. La puce embarquée montre vite ses limites dès que l'on sollicite des applications lourdes de création visuelle. Il faut également composer avec une connectique très réduite, cantonnée à deux ports USB-C et une prise casque, ainsi qu'une absence de compatibilité avec le wifi 7.
Le revêtement brillant de l'écran reste sujet aux reflets directs en extérieur. Ces limitations réservent ce modèle aux personnes cherchant une première machine bureautique d'appoint, prête à l'emploi et simple à transporter, qui n'ont pas besoin de raccorder de multiples périphériques.
Acer Aspire 14 AI : l'autre option face au Apple MacBook Neo
L'Acer Aspire 14 AI se présente sous le système Windows avec un processeur Intel Core Ultra 5 et une dalle Oled. Il vise un profil similaire d'utilisateurs à la recherche d'une machine abordable pour le travail quotidien. Cependant, son écran manque de justesse par rapport à celui du portable d'Apple et se montre tout aussi sensible aux reflets.
À ce jour, les deux modèles affichent une note actuelle identique de 3/5 dans notre comparatif. Vendu à un tarif strictement identique à celui du jour, l'Acer Aspire 14 AI propose une partie graphique plus polyvalente, mais le MacBook Neo conserve l'avantage d'une meilleure fidélité des couleurs et d'une conception silencieuse sans ventilateur.
Acer Aspire 14 AI
Points forts
- Autonomie importante.
- Processeur homogène.
- Partie graphique vaillante.
- Dalle Oled…
Points faibles
- …qui manque de justesse.
- Écran sujet aux reflets.
- Pas de wifi 7.
- Trop de logiciels préinstallés.

articles.title: Aragón pierde otro centro de datos: Capital Energy se retira de Épila y vende su conexión eléctrica a Blackstone
articles.text:
Aragón se ha convertido en uno de los territorios más atractivos para la industria de los centros de datos. Pero no todos los proyectos anunciados llegan a construirse. De hecho, la región ha perdido recientemente otro megacampus de centros de datos. En este caso, se trataba de Epilon, el campus que Box2Bit iba a construir en Épila, (Zaragoza). Con esta retirada, son tres ya los proyectos de este tipo que la compañía abandona en la región.
En esta “espantada”, Bit2Box, además, ha vendido a Blackstone los derechos asociados a 150 MW de capacidad de conexión eléctrica que había conseguido para Epilon y que ya no le van a hacer falta. El fondo de inversiones, por su lado, aprovechará esta potencia para reforzar su proyecto Rhodes, en Calatorao. Y es que los centros de datos requieren de un suministro eléctrico continuo y tan potente que la energía es ahora el bien más preciado para las empresas tecnológicas.
Un proyecto más que no se va a desarrollar. Según el portal Data Center Dynamics, Box2Bit anunció en su día tres campus de centros de datos en Aragón, pero, a día de hoy, ninguno seguirá adelante. Primero fue el Campus Ebro en Cariñena, valorado en 3.400 millones de euros, que fue descartado al quedarse fuera del plan de inversiones del Ministerio para los próximos cinco años. El segundo fue La Charluca, en Calatayud, que no consiguió obtener acceso a la red de transmisión y que tampoco llegó a desarrollarse.
Ahora se cancela también Epilon, que debía emplazarse en Épila, un municipio de Zaragoza.
¿Epeculación? Según las declaraciones de su alcalde, Jesús Bazán, que recoge ese DCD, los propietarios de las cerca de 100 hectáreas reservadas para Epilon no llegaron a recibir el primer pago y los derechos sobre el terreno expiraron el pasado mes de mayo. Bazán señala que no se puede descartar que el anuncio de Epilon tuviese motivaciones especulativas, primero anunciando un proyecto y obteniendo los derechos de terreno y capacidad de conexión y, posteriormente, transfiriendo estos últimos sin llegar a construir nada.
La conexión, un activo transferible que beneficia a Blackstone. Sea como fuere, la realidad es que la gran beneficiada ha sido Blackstone, que ha comprado los derechos de capacidad de conexión eléctrica y que ahora podrá utilizar para reforzar su enorme campus de centros de datos en Calatorao. El proyecto, al que se conoce como Rhodes, contempla alcanzar unos 430 MW de potencia informática y prevé una inversión superior a 13.000 millones de euros.
Con la cancelación de Epilon, los 150 MW procedentes de Box2Bit permitirán a Blackstone sumar capacidad de conexión que complementa los 600 MW que Red Eléctrica le había concedido inicialmente.
No sin problemas. A pesar de lo anterior, el macrocentro de Calatorao todavía tiene obstáculos administrativos y judiciales por delante. El Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Aragón ha admitido a trámite un recurso de Ecologistas en Acción contra el proyecto Rhodes, como informa eldiario.es. Según esta publicación, la organización cuestiona la aprobación parcial del Plan de Interés General de Aragón (PIGA) el pasado 28 de septiembre y la declaración de utilidad pública, que permite expropiar terrenos en suelo rústico para desarrollar estas instalaciones en beneficio de la promotora privada.
De momento, sabemos que Rhodes contaría con ocho edificios de centros de datos en una superficie de 223 hectáreas y que sus necesidades energéticas son aún mayores que lo que daba a entender el anuncio inicial: la documentación del expediente recoge una demanda de hasta 650 MW de potencia eléctrica, ampliable a 1.000 MW, frente a los 300 MW de los que se habló inicialmente. Ecologistas en Acción calcula que su consumo equivaldría al 40% del de toda la comunidad, mientras que la planta solar prevista dentro del recinto cubriría solo el 0,43% de esa demanda.

articles.title: pCloud Pass a bien été victime d'une cyberattaque, l'éditeur assure que vos mots de passe sont en sécurité
articles.text:
Quelques heures après les premiers signalements de connexions suspectes à pCloud Pass, l'entreprise suisse confirme avoir subi une cyberattaque. Si des adresses mail ont été exposées, l'éditeur assure que les données conservées dans les coffres-forts de son gestionnaire de mots de passe n'ont pas été compromises.
Nous vous en parlions ce vendredi matin. Dans la nuit du 26 au 27 novembre, plusieurs utilisateurs et utilisatrices de pCloud Pass ont reçu des notifications leur signalant la connexion d'un appareil inconnu à leur compte, malgré l'activation de la double authentification. Nous avions nous-mêmes reçu cette alerte et relevé plusieurs anomalies dans les infrastructures de pCloud. L'entreprise a depuis pris la parole sur Reddit pour apporter de premiers éléments d'explication.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
Des adresses mail exposées, mais des coffres-forts épargnés selon pCloud
L'entreprise suisse indique avoir rapidement contenu une cyberattaque visant son gestionnaire de mots de passe. L'attaque a toutefois entraîné l'exposition des adresses mail d'un nombre limité d'utilisateurs et utilisatrices de pCloud Pass, sans que l'éditeur précise combien de personnes sont concernées. D'après pCloud, les notifications reçues cette nuit auraient été déclenchées par des tentatives de connexion à leurs comptes.
L'entreprise assure en revanche que les mots de passe, les notes et les autres informations enregistrées dans les coffres-forts de ses clients n'ont pas été compromis. Elle rappelle que ces données sont chiffrées sur les appareils de ces derniers et que leur déchiffrement nécessite de connaître leur mot de passe maître, auquel l'éditeur lui-même n'a pas accès.
L'attaque aurait par ailleurs été circonscrite à pCloud Pass, épargnant les services de stockage en ligne de l'entreprise. Compte tenu de l'exposition des adresses mail, pCloud invite néanmoins ses clients à redoubler de vigilance face aux tentatives de phishing et rappelle qu'elle ne leur demandera jamais de communiquer leur mot de passe maître ou leurs mots de récupération.
Les explications de pCloud laissent les internautes perplexes
Sur Reddit comme à la rédaction, les explications de pCloud peinent à convaincre. Les notifications reçues cette nuit ne nous informaient pas d'une tentative de connexion à notre compte, mais bien de la connexion d'un nouvel appareil. Plusieurs internautes ont même indiqué avoir retrouvé cet appareil dans la liste de leurs sessions actives, malgré l'activation de la double authentification. On ignore aussi pourquoi les adresses IP associées à ces connexions appartenaient aux propres infrastructures de pCloud et pourquoi les liens intégrés aux notifications renvoyaient vers ce qui semble être un environnement de test interne à l'entreprise.
À défaut de savoir à quelles ressources les pirates ont pu accéder, il est également difficile d'évaluer la portée de l'attaque sur les coffres-forts. Si pCloud assure que leur contenu n'a pas été compromis, l'entreprise ne précise pas si les attaquants ont pu en récupérer des copies chiffrées. Or, comme nous l'expliquions hier à la suite de la cyberattaque dont a été victime 1Password, le chiffrement de bout en bout ne suffit pas toujours à garantir la sécurité des mots de passe lorsque les infrastructures du gestionnaire sont compromises.
Plus surprenant, pCloud consacre une partie de sa communication aux progrès de l'intelligence artificielle, qui accélèrent la découverte de vulnérabilités dans les logiciels, parfois avant même que leurs développeurs n'aient pu les identifier et les corriger. L'entreprise ne livre pourtant aucun détail sur la méthode employée par les pirates pour s'en prendre à pCloud Pass, ni sur le rôle éventuel de l'IA dans cette attaque.
Contactée à deux reprises par nos soins ce vendredi, l'entreprise n'a toujours pas répondu à nos questions.
Vous avez reçu une notification de pCloud Pass, que faire ?
Si vous avez reçu l'une de ces notifications, connectez-vous directement à pCloud Pass, sans passer par les liens intégrés au mail. Vérifiez la liste des appareils connectés et révoquez les sessions que vous ne reconnaissez pas. Par précaution, changez également le mot de passe de votre compte pCloud et celui de votre coffre-fort, et assurez-vous que la double authentification est toujours activée.
Attention, le renouvellement de votre mot de passe maître vise à sécuriser vos futurs accès au coffre-fort, mais ne protège pas une éventuelle copie de celui-ci déjà dérobée par les pirates. Redoublez enfin de vigilance face aux mails se réclamant de l'entreprise, les attaquants pouvant exploiter les adresses mail exposées pour mener des campagnes de phishing.

articles.title: Whatsapp: Diese 4 neuen Funktionen machen den Messenger besser
articles.text:
Whatsapp: Diese 4 neuen Funktionen machen den Messenger besser
Whatsapp zählt weltweit zwei Milliarden Nutzer:innen und ist damit der beliebteste Messenger. Damit das so bleibt, spendieren die Entwickler:innen den Apps für iOS, Android, macOS und Windows regelmäßig neue Funktionen – manchmal sogar in so geringen Abständen, dass es für einige Nutzer:innen unübersichtlich wird.
Was ist neu bei Whatsapp?
Damit ihr nichts verpasst, haben wir die Neuheiten der vergangenen Wochen für euch zusammengetragen. Darunter befinden sich die neue Planungsfunktion und ein E-Sim-Angebot.
Wie immer gilt: Könnt ihr das jeweilige neue Feature noch nicht finden, ist unter Umständen Geduld gefragt. Neue Funktionen bringt Whatsapp in Wellen auf die Smartphones seiner Nutzer:innen. Es kann also etwas dauern, bis euch neue Features erreichen. Außerdem solltet ihr sicherstellen, dass die App bei euch auf dem neuesten Stand ist.
Weihnachtsgrüße jetzt schreiben – und später versenden
Im Feiertagsstress kann der rechtzeitige Weihnachtsgruß an Freunde oder Verwandte schon einmal untergehen. Genau dafür liefert Whatsapp nun eine Funktion nach, die andere Dienste schon lange bieten. Ihr könnt jetzt Nachrichten vorschreiben und deren Versand für bis zu zwei Wochen später einplanen. Dazu tippt ihr eure Botschaft einfach ein und haltet den Senden-Button gedrückt. Vorausgesetzt, die Option ist bei euch schon aktiv, könnt ihr dann einen Versandzeitpunkt festlegen. Das funktioniert mit Text, Links, Fotos und Videos. Hier lest ihr alles Weitere zum Planen von Nachrichten auf Whatsapp.
Neue Funktionen für Whatsapp-Gruppen
In den vergangenen Wochen hat Whatsapp die Möglichkeiten in Gruppenchats stark erweitert. So können Mitglieder jetzt auch ältere Nachrichten an neue Gruppenteilnehmer weiterleiten. Außerdem lassen sich Nachrichten länger fixieren und ihr könnt Statusmeldungen speziell für eine Gruppe anfertigen. Ebenfalls praktisch: Nachrichten lassen sich jetzt nach Erwähnungen und Antworten filtern, sodass ihr alle an euch direkt gerichteten Botschaften leicht überblickt. Mit Blick auf die neue Obergrenze von bis zu 1.500 Personen pro Whatsapp-Gruppe sicherlich keine schlechte Idee.
Whatsapp als E-Sim-Anbieter
Wer auch auf Reisen im Ausland außerhalb der EU erreichbar sein will, muss sich um eine passende Sim-Karte kümmern. Whatsapp will seinen Nutzer:innen das ersparen. Die Meta-Tochter hat angekündigt, künftig eigene E-Sims vertreiben zu wollen. Die lassen sich dann über die App buchen. Um mögliche Roaminggebühren muss man sich dann keine Gedanken mehr machen. Was der neue Service kostet, ist bislang allerdings noch offen.
Whatsapp erkennt Daten eigenständig
Je nachdem, welche Daten euch Kontakte schicken, kann Whatsapp sie eigenständig und selbstständig Aktionen vorschlagen. Enthält eine Nachricht ein Datum, könnt ihr dieses direkt im Kalender speichern oder ein sogenanntes Whatsapp-Event daraus erstellen. Bei einer Adresse bietet der Messenger an, den Kartendienst zu öffnen, bei einer Mail-Adresse die entsprechende E‑Mail-App. Laut WABetaInfo muss sich dabei niemand Sorgen um die Privatsphäre machen. Der Messenger erkenne die Daten direkt auf dem Gerät und brauche dazu keinen Kontakt mit einem Server.

articles.title: Moloi: The Soweto founder taking African tech to the world
articles.text:
From teaching himself to code in Soweto to taking his technology business global, Seati Moloi is determined to challenge perceptions of where innovation comes from. The founder and CEO of Khoi Tech spoke to PHATHISANI MOYO about his journey from a curious township boy fascinated by video games to building an African-owned technology company and why he believes Africa must stop being a consumer of technology and start owning it.
When Seati Moloi and his siblings asked their mother for money as children, she had an unusual response. Rather than reaching into her purse, she would buy them a packet of lollipops and send them into the streets to sell.
The exercise had a small business lesson. If the sweets cost 50 cents, the children were expected to return with 80 cents. They would then share the proceeds.
His mother was teaching them how to work, make money and create something for themselves.
“She was effectively saying, ‘I’m not going to simply give you money; I’m going to teach you how to work, create something and generate revenue,’” Moloi recalled in an interview with TechCabal on Wednesday.
That lesson has stayed with Moloi, the founder and chief executive officer (CEO) of Khoi Tech, a Soweto-born wearable technology company that has grown from selling wireless earphones and smartwatches into digital health, employee wellness and workplace safety solutions. Having represented South Africa at London Tech Week twice, Moloi is now pushing the bigger idea that African companies should not only use technology built elsewhere, but create and own it.
But entrepreneurship was only one part of the education Moloi received at home. His parents also recognised their son’s insatiable curiosity about how gadgets worked.
Growing up in Soweto, a township rich in liberation history, during apartheid, he was fascinated by computers and video games. While other children were content playing them, Moloi says he wanted to understand how they were made. He wanted to create his own.
The boy who wanted to make video games
His fascination with technology began long before the internet made information and programming tutorials readily accessible. Moloi recalls being drawn to video games, but playing them was never enough. He wanted to understand what went into making them.
“I was fascinated by video games and wanted to create my own. I remember making a game based on The A-Team (the popular action-packed 1980s television series) using paper and pen. I even tried to contact the publishers,” he recalled.
His mother recognised that this was more than a passing childhood interest. Instead of getting him another game, she bought him a computer to explore the technology behind them.
Moloi says he taught himself BASIC programming using old Commodore computers. His father encouraged him to pursue mathematics and science at school, and by his final years of high school, he already knew he wanted to work with computers.
“I credit my parents for having the foresight to recognise the passion their child had and invest in it,” he said.
It was not a childhood without its difficulties. Moloi grew up in a tough environment during the final years of apartheid, a system of racial segregation and oppression, but he was also an ordinary township boy who played soccer and did the things children do.
What distinguished him, he says, was his curiosity and the encouragement he received at home.
“I was a township child with a keen interest in understanding how things were made,” he said. “I wanted to challenge the status quo and create things for myself.”
Building computers after work
After studying computer science at Pentech College in Cape Town and being groomed at Zakheni Computing, an enterprise technology solutions provider, Moloi and a few friends began assembling computers from individual components.
They would travel to suppliers in town, buy motherboards and other parts, assemble the machines, install software, and put together complete personal computers (PCs). The computers belonged to an era when hard drives were bulky, and storage was measured in megabytes rather than the gigabytes and terabytes familiar today.
Moloi remembers installing programmes such as WordPerfect and Lotus 1-2-3, as well as MS-DOS, before putting the machines to use or selling them to people who wanted computers in their homes.
“We could create something from individual components and sell it to people,” he said.
His parents, however, wanted him to gain corporate experience before committing himself to entrepreneurship. He eventually joined First National Bank, one of Africa’s oldest lenders, as a software developer, working on systems for automated teller machines and speed point terminals.
It was not quite the career he had imagined for himself.
Moloi entered a profession that was still largely white-dominated in the years following apartheid. Although he found the technical work relatively straightforward, the corporate environment’s inequalities made the experience uncomfortable at times.
“I didn’t particularly want to go into employment, but my parents insisted,” he said. “They wanted me to gain experience and understand how things worked in a corporate environment before venturing out on my own.”
He lasted about two years.
During the day, he worked as a software developer. In the evenings, he returned to assembling machines with his friends. They were beginning to attract customers, some of whom needed help using their new computers.
His first ventures included SMN Computers, a hardware business that assembled and sold PCs and eventually secured corporate clients, including the City of Johannesburg and Rand Water. They also worked with International Business Machines (IBM), a global technology and consulting company, that trained them in software development, especially websites.
But selling computers eventually became limiting. The company risked becoming what Moloi describes as a “box dropper,” competing with much larger players on the supply of hardware.
The team moved into software development through another business, Biza Telecoms, working on mobile applications and short message service (SMS) applications. Those experiences laid the groundwork for Khoi Tech, which was established around 2020.
From gadgets to data
Moloi founded Khoi Tech after identifying an opportunity in consumer electronics. He had always enjoyed exploring new devices and understanding how they worked. The company began developing wireless earphones and smartwatches under an African brand.
The name Khoi is derived from the word Khoisan, Southern Africa’s earliest known inhabitants. Its products included the Khoi Afripods wireless earphones and Khoi Afriwatch smartwatches.
The ambition was straightforward: create devices that people used every day, but sell them under an African brand. “Why isn’t Africa creating its own products?” Moloi said, describing the thinking behind the business.
The company received an important early boost through Telkom FutureMakers, the telecommunications group’s enterprise and supplier development programme, which supports black-owned businesses and entrepreneurs from disadvantaged backgrounds by helping them develop business ideas, access markets, sharpen their skills and scale their operations.
According to Telkom’s 2023 Integrated Report, the programme approved a R500,000 grant ($27,000) for Khoi Tech to develop its smartwatch prototype, which was launched in September 2022. The funding also helped the company build the backend systems needed to support the device.
The smartwatches generated health-related information that could help doctors, employers and other organisations. Khoi Tech began developing artificial intelligence (AI)-powered health monitoring systems that could use this data to support remote patient monitoring and provide insights into people’s health over time.
Moloi says he and his team engaged medical professionals to understand the challenges of monitoring patients outside traditional healthcare settings and accessing historical health information.
“We realised very early that we were not necessarily in the device business. We were in the data business,” he said. The idea was to sell devices, collect and store the information they generated, process it through Khoi Tech’s systems and make useful insights available to individuals and corporate customers.
The company began developing remote patient monitoring and employee wellness solutions, alongside applications for driver safety and the mining industry.
For underground miners, wearable devices can help companies monitor employees and identify their locations. In transport, the technology can support driver wellness and fatigue-risk management.
The move also changed how Khoi Tech approached manufacturing. It works with contract manufacturers in China to produce devices according to its specifications, while developing its software and backend systems in South Africa.
“We realised that we were not necessarily in the device business. We were in the data business. We use the devices to extract data and store it in our databases. Our solution is mainly focused on the backend system,” Moloi said.
Getting the devices approved was not a simple process. Khoi Tech had to submit them for testing and certification by the Independent Communications Authority of South Africa (ICASA), South Africa’s telecommunications regulator, to address component defects and repeat parts of the process.
It took about two years to secure certification and approval.
Moloi would have preferred to manufacture everything locally, but says the cost was prohibitive given the company’s resources. The experience reinforced the importance of developing the software and intellectual property that sit behind the products, rather than relying on hardware sales alone.
A moment to pinch himself
For a founder who began his journey in Soweto, taking Khoi Tech to London Tech Week was a particularly meaningful milestone.
The company was selected as part of a South African startup cohort supported by the United Kingdom-South Africa Tech Hub, Telkom and Disraptor, a South African technology venture builder. Khoi Tech’s 2026 participation marked its second consecutive appearance at the event.
Moloi remembers the first experience on the tech world stage as almost surreal.
“It was one of those moments when you wanted to pinch yourself several times to see whether you were still alive!” he said.
There was pride in standing before international organisations and presenting technology developed by a company from Soweto. Some people he met, he says, were surprised by what the team had built, particularly its solutions for corporate customers and the mining sector.
Dinner with the Mayor of London and explaining how the company developed its technology was another highlight. Moloi found the experience challenged a familiar belief that innovation of this calibre must come from established technology hubs or wealthy countries.
“There is sometimes an assumption that because we come from this part of the world, we cannot be innovative or think at that level,” he said.
The ambition to own the technology
Moloi speaks passionately about technology sovereignty. He believes African countries cannot remain dependent on foreign companies for the platforms and systems that underpin everyday life.
He points to reliance on global technology companies such as Microsoft, Google and WhatsApp, arguing that local talent can develop alternatives that serve African markets.
“It’s everything, my brother,” he said when asked why ownership matters.
For him, sovereignty begins with controlling the technology stack that supports a country’s economy and security. South Africa’s broader digital economy accounts for an estimated 10% to 15% of gross domestic product (GDP), according to the GSMA’s 2024 report on digital transformation in South Africa. Retaining more of that economic value through locally developed technology, intellectual property and platforms is central to his argument.
He makes the point with a familiar example: if WhatsApp were switched off, South Africans might have to return to SMS because they have not built a comparable platform of their own.
His argument is not that the continent should isolate itself from international companies. Rather, it should develop the capability to build its own systems, collaborate from a position of strength and retain more of the value created by its innovations.
Moloi believes countries such as China and Singapore offer lessons in developing technological independence. He was also invited to join a group of entrepreneurs who recently travelled to Silicon Valley with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, but declined, saying he was more interested in learning from the East.
“If you go to Shenzhen, for example, you will see that it is living in 2050,” he said.
His frustration reflects a concern echoed across Africa’s technology industry for years. The continent continues to struggle to create the conditions needed to turn that potential into globally competitive, locally owned technology businesses.
TechCabal previously reported that even companies such as Khoi Tech face challenges accessing investors and networks outside established technology hubs. Much of Africa’s talent still builds on technology developed elsewhere rather than owning the products and platforms shaping the digital economy.
For young people growing up in townships, Moloi wants his journey to offer hope and a different picture of what is possible.
“Being born in Soweto or any other township should not be seen as a limitation,” he believes.
The Soweto-born founder hopes young people will use the tools available to them, including artificial intelligence, to build solutions that address the needs of their communities and the wider continent.
“They need to take the baton and continue the race,” he noted.
Moloi believes that the future begins with recognising that a child from Soweto can do more than use technology built elsewhere. That child can help create it.

articles.title: Apple, Samsung, and Xiaomi are all planning to sell fewer phones in 2027
articles.text:
Bottom line: Smartphone makers are lowering their 2027 sales targets as the memory chips used in their devices become significantly more expensive. Apple, Samsung, Xiaomi, Oppo, vivo, Huawei, Transsion, and Lenovo have all lowered their shipment targets for next year, with reductions ranging from 5.6% to 29%. Honor is the only manufacturer planning to maintain its shipment volume, as analysts expect the memory shortage driving these cuts to persist until at least 2028.
Jiemian News reported the targets, citing supply chain sources. None of the manufacturers had responded to requests for verification by the time of publication. The figures represent internal targets and could still change, but the overall direction is consistent across nearly all major brands.
Apple is targeting approximately 220 million units in 2027, down from roughly 233 million. Samsung's target is falling from about 232 million to 210 million, a 9.5% reduction. Both companies are among the least affected major players, reflecting their strength in the premium segment, where manufacturers have more room to absorb higher component costs.
Chinese smartphone brands face deeper cuts. Xiaomi is lowering its target from approximately 120 million to 90 million units, a 25% reduction. Oppo's target is falling from about 105 million to 90 million, a 14% decline. Vivo is reducing its target from 85 million to 60 million. Motorola's parent company, Lenovo, is cutting its target from approximately 50 million to 40 million units, while Transsion is lowering its goal from 66 million to 58 million. Huawei, which targeted approximately 60 million units this year, is reportedly planning to ship fewer than 50 million.
Mid-range and entry-level models account for most smartphone sales by volume, but they also have the thinnest profit margins. These segments are therefore expected to bear the brunt of the reductions.
Memory costs have already changed what goes into the phones themselves. Honor CEO Li Jian spoke after the Honor 700 series launch at the end of November. He said many products in the industry "have had to make trade-offs: some chips have been downgraded, some imaging systems have been downgraded, and some memory systems have been downgraded, relying on piecing together specifications to find a balance."
This means buyers could end up with less powerful processors, simpler camera modules, or less RAM at the same price. In other cases, they may have to pay more for essentially the same specifications. Either way, smartphones with weaker specifications or higher price tags are harder to sell, and the lower shipment targets reflect that reality.
The 2027 plans follow a turbulent 2026. Early in the year, rising memory prices prompted Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo, and Transsion to collectively reduce their smartphone orders. Xiaomi at one point lowered its annual target to fewer than 100 million units. In July, however, the company judged that memory prices might be approaching their peak, prompting it to restore some low-end orders and raise its target to 110 million units. Its current 2026 target of approximately 120 million is now well above both earlier estimates.
The global picture has also deteriorated. Forecasts for worldwide smartphone shipments this year have shifted from an expected decline of approximately 3% at the beginning of the year to a projected contraction of around 14%.
Honor is keeping its 2027 target at approximately 50 million units, matching its goal for this year. IDC data showed that Honor was the only leading Chinese smartphone manufacturer to record quarter-over-quarter shipment growth in the third quarter. "Mid-range phones face even greater cost pressures than flagship phones," Li said. "While others are retreating, Honor is determined to move forward." Whether the company can maintain this trajectory will depend on securing memory supplies at commercially viable prices, something its larger competitors are also fighting to achieve.
Counterpoint Research's November memory tracker reported that third-quarter DRAM revenue increased by 369% year over year. The average selling price reached $1.90 per gigabit, while Samsung held a 38% market share. "The current market is in a price-driven supercycle, rather than a shipment-driven cycle," senior analyst Jeongku Choi said. He added that buyers are now competing for supply security rather than lower prices.
Forecasts suggest that the pressure will continue throughout next year. A Goldman Sachs report published this month projects a global DRAM supply deficit of 5.1% in 2027, potentially making it one of the worst shortages in more than 15 years. The report also projects a 2% decline in smartphone NAND demand that year. Counterpoint research director MS Hwang said memory prices should remain elevated next year, with no major new wafer fabrication plants expected to come online before 2028.
Goldman Sachs expects conditions to improve after that. The firm projects the DRAM supply-demand gap will narrow to 1.2% in 2028, with prices for both conventional DRAM and NAND potentially falling by around 20%. Viewed in this context, the 2027 shipment reductions represent a defensive response to a temporary market cycle rather than a permanent retreat. However, manufacturers may revise their targets again as memory supply contracts are finalized and demand becomes clearer.

articles.title: Texas lifts freeze on 1,800+ data center projects in Greg Abbott U-turn — companies rush for permits before Gina Hinojosa's January arrival
articles.text:
Texas lifts freeze on 1,800+ data center projects in Greg Abbott U-turn — companies rush for permits before Gina Hinojosa's January arrival
The state had paused the approval of new permits at the behest of outgoing Republican governor Greg Abbott, but the halt was short-lived.
After slamming the brakes on more than 1,800 data center projects in August, Texas has once again started approving them following a new directive from outgoing Republican governor Greg Abbott's office. The move came after the same office also paused the approval of permits, saying that Abbot's "top priority is to protect Texans’ safety and quality of life” amid concerns over the amount of power new data centers would require. At the time, the move meant that 474 gigawatts of new power requests became subject to the moratorium. But with Democratic governor Gina Hinojosa's January arrival edging ever closer, Abbott has done a 180-degree pivot, with the FT reporting that data center builders are rushing to get their approvals in before the new governor arrives. Hinojosa has already pledged to rein in new data center construction.
As recently as October, Texas suspended a further 17 data center construction permits and shut down an automated portal that was found to still be approving new permits. That system will surely be switched back on now that Abbott's office has confirmed that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which is in charge of the state’s electrical grid, has finished gathering the information that it needed on how data centers affect local communities.
But even with ERCOT's investigation complete, the processing of new power requests isn't one that is expected to happen quickly. With that in mind, some developers have already taken matters into their own hands, choosing to build their own power centers to reduce or eliminate their reliance on the local grid. The region's large gas supplies are helping this effort, as is what is considered to be a "lax" regulatory environment. This all means that the possibility of using gas turbines to power new data centers is a viable one, although some are looking beyond traditional gas-powered options. In Mississippi, Elon Musk's xAI installed eight converted jet engines to power its data center, despite the known health risks posed by their use.
While it remains to be seen what impact the arrival of incoming Governor Hinojosa will have on data centers in the area, there's little doubt that they will be a hot topic. Locals continue to be concerned about the environmental impact these facilities have, while increased costs associated with powering their own homes are another issue. Texas isn't alone in facing these problems, with New York announcing a year-long ban on data center projects larger than 50 megawatts that came into force earlier this year. In Northern Virginia, Amazon abandoned plans to build four new data centers after public outcry. The land will now be used for housing instead.

articles.title: Intel "Razor Lake-AX" Split Into MoP and MoB Lines, iGPU Tipped at RTX 5070 Ti Laptop Level
articles.text:
Friday, November 27th 2026
Intel "Razor Lake-AX" Split Into MoP and MoB Lines, iGPU Tipped at RTX 5070 Ti Laptop Level
More details have surfaced regarding Intel's next-next CPU lineup known as "Razor Lake." Specifically, the Intel Razor Lake-AX chip, which will reportedly come in two parallel product lines. According to prominent Intel leaker Jaykihn, Razor Lake-AX will be split into MoP (memory-on-package) and MoB (memory-on-board) lineups. The MoP version officially supports up to 96 GB of LPDDR5X and comes in 16-core and 28-core CPU configurations, targeted at laptops and mini PCs. This is the version that was pictured yesterday with empty memory pads that the OEMs will fill themselves. The MoB line, on the other hand, goes up to 192 GB and uses the 28-core CPU part. Jaykihn also floated the possibility of a 52-core MoB option with dual compute tiles, but apparently that line is still in its definition state and won't come to laptops.
On the graphics side, we got a new tip from leaker Haze today, who posted a single line claiming "Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti mobile like performance." This was a quote tweet of his earlier claim that the Razor Lake-AX chip uses on-package memory. Although he doesn't point out which configuration he's talking about, it's probably the flagship with 32 Xe3P GPU cores. This is a single line from a leaker, so take it with a grain of salt. If true, that would be quite an impressive feat for the Razor Lake-AX chip. Memory bandwidth will also be important for gaming performance since the AX chip only supports LPDDR5X. The Razor Lake-AX MoP line is expected to be announced or launched sometime in late 2027, but the timeline is hazy right now since the product is so far out.
Sources:
				Jaykihn on X, 				Haze on X, 				via Wccftech
