articles.title: Après les 60 fps, les 180 fps : la surenchère des vidéos de GTA 6 sur PC continue
articles.text:
À en croire une séquence qui tourne sur X depuis le début d’après-midi, GTA 6 tournerait déjà six fois mieux sur un PC pirate que sur une PS5 Pro.
Son auteur, D Everett Hinton, affirme dans une vidéo publiée sur X atteindre 30 images par seconde natives, propulsées à 180 grâce à la génération d’images, le tout en HDR10+ avec un moteur graphique « entièrement réécrit ».
Il assure au passage que la plupart des autres extraits en ligne sont faux, contrairement au sien. Pourtant, son nom n’apparaît dans aucun des projets recensés par les sites qui suivent la course des portages, et pas une seule ligne de code n’a été publiée.
En regardant l’extrait de plus près, les zones d’ombre s’accumulent vite. La vidéo se limite au prologue de la prison, en intérieur, loin de la charge d’un monde ouvert ou d’une course-poursuite en voiture.
L’image est vendue comme du 32:9 (le format des écrans ultra-larges), mais elle tient en réalité dans un fichier 1080p encadré de bandes noires.
L’auteur reconnaît d’ailleurs lui-même que les 30 images par seconde sont mesurées en 16:9, et non dans la définition géante de 5 120 par 1 440 pixels. Quant au compteur affiché à l’écran, il est fait maison et n’indique ni la carte graphique ni le processeur utilisés.
180 images par seconde, dont 150 inventées
Un détail technique vend immédiatement la mèche : le chiffre affiché vaut toujours exactement six fois la cadence réelle (30 donne 180, et 27,6 donne 165,6).
Ce ratio correspond au mode 6X du DLSS 4.5, qui demande aux cartes RTX 50 d’inventer cinq images intermédiaires pour chaque image réellement calculée.
Concrètement, le jeu continue de tourner à 30 images par seconde : la physique et la réactivité à la manette ne progressent pas d’un pouce. Nous avions déjà expliqué le grand paradoxe de la génération multi-images, qui gonfle spectaculairement les compteurs sans offrir la fluidité d’un vrai rendu natif.
Sans preuve formelle, l’hypothèse la plus crédible reste celle d’une simple capture de la version console à 30 images par seconde, passée ensuite à la moulinette de la génération d’images. La manipulation a d’ailleurs déjà été montrée mi-novembre avec une PS5 Pro reliée à un PC équipé d’une RTX 5090 pour afficher 180 images par seconde.
Ce n’est donc pas un montage grossier, puisque l’on voit bien GTA 6, mais plutôt le mirage des 60 fps de cette semaine multiplié par trois.
    Pour aller plus loin
DLSS 4 et Multi Frame Generation : le grand paradoxe de la technologie star de Nvidia
            
Où en sont vraiment les portages ce soir
Si l’on coupe la génération d’images pour regarder les mesures réelles, le tableau est beaucoup plus modeste.
Tous ces chiffres proviennent des auteurs ou de leurs testeurs (et restent à vérifier de manière indépendante), mais aucun projet n’approche encore les 30 images par seconde en monde ouvert :
- Vice-Tay affirme avoir tenu 30 minutes à une médiane de 21,1 images par seconde sur une RTX 4090, cinématiques comprises. C’est le seul projet à revendiquer le seuil de jouabilité fixé par les sites de suivi, sans validation extérieure pour l’instant.
- VIctory-Nvidia annonce entre 26 et 30 images par seconde en 1440p avec le DLSS sur une RTX 5070, uniquement dans les salles du début. De son côté, PortWatch VI indique y avoir relevé 20 images par seconde sans génération d’images ni plantage.
- ScarlettPort plafonne autour de 7 à 8 images par seconde sur une RTX 3060, tandis qu’un testeur évoque une médiane de 22 images par seconde sur une Radeon RX 9060 XT.
Côté juridique, GitHub n’a publié aucun nouvel avis de retrait au nom de Take-Two depuis la vague de mardi (3 007 dépôts supprimés).
Selon la documentation de Vice-Tay, c’est l’auteur de CGBJ qui a choisi de retirer lui-même son projet, dont une branche privée sert de base à la démo multijoueur de jeudi soir.
Pour s’y retrouver dans cette course, le tableau des scores de PortWatch VI reste la meilleure boussole.
    Pour aller plus loin
Où en est GTA 6 sur PC ? Ce site suit la course des portages
            
Comment repérer une fausse démo (et éviter les pièges)
Au-delà du buzz, ces vidéos spectaculaires servent souvent d’appât. Kaspersky dit avoir déjà bloqué 27 416 malwares déguisés en GTA 6, et une fausse version PC du jeu est devenue une arnaque à grande échelle. La règle d’or consiste donc à ne jamais télécharger un fichier promettant GTA 6 sur PC, et à garder les mêmes réflexes qui dégonflaient déjà les prétendus 60 fps :
- Un compteur multiplié exactement par deux, quatre ou six trahit la génération d’images, qui ajoute des images sans accélérer le jeu.
- Un relevé sérieux affiche toujours la carte graphique, le processeur et la définition réelle.
- Un simple couloir de prison ne dit rien des performances réelles en voiture ou en pleine poursuite.
- Sans code publié ni test indépendant, une démo reste une simple promesse, et le lien de téléchargement qui l’accompagne mène souvent à une arnaque.
    Pour aller plus loin
Sur le dark web, comment une fausse version PC de GTA 6 est devenue une arnaque à grande échelle
            
    Pour aller plus loin

Une prouesse réelle, mais loin des 180 fps

articles.title: Galaxy Watch 9 tem 47% OFF na Black Friday da Amazon
articles.text:
Galaxy Watch 9 tem 47% OFF na Black Friday da Amazon
Galaxy Watch 9 equipado com maior bateria e processador Snapdragon Wear Elite atinge o 47% em oferta na Amazon
O Galaxy Watch 9 BT (40 mm) anunciado há poucos meses por R$ 2.999, encontra-se com 47% de desconto em oferta na Amazon. O novo smartwatch da Samsung custa apenas R$ 1.599 em até 12x sem juros. A poucas horas oficialmente da Black Friday 2026, este é o menor preço para adquirir o modelo desde o lançamento.
O menor preço que já encontramos para o Galaxy Watch 9 BT 40 mm foi R$ 1.419,10, na Black Friday de 2026 (Magalu). Fora de datas promocionais, o melhor foi R$ 1.488,87 (Mercado Livre, 11/11/2026), e esta oferta está R$ 110,13 acima.
A Samsung implementou novidades interessantes ao Watch 9. Equipado nativamente pelo sistema Wear OS 7 com One UI 9 Watch, a função “levante para falar” aciona sem a necessidade de usar o botão lateral, o Google Gemini. O assistente de IA atua principalmente na entrega de sugestões personalizadas a partir dos dados coletados.
O relógio inteligente conta com o sensor BioActive que monitora funções importantes de saúde como batimentos cardíacos, pressão arterial, índice de condicionamento físico, realização de eletrocardiograma e etc. Além disso, possui um treinador personalizado para praticantes de caminhadas e corridas.
O Galaxy Watch 9 chega com uma bateria maior ao antecessor, capacidade de 390 mAh contra 325 mAh do Watch 8. A evolução do componente gera uma autonomia 20% maior, de acordo com a Samsung. Portanto, na teoria é possível ganhar mais algumas horas de uso no dia a dia.
O novo smartwatch continua com 2 GB de RAM e 32 GB de armazenamento para salvar músicas, mas agora vem equipado pelo processador Snapdragon SW6100 Wear Elite de 3 nanômetros. A configuração sugere proporcionar uma navegação bem fluida entre os aplicativos.
A tela Super AMOLED de 3.000 nits garante ótima visibilidade mesmo sob sol forte e segue com a proteção de Cristal de Safira, um vidro mais resistente contra arranhões; já a caixa de 40 mm utiliza alumínio. Enquanto a certificação IP68 promete vedação avançada contra a entrada de poeira e água, incluindo imersão ou mergulhos.
Por fim, o Galaxy Watch 9 por R$ 1.599 em até 12x sem juros, conta com conexões avançadas de Bluetooth 6.0 e GPS de dupla frequência no qual possibilita obter dados de geolocalização mais apurados.
O Achados do TB desde o início do mês vem dia a dia monitorando preços e reunindo as melhores ofertas de itens de tecnologia. Por isso, acompanhe os nossos canais do Telegram e WhatsApp amanhã para receber as melhores promoções!

articles.title: IBM quantum computer solves problem classical computers can’t in just 15 minutes
articles.text:
IBM quantum computer solves problem classical computers can’t in just 15 minutes
- Date:
  November 23, 2026
- Source:
  IBM
- Summary:
  IBM and University of Chicago researchers have demonstrated that a quantum computer can complete an extraordinarily complex calculation in just 15 minutes, beyond the practical reach of leading classical computing methods. A novel error-detection technique also allows scientists to establish confidence in the accuracy of the results, overcoming a major hurdle in quantum computing.
- Share:
An IBM quantum computer has completed an extraordinarily complex computational task in just 15 minutes, while leading methods for simulating the calculation on conventional computers would require prohibitively long runtimes. Perhaps even more significantly, researchers were able to establish statistical confidence in the accuracy of the quantum computer's results, addressing one of the biggest obstacles in the field.
The achievement, led by IBM and researchers from the University of Chicago, satisfies the fundamental criteria for quantum advantage. This milestone occurs when a quantum computer performs a computational task beyond the practical capabilities of leading classical computing methods while producing results that can be trusted.
In their new paper, "Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity," the researchers demonstrated that both objectives could be achieved simultaneously using a novel design for encoded quantum circuits. The experiment represents one of the largest demonstrations of logical quantum computing to date. The researchers have also made their circuits and experimental results publicly available through the Quantum Advantage Tracker.
Solving Quantum Computing's Verification Problem
Unlike conventional computers, which process information using bits that represent either zero or one, quantum computers rely on quantum bits, or qubits. These can exist in combinations of both states and interact through a phenomenon known as quantum entanglement. These properties allow quantum computers to approach certain computational problems in fundamentally different ways.
For years, scientists have tested the capabilities of quantum computers using a benchmark called random circuit sampling (RCS). This technique involves running a series of randomly selected quantum operations and generating samples from a complex probability distribution. As the circuits grow larger and more complicated, reproducing their output with a classical computer becomes increasingly difficult.
However, this approach creates a fundamental dilemma. If a computation is too difficult for a classical computer to reproduce, how can researchers establish that the quantum computer performed it correctly?
As computational complexity increases, independently verifying the results becomes progressively more difficult and eventually impractical without making strong assumptions about how accurately the quantum hardware operates.
To overcome this problem, the IBM and University of Chicago team developed a more structured alternative to random circuit sampling. The researchers mathematically demonstrated that their approach preserves the same computational hardness criteria as conventional RCS while introducing a structure that allows errors to be detected during the computation.
"Verification remains one of the biggest challenges in firmly establishing experimental quantum advantage," said Bill Fefferman, Associate Professor at the University of Chicago. "This experiment develops techniques to better characterize the fidelity of hard quantum states under noise, increasing confidence that the quantum computer is solving a computationally hard problem."
Soumik Ghosh, PhD student in Fefferman's group at the University of Chicago, added, "Beyond strengthening experimental validation, advances in verification have the potential to unlock practical applications for the next generation of quantum computers."
70 Logical Qubits and Tenfold Lower Error Rates
One of the greatest challenges in building powerful quantum computers is their extraordinary sensitivity to errors. Quantum information can be disrupted by environmental disturbances, imperfections in hardware, and inaccuracies in the operations used to manipulate qubits. As computations become longer and more complex, these errors can accumulate and undermine the reliability of the results.
Quantum error correction addresses this weakness by encoding quantum information across multiple physical qubits to create more reliable units known as logical qubits. This approach allows certain errors to be identified and, depending on the technique, corrected or accounted for without destroying the underlying quantum information.
In one of the largest known demonstrations of quantum error correction, the researchers performed computations using 70 protected logical qubits. The experiment involved 2,415 logical two-qubit operations and 468 logical "T gates."
Quantum gates are the fundamental operations that manipulate quantum information, much like logic gates in conventional computers. Two-qubit gates allow qubits to interact, while T gates enable additional types of quantum operations needed for universal quantum computing. Together, these gate counts illustrate the considerable complexity of the experiment.
By encoding the quantum circuits, the researchers achieved effective logical error rates 10 times lower than the underlying physical error rates. This substantial reduction allowed the quantum computer to maintain remarkably high fidelity, a measure of how closely the actual quantum state matches the intended one, despite performing thousands of complex operations.
A New Era of Quantum Advantage
"We are now firmly in the quantum advantage era," said Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow. "We have demonstrated a quantum computation beyond the practical reach of classical computers that establishes, with statistical confidence, a lower bound on how faithfully it was executed. This milestone gives scientists, developers, and businesses a new foundation for trusting quantum computers as they scale to problems far beyond what we can achieve classically."
The researchers found that many leading classical simulation techniques would require impractically long periods to reproduce the computation. IBM's quantum computer, by comparison, accomplished the task in approximately 15 minutes.
Although the experiment was designed to demonstrate quantum advantage rather than solve an immediate real-world problem, it addresses two essential requirements for making large-scale quantum computing practical: controlling errors and establishing confidence in computational results.
By demonstrating both capabilities in a computation beyond the practical reach of leading classical methods, the researchers have taken a significant step toward a future in which quantum computers could reliably tackle scientific and industrial problems that are currently out of reach.
Story Source:
Materials provided by IBM. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Simon Martiel, Jay-U Chung, Alireza Seif, Soumik Ghosh, Ian Hincks, Abhinav Deshpande, Bill Fefferman, Jay M. Gambetta, Ali Javadi-Abhari. Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity. arXiv, 28 Jul 2026 DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2607.25941

articles.title: From Fan-Out to Fast: Sub-100ms API Design in Distributed Systems
articles.text:
Transcript
Saranya Vedagiri: How many of you got the chance to take the Tube today? So many of you have taken the Tube. Have you ever wondered why is the line paused again, anytime in your experience when taking the Tube? I just see a couple of you leaning in. I would like to take the Tube design just like a system design in a distributed system. Just like how we have the map in our hand, it feels as if London is manageable. A couple of lines, a transverse, and you feel like everything is good. That's not the same when you take the actual journey. Your actual journey can have pauses and unexpected reason. That's not what you want. That's similar to a distributed system. When you look at the system diagram, it feels so comforting. A couple of boxes and arrows moving from one to another. You expect everything to go great.
That's not really what happens. When the downstream slows down, you have to retry. Then, when a cache miss happens, you again retry. You fall back to a database. All of this adds time. That is why latency is important. What we are going to do today is considering latency as a route plan. We are going to take each and every hop, make sure there is a budget assigned to each hop, and see how we can get the journey better and make sure one station is not acting as a bottleneck for your complete journey. Today, the title of our discussion is, "From Fanout to Fast: How Do We Build an API within sub-100 milliseconds in a Distributed Environment?" If you are a senior engineer, I will give you concrete patterns which you can go back and apply. If you are an architect, let's look at some of the tradeoffs and system constraints. If you are a leader, let's make sure you have enough information so you can prioritize what is right for the team.
I'm a staff engineer at eBay. I have nearly two decades of experience in the IT industry. Lately, most of my involvement is towards building low latency systems which are scalable and reliable. From my experience, one thing is very sure, building a low latency system is doable once, but if you have to keep it the way that it is always, then it needs a lot of engineering. That's where the real engineering is. Let's see how we can do that. This is why a repeatable process is important. We don't have any quick shortcuts to get it done.
The Cost of a Millisecond
Let's understand, what is the cost of a millisecond. When you compare 120 versus 80, it doesn't sound too dramatic. Users don't experience latency as numbers, they experience it as friction. Friction really compounds. What do we do about it? What we are going to do is we are going to see how we can take the complete request path and divide it into some components or parts and make sure we cap each part with a budget. We also know that when scale comes into picture, your latency drifts. Have you seen the scenario where the system that you are building, let's say you put up a cap limit of your latency to be like 30. This is in a normal scenario. When peak traffic hits, your graph suddenly bumps up to 60. When there is a dependency wobble, you see that the latency shoots up again to 120.
There's no steady graph, but there is always a bump here and there. What has changed? There is no change in your code. The code has remained the same throughout. What has actually changed is the frictions that happen, is the systems which are going down, is the retries which are happening, your thread contention, your queuing, all of these aspects have added to this. A better way to handle is to look at the complete request journey.
Outline
Here is what we will cover. We'll start off with assigning a budget to latency, and make sure every hop has its own budget. Then we'll take a look into a complete journey, and see all the things that could go wrong. We'll see a scenario and how that could be fixed. We'll move on to tradeoffs. Then, without measurement, there is no success. We don't know how far we are without measuring. We'll look at that. We'll look at what the future holds, and we'll wrap it up.
Chapter 1: Latency Budgets - Defining and Managing Performance Targets
Latency budget. This is nothing but what your goal is versus what your system design is supporting. Let's say you want to build a recommendation engine which needs to respond within 50 milliseconds, because it's going to be used in multiple different components in your pages, exposed in emails and everything. How is your system design supporting this? That's what we need to see. How does it help, actually? When you have a concrete plan, it helps you with two things. One is prioritization. You don't really need to spend 100 milliseconds on a nice-to-have if you already know what is your cap limit. The other thing is alignment. It makes better alignment between the different teams. We don't need to explain each team between the product, the engineering, your quality teams about various aspects, because everybody comes to an alignment with one cause that they have to deliver things at a low latency.
Now what we will do is we will take the complete path from the client to the way that the client can receive the response and divide it into sub-parts, and make sure each part does not take more than what it is allocated. Here is a rough estimate of how we could break this down. There are a few things where we can utilize some buffer, but there are a few things which you cannot utilize a buffer. The edge layer, there's nothing we could do about it. Most of the content pull up your TLS, and the initial routing needs to happen here, which is going to take time, and you have to give it that. Let's cap it with 10 milliseconds. The next one comes the gateway. That's where your authentication and throttling happens, and you have to give it a 5 millisecond. Then next comes the application logic.
This is where it can be done in a single microservice or more. Just a pointer here. I think we have been overusing the terms of microservice where teams have started to really subdivide it into so many services that what could be done by one service is being done by four now. What we are forgetting is the network hop, which is involved in all of these things. We cap it at 30. Then the next one is the data access layer, where you definitely need an entity service, which is actually writing to your database, which could be whatever database that you're choosing. Then comes the buffer. It's better to save some buffer. Here we are adding 10 to 15 milliseconds as a buffer just to make sure there is enough time. Reality exists, so whenever there is a delay, you are just serving your buffer to make sure you have that time with you.
Chapter 2: The Request Journey - Tracing the Path of a Fast Request
Next, we look at a sample journey, a request journey, and see how things can go wrong in this journey. This is simple, considering we already saw the budget allocation. Your request travels from the client to the edge, and then the authentication, then it moves to your application logic, your persistence layer, and the way back. Now some teams don't realize that there is a component for serialization when you send your response back. That is where the JSON payload translations happen. Sometimes they wonder, why is my application logic fast, but my API itself isn't? This is one reason. Having seen the path, where does the latency hide in all of these things? The network hop. When we take the network hop, we have the TLS handshake, the connection pools, we have DNS lookups, everything. What I would suggest is, if it's possible, removing one hop saves a lot of time than actually rewriting thousands of code.
If you think about this, so let's say we have an item service, which needs to call a couple of other services, like the item, detail service, which calls the seller details to fetch all the seller details. Then the feedback rating, the feedback reviews, the completed text of it, the image URL, everything. It has to call a number of downstream services. Now if each service takes a particular time, so now it is important to see whether we need to talk to all of these services synchronously or asynchronously, and how much of it is actually exposed to the outside clients. If it is an internal service, do we want to use gRPC? What that helps with, it helps with communication between two services, which could be faster if there is more data payload with sharing. If it is a REST service and if it is public-facing, then it makes sense to use JSON, because it's more meaningful when you read it.
The other thing is serialization. As I said, when your payloads are increasing, you have to pay for serialization. What can happen? For example, if I'm returning item details, I have a lot of information with me, title, description, SKU details, what is my last transaction, who bought my last item, so many information. Do I have to send all of this information for my client? My clients for an item service, could be search, could be cart, could be checkout, could be an email, could be some metrics. All of these clients, do all of them need the same information? Is there some customization which could be done based on who the client is? Do you need to use a REST service or do you want to use a GraphQL, because it is a read service. All of these discussions need to be done and decided. These are some things which could hide your latency.
Cold caches. What if there is a cache miss at the wrong moment? Then you have to fall back to the database, which adds up your latency. DB query shape. There are a few queries. Like, if you miss the tuning of the queries, if you miss the constraints, if the constraints are not built right, then it is going to take time, and you end up tuning it at the wrong moment after you are live. These are some things to be checked beforehand. Queuing and contention comes into play when we are using threads. If a downstream fails, the queue size increases, the thread contention increases. Now eventually you try to retry because you have not got the response. Your request comes pouring in. Now you have a lot of things to handle and the system eventually fails. Then the dependencies. When you have more dependencies, your total SLA is dependent on it, because that's from the slowest downstream that you are calling. Observability. If you're adding too much log, where is your tracing information? How much are you tracing? Are you doing 1%? Are you doing more than that? All these tiny pieces make a huge impact.
Chapter 3: Scenarios and Fixes - Addressing Common Latency Pitfalls
Now let's take a scenario and look at the fixes for it. Here is the case when we faced that. The p95 was looking fine, but the users still timed out. What happened was we got issues raised, from one of the clients, saying, I'm getting a lot of timeouts. When we look at our dashboard, our dashboard is green. We don't see pretty much. We don't really see that, because we are taking in billions of calls. For the client, they have millions of calls. Then even a small failure, in this case, it was less than 1% for us, but nearly 1% for them. If you take the example of the item service, if it's coming from the checkout, then every single transaction is valuable. Any single transaction, we don't want to result in a failure. That's exactly what we wanted to look at. How do we face this?
How do we investigate this problem? How do we solve this problem? When you're having your majority works, your p99 works, your p95 works, but that's where, in your p99, it's not the way that it has to. First of all, let's see how we went about investigating this. We need to take from the client how much logs they have. Try to map those into your system. Like, are you able to trace it out? This is why, if there are leaders in the group, it is important to make sure you have added all the observability metrics for your services, because there is no time after having an incident that you go back and add all of these things. Now, if you have not built dashboards for your p99, this is the time to build that. If you're having those dashboards, look at it. Now, what is the difference between a successful transaction and where it has timed out?
What is the bottleneck that you're seeing here? It could be some downstream is not returning, the cache lookup was a failure, we had to go back, retried so many times, it didn't work. What is that exact problem? Note down all those problems that you're seeing and compare it with the dashboards that you have. Does it correlate? Are you looking at your thread health? Are you looking at your queue size? Does it correlate somewhere? Are you looking at your DB dashboards. Did you receive peak load during that time? Did you look at the cache dashboards? Are you having cache misses? Are the cache calls increased? Look at all of that information which you have and see what corresponds. Now when you look at the cost, it's always tempting to say that it can be the retries that we did, or it is the cache request which has failed.
There can be so many causes which is not really evident at the first glance, and those could be retry amplification. I've seen some of the codes when reviewing. Every time there is a retry, they increase the retry timeout. First time it is 500, second time they add it to 1,000. What is the benefit of this? If you want to build a high latency system and you retry, you're capping it at 500 and 1,000, you're not in the game. Your service is already going to lose it. Make sure your retries make sense. If you're looking up from cache, if it is Redis Cache, usually it responds in 5 milliseconds. Do you want to cap it at 8 or 10, and then do a retry? Don't wait for 50 milliseconds and do a retry. Probability of you capping it lower and then doing a retry might result in a better one.
Maybe you are reaching a different pod. The other one would be thread pool starvation. Here, if an application is using just one thread pool for the entire journey, it has a good potential to bring the system down. We'll talk more in detail about thread pool in the coming slides. The next is database tail latency. There are situations where database is taking more time, maybe bad query, maybe you hit a wrong shard, hotspots, things like that. Observability gaps. You're logging too much of information. Then your GC or the JVM pauses. What do we do about it? In our case, we did three things, which actually helped us. The one is payload reduction. We were retaining a lot of information. Look at your maps. We had a key-value pair map, which was having user-related information. It had thousands of keys in it. We were returning this to 400-plus applications.
Not every application actually needs this. They probably need only 5 or 10 keys, but we were returning everything because that's all associated with the user. We didn't have the ability to request for a certain case. Now, once we changed that, that was helpful. Look at your response. Scan through each field one by one. Look to see if everything is making sense for the client, from the client perspective. Then, your retry discipline. Retry only if you're making idempotent calls. Here, again, you have to cap your limit and make sure you're giving thread pools separately for each of the downstream. That is what it is with thread pool guardrails.
Chapter 4: Tradeoffs - Balancing Speed with Other Priorities
I think now we started off with why a millisecond is important. We looked at budget. We also saw a request journey. How things could go wrong in that journey. Now it is time to look at some of the tradeoffs that are available. The first one is async fanout. We know what fanout is. Like one request turning into multiple. When we have such a fanout scenario, there are multiple options by which you can execute. One is doing things serially, the obvious way: one after the other. Or, see how much you could parallelize it in a couple of threads. Like whether you want to do two things at once. Then maybe your output needs to be fed for the other downstream calls. You take a judgment about it and do it. Then, if you're doing asynchronously, you also have options of running it in a separate background thread, or you want to drop an event.
Or let's say you make a fire and forget call. Like, what are the options that you have? What is making sense for your application at that moment? Maybe let's take an example to understand this better. If we take placing on an order as an example, when you take place order, there are a number of things which have to happen immediately, like after you hit on that place order button. One thing is you're supposed to receive your order confirmation email, the inventory has to get reduced. Your payment has to be made. You have to detect from the buyer, credit to the seller. Your metrics, you need to drop the metrics. Maybe giving this information to a couple of other downstream services which actually takes in this for the feedback and other things. Now when there are a lot of things, not all of these things have to happen serially.
When you take the item service response, where item has to call image, call seller details, call feedback and everything, again here there are a couple of things which needs to happen at the moment for sending the response back, but the couple of things need not happen synchronously. That is why we need to decide what needs to happen when, and see if you can move certain parts below the radar. When you want to do that asynchronously, making your configuration for a thread pool is very important. What is a thread pool? Let's compare it with, maybe you have a fixed number of workers in your kitchen. Let's say two workers. You have orders piling in. What happens? The two workers may not be able to do all the orders, and your orders are piling. Let's say you have very few orders, there's a very good chance that they bump onto each other.
Now, having this right configuration is very important. How could we go about it? What could help us to define what is the right configuration? This is where we need to check, what is our application doing? Is it an I/O intense work? Is it doing an I/O intense work, or is it doing a CPU intense work? Some examples could be, for CPU intense work, are you doing any algorithm processing? Are you doing image processing? Are you validating fields using your rules engine? Are you doing any encryption, decryption, or maybe tokenization? What are you actually doing? If you're doing all of these works, it is CPU intense work. Closer to your CPU cores, if you're using an 8-core system, maybe 8 threads, you should be good with this, with a normal load. Let's say if you're doing an I/O intense work, calling your REST service, calling your downstream, or waiting because you don't get the response, you have to wait.
You're looking at file. You're making a cache call, database call. All of these are I/O intense work. Since there is a waiting time involved, we need to make sure that you're adding more threads, taking this into account. A small example could be, if you are waiting for 80 milliseconds, and that particular downstream is capable of giving you a response in 20, the formula is the number of cores that you have times 1 plus 80 by 20, which nearly comes to about 40 threads. When you're having your CPU intense work, you are only at 8. If you're having an I/O intense work, you are at 40 now. Using the right number is very helpful. Your service could be doing both. Then you need to carefully check what your service is doing and make sure your limits are set based on that. This is no hard and fixed number.
It is more as a starting point where you should actually fine-tune it based on your results, based on the dashboards that you're seeing. Go back and fine-tune this. Also, there is one more important thing to understand, is, what is your incoming traffic? How much concurrent requests are you going to receive? That is also important to determine this thread count. A simple way could be from Little's Law, where, what is your latency? Latency into number of requests per second. If your latency is 50 milliseconds for your service and you are expected to get 500, then it's about 25 concurrent requests that you are seeing. This is even before the retries that you have to do, system getting abnormal, and things like that. This is just a starting number. Make sure you cap your threads at the right number. Along with the thread pool, the other thing which we need to be careful about is queuing.
Once you have set some number with your thread pool, if there are more requests, you need to make sure your queue size is also right, because that's where the next requests are going to be queued in. Now, let's say both your thread pool and your queue is full, then, what next? You need some rejection policy set up. What is your rejection policy? Have you carefully analyzed your rejection policy? Are you going to outright reject your request? Are you going to pick up any low priority work and remove that from your queue? What is that? You have to define that correctly, which will help you. Also, the other thing could be the memory, which you have to check, and things like that.
Next comes the caching. We don't expect everything to be returned by the service. You don't need to go to database to return every information through the service. There are moments that you have to leverage using cache. What type of a cache? What data do you put in your cache? What is the key that you're going to use in your cache? That's where all these engineering concepts lie. Are you going to use a single cache to look up all the information? Let's say, for the item information, do you want to add feedback into the cache? Is the review itself making sense or do you want to add the feedback score? Is adding item description making sense or do you want to add the price. What is making sense? What is the time? What is the benefit this is going to give? Of course, it's going to give you latency importance.
Because 5 milliseconds versus 30, and that's the tradeoff. Make sure you are building cache, which are multi-level, if possible. You don't want to make your cache bulky also. The payload in the cache shouldn't be bulky. You want to make sure that you are giving the right data, checking the payload size as well. Make sure it's not like more than a few KB. Using a cache is not going to solve all the problems until you have invalidation set right. If you're not invalidating your data as the data changes, if you're not making it accurate, then there is a chance that you're not showing the clients the right information. Then there is no point in using the cache. Invalidation becomes very important. How are you going to invalidate this data? There are a couple of options. If you set a fixed TTL, then till that time, the data is there and then it moves away.
Is that the practical approach that you want to take? Sometimes you want to change it when the actual data is being changed by the user. Then you want an event-based approach. You also have like version-based. Choose version-based only if you are sure about, is there a reliable plan to choose the exact version because you don't want to get into trouble of choosing what is the right version to be picked up. There is also another concept of stale-while-revalidate. This is where you know the information is stale, but it's ok to return that. You have to determine who are your clients. You don't want to have a checkout reading price from a cache. You want the most accurate information. You need to go to the DB for it. Choose what is your application doing, the responsibility of the application. How much delay is your client acceptable? That could be different between different clients.
If you're sending an email, it's fine to build something which is not really accurate, which can be eventually consistent. That is fine. Choose based on your clients as well. Then, we also have the option of using group-based, where it is best advised for derived or aggregated views. A general rule of thumb, maybe if you're experimenting it for the first time, will be start it with a TTL and then fine-tune it. Once you fine-tune it, use the event-based approach.
You know that you want to cache. You know how you can have the right data. Now you need to understand that data classification is important. You don't want to get into any of those compliance issues where you have added the wrong data, especially when you're in the financial industry. What are the data classifications available? Public data, anything which is public. When you search for an item, you get all this listing information. You get seller details, like what is the seller's name? Where is he selling this item from? These details. These are all publicly available. It's ok to cache it. What about internal data? Some of those unique IDs. You have UUID. Do you want to expose it outside? What about your item ID? Do you want to expose it outside? These are things that need to be determined. This is something that you need to work with your InfoSec team to understand what is the organization's level of classification, and how much they want to expose it, add it to a cache, and things like that.
What about confidential data, like name, address, phone number, things like this? Definitely, we need to encrypt it or tokenize it. Whatever is the best fit or recommendation from the InfoSec team. Now this is a time where we need to think, does it make sense to add it in cache? We are going to cache because we want to reduce the time. Now if you're adding a confidential data in the cache, be mindful that you need to pay for decrypting it or de-tokenizing it. Are you ready to accept that? Is your system ok to do that? Then, about classified information. Your SSN number, your passport number, all of this information, a strict no. You cannot cache this data.
Next, we'll move on to circuit breakers. Circuit breakers are very helpful. It helps you contain your problem area to a specific region. It doesn't allow the entire system to be brought down. Instead, it contains the problem in one specific area. In that way, circuit breaker is very important. If you take a mental model. What happens, let's say when a downstream fails, and you have 10 downstream calling, and one of the downstream suddenly starts failing, the queue starts to build up, your thread pool queue is also high, your backup queue is also high. Now, as per your system logic, you try to retry and you also have incoming requests. There is a complete possibility of system being down. You are actually having a self-inflicted failure. Even if there is a request which does not need this downstream A, the request could fail for them. A circuit breaker helps in that.
It helps you contain that. It is important to use this. When the circuit breaker is open, it's not going to allow any request. It's going to allow time for the particular downstream to prepare itself, to come back up. When it partially opens up to send a few requests is to see whether it succeeds. Once it succeeds, it sends the remaining requests. This is very helpful.
Then, what about fallbacks? Maybe we could take this example. When you're viewing an item on a search, you actually see this hottest item trigger, or you see this, five people are viewing onto this item. I have 10 purchased this item two hours back, or an hour back. All of these are hot information which are available. You need to be more accurate to give this information, or maybe nearly accurate. What if we don't have this? What if the service which returns this information are failing? Then you probably go and use your fallback text, which is like, maybe, yes, this is a hot item. Many people are viewing. We had more transactions. Don't give the exact number. This is the use of fallback. Consciously decide based on what your service is doing. Check if there are any places where you could use this tactic of a fallback.
It doesn't have to be a static text. It could also be defaulting to certain numbers based on the situation. The other one is data partitioning, which is mostly underrated. The main theme is to avoid hotspots. Why do we want to avoid hotspots? Because we want to distribute the traffic to all the shards possible. When you're deciding about partitions, make sure you choose a key which will give you a unique distribution across. Don't choose something like, I'm going to put all my hot sellers into one shard, like the top sellers into one shard. When there is a specific season, for example, Thanksgiving in the U.S., it's going to make all the requests go into that shard. It does not make sense to divide your sharding based on this theme. Rather use a key which is very generic: maybe the ID of the user itself, maybe his login name.
Use things which are generic, and make sure that gives a default distribution or a common distribution into all the shards. Sometimes due to regulations, it is also required that you need to split your data based on the region. Like EU region, you need to have a separate shard. U.S. region, you need to have a separate shard. This does not solve the problem because, again, if you have a seasonal event, it's going to go into that particular shard. That is why it is important to subdivide it based on the other keys that you have.
Chapter 5: Measuring Speed - Tools and Metrics for Performance
Now that we have seen a quick recap, we started with why is latency important, why is being fast important. We saw a request journey. We saw a list of tradeoffs. Now, until we measure, we don't know how good we are performing. That is why measuring things is really important. A measure could tell you how long things went well, or did not go well. Tracing will tell you why something happened. If you're not having tracing, you are missing out on something, on identifying why the problem even happened. Tracing is very important. If you haven't built it, it's time to actually build this. There could be themes, with the teams coming up saying, "My Redis is failing. My DB looks fine, but my cache calls are failing." How are we figuring out all of these things? Only because we have tracing built. You are able to take just the unique ID, look through the complete request, and see where exactly the problem has happened.
If you are able to identify, that's because you have tracing built in. Let's move on to having SLOs. Before maybe going into SLOs, I want to touch base on SLIs, service level indicators. They are like direct metric information. Let's say you are getting 100k requests per second. Then let's say around 95k requests have succeeded, and the remaining 5k were not successful. This 95% is your success rate, or your application's availability is just 95%. The same thing, you could track for your error rates, you could track for a specific error also. You have that specific downstream, you can tie it based on the feedback system, what is the availability of the feedback system. All of those things could be done. You could also have measures like, how many of my requests is responding well within 200 milliseconds? If the number was 99.8, then that is the time that you have done it.
How do we tie this to a goal? That's where SLO comes in, service level objective. Let's say you want to make sure in a 30-day period, I want the availability of my system to be 99.9. Then that is your SLO. What happens when you set this up? You are going to be alerted. The team is going to be alerted. The leaders are going to know, when an SLO, the buffer, the time that you had, if you're utilizing that buffer in a week, which you had set for a month, then it is time to pause on all your velocity works that you're doing, and first fix the system. Did I make a wrong judgment about the SLO? My SLO number itself, did I do a mistake in configuring that, or should I go back and check my application service? Check the path, where is it going wrong?
Has it been happening consistently? Then there is something to do about it. Then there is some refactoring which needs to be done. There is no one solution which can fix it. You have to do small things at every journey to make sure that you're getting it right. This is where SLO is very helpful. Thread pool observability. We saw about thread pools and the importance of thread pool. Now, if we don't have an observability dashboard, you are not going to know whether your queue is getting built up. Am I getting an alert for it? Setting up alerts, before that, you need a dashboard. We need dashboards for active threads. What is my queue size? What is a completed task count? Then, what is my rejection rate? If I have information for all of these, then it's helpful for me to fine-tune during the next iteration.
Chapter 6: Culture and Future - Building a Performance-First Mindset
Now that we have seen about how we could measure, how we could fix it, we have seen a lot about technical things going wrong, technical aspects going wrong. Now it is time to look at the human side of things. What is within our control? What can we do as a team to get this done? That's where culture comes into picture. During planning, are we talking about SLA? Are we talking about latency? Are we talking about what is our goal? During retrospective, did we talk about the last incident which happened? What was the last issue where you had to come back online and check things on a weekend? Did you have to spend your night over it? What was that incident? Are we discussing it as a team? Are we trying to fix our dashboards? Are we trying to fix our alerts? I know that teams set up alerts only in Slack, and your Slack thread is filled up with all these alert messages, nobody is looking into it.
Are we looking into that? These are things collectively which a team needs to take up, like during your planning session, during your retrospective. This is nothing but performance and review. What are some of the anti-patterns which we need to avoid? Considering staging data. Let's say you're doing a load test in staging and taking that number for your production. That's no way the same. Your environment in your lower region is not the same as what you're doing in production. Do not take that as a benchmark. If you're going live, maybe start with 1%, 2% traffic. Or even better, start it with traffic mirroring, if that is allowed. You mirror your traffic and see whether your new flow that you've added is performing at the same level as earlier in production. Is it delaying your latency? Is there something that you need to restructure? The other things could be synchronous logging, where you're logging too much information.
What is the future holding for us? There are a lot of things, like capabilities around adaptive routing where routing could be done to regions which are having less traffic. AI-assisted predictions, you can have models to predict, this is the hot cache. Make sure you can warm it up beforehand. You can use predictive warming. Edge-native executions, all of these are in the future.
The 48-Hour Playbook
Let me give you some information which you could try before the weekend. When you go back, what could you do? Choose a simple flow in your application, from end to end. Note it down. Work with your lead. Is there any journey that could be removed? Is there any duplicate logic? I've also seen these patterns when I'm reviewing code between the teams. If there is a dependency X, and you have three flows, like A is calling B, B is calling C. You always have this X which is getting called in all the flows. You tend to have that one service which everybody wants. What do we go about it? Is there anything that you can do about changing it? These are all things that you can check. Now, instrument it, and budget. You'll note down what is the graph. If you don't have a p99 dashboard, create one.
Note down what was the current latency. If it is at 500, yes, note it down. Look at the different junctions, your paths. Note down what each path has taken up. Now, where do you want to go from here? What is your budget? Cap it. Make improvements. Remove that unnecessary call. Rephrase it. Add thread pools. Parallelize it, if it's possible. Add cache if it's not there. Do all of these things, and take a result out of it. Run an L&P and take a result out of it. Now you can check the before and after metrics. I would like to leave with one quote. We are what we repeatedly do, so excellence is not an act, but a habit. I hope we inculcate that as a habit.

articles.title: Huawei says it can build better memory chips than Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron, but the proof is still to come
articles.text:
Forward-looking: Tech giant Huawei will reportedly present a white paper on its in-house HBM chip design that some industry insiders speculate could outperform existing products from market leaders Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The presentation will be made at the International Solid-State Circuits Conference in San Francisco on February 16, 2027.
Huawei's novel HBM design reportedly supports twice the data-pin density of the current products from the three leading players. According to Bloomberg, the new interface uses 4,096 data pins split across 64 channels - twice the width of the 2,048-bit interface of existing HBM products from Samsung and Hynix.
To pack twice as many connections into the same physical footprint, Huawei is reportedly using five-layer wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding to fuse memory controllers directly onto stacked DRAM dies. In theory, the new architecture could deliver higher memory bandwidth and better efficiency, allowing more data to be transferred to the processor at the same time while consuming less power.
If the theoretical improvements translate into real-world gains, Huawei's HBM chips could be better suited for model training, AI inference, data ingestion, and other complex tasks than competing products. However, five-layer wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding could be difficult to scale, especially without access to advanced lithography, so it remains to be seen how Huawei will overcome the challenge.
Despite the promise of faster and more efficient HBM technology, it's important to exercise caution about Huawei's new design, as tech companies - both hardware manufacturers and software vendors - are known to announce their research results extremely early in the developmental phase, often without an actual working prototype or a sandbox build for external partners.
Huawei's move to design its own high-bandwidth memory is part of a greater push from Beijing to establish domestic semiconductor capabilities amid crippling trade restrictions by the US, which prevent established chipmakers and memory manufacturers from supplying hardware to mainland China, ostensibly over national security concerns.
Despite facing a multitude of sanctions from the US government over potential national security concerns, Huawei has gone from strength to strength in recent years, developing its own processors, AI accelerators, data center supernode architectures, operating systems, AI and Development Frameworks, and domestic EDA tools to bypass US export controls and Entity List restrictions.

articles.title: There are a few in-store Black Friday carrier deals, if you hunt for them
articles.text:
I headed to my local mall this Black Friday to check out the in-store carrier deals and see if there was anything worth venturing out for. Unfortunately, there wasn’t a ton.
Now, before we get into this, I should note that I went right at opening so I could get a good look at most of the deals before the rush (hence why there aren’t a lot of people in the background).
I should also add that I probably missed some deals, purely because when I asked about them, the salespeople wouldn’t share every deal and instead pushed me into specific offers based on my device and current plan, which was annoying if I wanted general ideas while shopping around.
I will give credit where it’s due, as Freedom was the one that had every available in-store plan listed at the door, so you could see the options.
Freedom Mobile
Honestly, Freedom had a few in-store Black Friday deals that caught my attention, and they were actually displayed:
- $25/15GB CAN/US when you bring your number to Freedom
- $35/40GB CAN/US/MEX with 1GB of Roam Beyond data for 120+ destinations globally (when you buy a phone) (avail. online)
- $40/70GB CAN/US/MEX with 1GB of Roam Beyond data for 120+ destinations globally (avail. online)
- $45/125GB CAN/US/MEX with 5GB of Roam Beyond data for 120+ destinations globally (avail. online)
Notably, most of these are already available online, so you can probably save yourself the trip into a store.
Rogers/Fido/Chatr
Rogers had a fair amount of deals across the board. Now, they only told me of a few 5G+ plans that were being offered, but some of the deals honestly weren’t bad if you wanted to switch. The one I’m most surprised about is Fido not getting the Pixel 11 down to $0/mo, since from my experience, the Pixels normally get great deals around black friday and the holidays.
Rogers
- Samsung Galaxy S26 as low as $0/month (avail. online)
- iPhone 17 as low as $0/mo with an eligible trade-in
- Add a line with a new phone and get up to $300 for every eligible additional line activation
- Get up to $200 in credits when you activate Rogers Xfinity TV + internet
- Rogers: $45/60GB BYOD plan with roaming
- Rogers: $60/100GB BYOD plan with roaming
Oddly, the Rogers store had a sign advertising a $40/100GB CAN/U.S., but the reps didn’t talk about it at all, so it’s not entirely clear how that deal works.
Chatr/Fido
- Chatr: prepaid plans starting at $35/30GB Canada-wide with autopay data bonus (avail. online)
- Fido: Google Pixel 11 as low as $9.99/mo on select plans (avail. online)
Bell/Virgin
Honestly, Bell didn’t have a ton of advertised deals like the others. They kept them rotating on a digital board, which was kind of annoying, but their sub-brand, Virgin, did have a few that intrigued me. I also should note that all plans are 5G unless otherwise noted.
Bell
- Samsung Galaxy S26 from $1/mo
- iPhone 17 from $1/mo wth six months of Apple Music free
- Gigabit Fibe 1.5 for $70/mo when bundled with select mobility plans with Autopay (also gets you a $100 prepaid Mastercard)
- Plans starting at $40/mo
- $200 Prepaid Mastercard with eligible internet and TV bundle
Virgin
- $50/60GB CAN/US/MEX (avail. online)
- $45/60GB (avail. online)
Telus/Koodo
Telus was another brand that didn’t explicitly advertise deals as much as I thought it would, but the store did have some options available, especially from their sub-brand Koodo.
Telus
- $60/60GB of 5G data
- $55/15GB of 5G data
- $65/100GB of 5G data
- iPhone 17 Pro for $0/mo with Bring It Back and trade-in
Koodo
- $30/15GB 4G with a Koodo prepaid bonus
- $40/10GB of 5G data
- $35/20GB of 5G data
- $45/60GB of 5G data (avail. online)
- $55/100GB of 5G data (avail. online)
Best Buy Express
The Best Buy Express store had a few notable offers:
- $200 bonus gift card with eligible internet and TV bundle
- $300 bonus gift card with iPhone 17 Pro Max
- Save up to $400 on select laptops
- Save up to $150 on the Sony WH-CH720N headphones, which cost $99.99
Other Deals
T Booth Wireless
- iPhone Air 256GB: $10/mo
- Samsung S26 256GB: $5/mo
- Google Pixel 11: $0/mo
Wirelesswave
- Samsung Galaxy S26 FE: $0/mo
- Samsung Galaxy S26 FE 128GB: $1/mo with Return IT and $200 to spend in-store
- Samsung Galaxy S26 256GB: $0/mo with Return It and $300 to spend in-store
- Samsung Galaxy Ultra 256GB: $25/mo with Return It and $300 to spend in-store
- iPhone Air 256GB: $5/mo
- Google Pixel 11 256GB: $0/mo OR $1/mo with return it and $300 to spend in-store
What you should know
Honestly, I was more surprised by the lack of advertising for a lot of the deals. While some were displayed, I had to call back later to confirm a lot of deals because they weren’t explicitly mentioned or posted outside the store. Some used a rotating digital board, which, while it works, also really limits what the brand can display, in my opinion. I did like how Freedom and Rogers displayed deals, purely because I could see the (honestly pretty decent) offers.
You can check out all of our Black Friday coverage here.

articles.title: YouTube sur Android Auto : cette nouveauté vidéo va tout changer en voiture
articles.text:
Regarder YouTube au volant va être possible avant l'heure. Enfin, à condition que la voiture soit à l'arrêt, naturellement.
Morphe est un outil open source qui modifie des applications Android pour y ajouter des fonctions ou en retirer la publicité (YouTube, YouTube Music et d'autres services de streaming), est disponible en version 2.4.0. Cette mise à jour concerne les versions modifiées de Reddit, de YouTube et de YouTube Music. La principale nouveauté ici, c'est la lecture de vidéos YouTube sur Android Auto.
YouTube dans le lanceur d'Android Auto
D'après les notes de version, un nouveau correctif permet à une version de YouTube modifié par Morphe d'être reconnue comme une « application vidéo pour véhicule à l'arrêt ». L'application apparaît alors dans le tiroir d'applications d'Android Auto, et il est possible de regarder des vidéos, tant que la voiture ne roule pas. La fonction est pour l'instant proposée en accès anticipé. Elle est aussi compatible avec DriveDeck.
Justement, Google travaille de son côté sur une fonctionnalité comparable pour les smartphones sous Android 17 ou version ultérieure. Cette mise à jour, officielle cette fois-ci, est attendue d'ici la fin de l'année.
Aujourd'hui, sur Android Auto, les utilisateurs peuvent seulement écouter le son des vidéos YouTube, et l'application doit être pilotée depuis le téléphone qui est, on le rappelle, interdit au volant et désormais passible de retrait de permis.
D'autres correctifs concernent l'affichage. L'un détecte quand YouTube est affiché sur l'écran du véhicule et adapte la disposition aux écrans horizontaux. Un autre masque la barre de navigation pour mieux exploiter l'espace disponible. Morphe permet également à des alternatives à Android Auto, comme DriveDeck, Gearslip, AARE et Flywheel, de parcourir la bibliothèque de YouTube Music.
Un mode Ghost et d'autres changements
La mise à jour apporte aussi des modifications qui ne sont pas liées à Android Auto. Le changement majeur est un mode Ghost, comparable à la navigation privée. Les vidéos regardées n'apparaissent pas dans l'historique et n'influencent ainsi pas les recommandations. Il peut être activé pour toute une session, ou pour une seule vidéo via le bouton à trois points, sans déconnexion du compte.
Côté YouTube Music, les paroles peuvent maintenant s'afficher en plein écran, avec la prise en charge de polices personnalisées. Il est également possible de désactiver les gestes qui font changer de morceau en glissant le doigt sur la pochette. Un bouton de diffusion direct vers Sonos a enfin été ajouté. Il permet d'envoyer le son vers des enceintes UPnP de Sonos ou d'autres marques, à condition qu'elles soient connectées au même réseau Wi-Fi.
Source : Android Authority

articles.title: pCloud confirms password manager hack after suspicious login alerts
articles.text:
The pCloud Pass password manager suffered a cyberattack, with users reporting that unknown devices had connected to their accounts even with two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled.
The incident was first reported by numerous pCloud customers who began receiving email notifications informing them that a new device had connected to their pCloud Pass accounts.
In two Reddit threads, customers worldwide reported receiving notifications warning that an unfamiliar device named "pd" connected to their account from the IP address 45.131.244.7 in Luxembourg, which users say belongs to pCloud's own infrastructure.
Several customers reported receiving the alerts despite having two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled on their accounts. However, when customers checked their accounts for connected devices, some found no unfamiliar devices listed.
Other pCloud customers reported receiving the same notifications despite never having used the company's password manager, including one who said the notification was sent to an email address associated with a pCloud storage account they had requested be deleted almost a year ago.
In response to the reports, pCloud confirmed its password manager had suffered a cyberattack, which the company says was quickly contained.
"A cyberattack targeting pCloud Pass occurred, which was promptly contained by the pCloud team," reads pCloud's statement.
"Unfortunately, a small number of pCloud Pass user email addresses were exposed and login attempts were made. Our system sends a notification automatically to each of these addresses."
pCloud says the attack was isolated to its password manager and that its cloud storage services were not affected.
The company says that passwords, notes, and other information stored in pCloud Pass have not been compromised, explaining that the data is encrypted on customers' devices and can only be decrypted using their master passwords.
However, pCloud did not disclose whether any encrypted password vaults were accessed or stolen during the attack.
This matters because threat actors who obtain encrypted password vaults could try to crack them offline without being subject to the service's login rate limits or two-factor authentication protections.
This was demonstrated in the 2022 LastPass breach, when attackers stole backups containing encrypted password vaults.
Researchers later linked the breach to cryptocurrency thefts in which attackers are believed to have cracked weak or reused master passwords to access stored cryptocurrency wallet private keys and seed phrases.
A reader who contacted BleepingComputer also noted that the "Open settings" link in the email notifications pointed to passqa1.pcloud.com, which appears to be a quality assurance (QA) environment rather than the password manager's production website.
BleepingComputer confirmed that the link pointed to the same hostname in a copy of the notification shared with us.
In its statement, pCloud also discussed how advancements in artificial intelligence are accelerating the discovery of software vulnerabilities, but did not specifically state that this was an AI-powered attack.
The company is also warning customers to watch for phishing attacks, stating that it will never ask for their master passwords or recovery words over email, phone, or chat.
The pCloud Pass incident is the latest in a series of cyberattacks impacting password managers this month.
Earlier in November, mSeven Software warned mSecure customers to change stored passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and remove passkeys after a hacker reportedly stole an encrypted customer database.
On Wednesday, 1Password disclosed a data breach after a threat actor compromised an employee's GitHub account and deployed malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data.
However, 1Password said customers' password vaults and the encryption keys protecting them were not compromised.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Payaza acquires Ghana’s Seesail to bring commerce tools, finance to Africa's small businesses
articles.text:
Nigerian payments infrastructure company Payaza has acquired Seesail Technologies, the Ghana-founded commerce platform for small businesses.
Payaza offers payment collection, payout and merchant tools to businesses in Africa and international markets. It handles card, mobile money and bank payments in more than 40 currencies and operates in more than 27 countries.
Disrupt Africa reported recently Payaza had been authorised by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) to provide payment gateway services, just weeks after getting regulatory approval in Zambia.
The deal to acquire Seesail will see the entire team join Shopaza, a Payaza product, and co-founder and CEO Victor Blavo becomes general manager for Africa.
“We watched Seesail from the inside through the payments they ran on Payaza. They built real traction with very little. We believe in the dream, and we are bringing the jet fuel so they can move as fast as they can,” said Seyi Ebenezer, CEO of Payaza.

articles.title: Por qué GTA 6 no permite volver a jugar las misiones
articles.text:
Rockstar Games confirmó que GTA 6 no incluirá una función para volver a jugar misiones ya completadas, una herramienta que sí estaba disponible tanto en GTA 5 como en Red Dead Redemption 2. La decisión responde a un conflicto directo con la estructura narrativa del juego, según explicó el estudio.
El director sénior de diseño de Rockstar Games, Scott Butchard, abordó el tema en una entrevista con Kotaku. Según su relato, la posibilidad de repetir misiones estuvo sobre la mesa durante las primeras etapas de desarrollo, pero el equipo decidió no incorporarla a medida que el proyecto avanzaba.
“La repetición de misiones fue sin duda algo que barajamos en las primeras fases del desarrollo, pero actualmente no la ofrecemos”, declaró Butchard en diálogo con el medio. “A medida que el juego iba tomando forma, nos pareció que entraba en conflicto con la historia que intentábamos contar”, agregó.
Las decisiones del jugador pesan sobre la trama
El argumento central de Rockstar gira en torno al peso de las decisiones del jugador dentro de la historia. Butchard sostuvo que volver a jugar misiones de forma aislada “restaba importancia a las decisiones” tomadas a lo largo de la partida, al describir esa dinámica como “quedarse al margen del juego”.
GTA 6 permite ramificaciones narrativas significativas: los jugadores pueden decidir si matan o perdonan a ciertos personajes, completar objetivos de distintas maneras y moldear el vínculo entre Jason y Lucía según sus propias acciones. Estas variables generan opciones de diálogo y escenas cinemáticas diferenciadas, un nivel de ramificación que explicaría la complejidad de implementar un sistema de repetición de misiones equivalente al de entregas anteriores.
El precedente de Red Dead Redemption 2
Red Dead Redemption 2 también ofrecía variaciones que afectaban el carácter de su protagonista, Arthur, aunque con un alcance menor al de las decisiones presentes en GTA 6. Ese título sí contaba con un menú de repetición de misiones, lo que marca una diferencia respecto al funcionamiento actual del nuevo lanzamiento.
Rockstar no descarta cambios futuros
Butchard fue preciso en su formulación: el juego “actualmente no admite” esta función, una frase que deja abierta la puerta a una eventual incorporación mediante una actualización posterior. Sin embargo, el estudio no confirmó ningún plan concreto en ese sentido.
La ausencia de esta herramienta generó controversia entre los jugadores, en particular porque GTA 6 incluye algunas de las misiones mejor valoradas de la franquicia, como la misión final del Capítulo 1. Dado que completar el juego puede demandar entre 50 y 100 horas, resulta poco probable que la mayoría de los usuarios reinicie la partida completa solo para revivir una secuencia puntual.
Aun si Rockstar no incorpora la función de manera oficial, existe la posibilidad de que la comunidad de desarrolladores de mods encuentre una solución alternativa cuando se lance la versión para computadoras, un paso que la compañía no ha confirmado todavía pero que se considera habitual en sus títulos anteriores.
El avance de la adaptación no oficial para PC
Entretanto, una versión no oficial de GTA 6 para computadoras continúa en desarrollo pese a los intentos de Take-Two Interactive y Rockstar Games por frenar su distribución, que ya incluyeron el cierre de más de 3.000 repositorios vinculados con el proyecto.
Según información difundida por comunidades de jugadores, la iniciativa, basada en una copia filtrada para Xbox Series, trasladó parte de su desarrollo a espacios privados y ya cuenta con las primeras modificaciones creadas por usuarios, además de un lanzador propio en preparación para facilitar su ejecución a quienes no tienen conocimientos técnicos avanzados.

articles.title: Vendu 115 euros par erreur, le Galaxy S26 Ultra a pourtant bien été livré par Amazon à quelques chanceux
articles.text:
Le Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra équipé de 256 Go de stockage est soudainement passé de 239 800 yens (environ 1 371 euros) à seulement 20 185 yens, soit à peine 115 euros. Cette vente flash involontaire a rapidement disparu du site, mais plusieurs acheteurs nippons confirment avoir pu passer commande et ont déjà reçu leur Galaxy S26 Ultra à ce prix dérisoire.
Grosse erreur de Samsung sur Amazon Japon
Généralement, lorsque ce genre d’erreur se produit sur le prix d’un produit, le commerçant invoque un bug logiciel pour rembourser les clients et annuler la commande. Mais cette fois, Amazon Japon a décidé de valider les achats effectués par les clients chanceux. Une aubaine donc quand on sait que le Galaxy S26 Ultra a été lancé à 1 469 euros et qu’on le trouve aujourd’hui autour de 1 000 euros. Amazon n’a pas communiqué officiellement sur cet incident, ce qui laisse penser qu’il s’agit bien d’une erreur de leur part qu’ils ont rapidement réglée.
Difficile de faire une meilleure affaire pour le Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra
Même lorsque le Galaxy S27 Ultra sortira, il n’y a aucune chance de trouver un Galaxy S26 Ultra neuf à ce prix. Pour rappel, le dernier smartphone haut de gamme de Samsung est équipé d’une puce Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, d’un capteur photo principal de 200 mégapixels et d’un téléobjectif de 50 mégapixels avec zoom optique 5x. Il est également certifié IP68, intègre le stylet S Pen et profite d’une batterie de 5 000 mAh qui se recharge à 60W.

articles.title: La calidad/precio no era solo una guerra de especificaciones. Nothing acaba de ganar con un móvil que reivindica algo más
articles.text:
Cuando alguien busca un móvil caro suele fijarse en las especificaciones, pero también en otros aspectos. El diseño y los materiales son importantes, porque un móvil bueno también debe parecerlo. ¿Y conforme descendemos de categoría? La atracción suele llevársela la relación entre la calidad y el precio. Que nos llevemos lo máximo por lo mínimo, aquí no importa tanto el diseño.
Nothing Phone (4a) Pro - Triple Cámara 50MP, Ultra Zoom 140x, Smartphone Unibody Metal, Batería Larga Duración, Carga Rápida 50W, AMOLED 144Hz, Glyph Bar, 8GB+128GB - Plata
Si algo tiene de rompedor Nothing es que cada uno de sus teléfonos es único. Ves un Nothing y lo sabes, cueste 600 euros o 300. Y esa pasión por distinguirse es justo el broche que necesita el Nothing Phone (4a) Pro, un móvil que pude analizar y que terminó sorprendiéndome porque lo tenía casi todo. Por eso me parece acertado que fuese uno de los ganadores en los Premios Xataka Verisure 2026.
El interior no tiene por qué estar reñido con la superficie
Cuando alguien me pide una recomendación suele añadir una cifra que acorta mucho la búsqueda: "que no cueste más de 300 euros". Hace un par de años resultaba más o menos sencillo encontrar un buen móvil que no rebasase el listón, con la crisis de la memoria RAM la búsqueda se ha complicado. Mucho. Tanto, que mi respuesta suele ser la misma: si te gastas un poco más, tendrás un teléfono capaz de aguantarte años.
Protege tu hogar frente a robos y ocupaciones con las cerraduras inteligentes de Verisure, disponibles como parte del sistema de alarma Verisure. Al margen de permitir abrir la puerta usando las llaves o desde el móvil, alertan ante cualquier intento de manipulación y transmiten la información a la unidad central de la compañía para generar un salto de alarma. Descubre la solución que mejor se ajusta a las necesidades de tu vivienda o negocio.
El Nothing Phone (4a) Pro ha sido una de mis recomendaciones más firmes de este año. Creo que equilibra a la perfección las características con el precio, por más que este haya subido durante los últimos meses. En su día me pareció una elección acertada por 429 euros en su oferta de lanzamiento, hoy es difícil encontrarlo por menos de 600 euros (en su versión de 12/256 GB, que salió por 549).
Nothing le tiene pillado el punto a la receta. Añade un conjunto de especificaciones de muy buen nivel, sin que sean lo máximo disponible; coloca una pantalla AMOLED de generosas dimensiones; la batería queda en la línea de lo razonable, y corona el conjunto con un envoltorio repleto de luces y con muy pocas sombras. El resultado es un móvil que sorprende la primera vez que te encuentras con él y que termina conquistándote cuando lo llevas en el bolsillo.
¿Por qué tener un móvil aburrido cuando puedes destacar con un diseño que se sale de lo común? Y todo sin abandonar la batalla de las características, porque en las gamas donde pelea Nothing este aspecto es vital. El Phone (4a) Pro es un luchador que puede medirse hasta con móviles el doble de caros. Sus especificaciones son inferiores, sí, la experiencia no tanto. Puedo dar fe.
Un algo más que termina marcando la diferencia
La pantallita redonda del Nothing Phone (4a) Pro (la Glyph Matrix, con 137 miniLED, heredada del Nothing Phone (3)) no es solo una anécdota, ya que puede funcionar para las notificaciones y hasta como visor de la cámara. Un visor algo tosco, aunque válido para encuadrar un selfie con la cámara trasera sin darle la vuelta al teléfono. Y no todo son luces: el móvil remata su diseño de inspiración industrial con aluminio, transparencias y un módulo de fotografía diferente.
Ese esfuerzo por mimar los detalles es lo que hace del Nothing Phone (4a) Pro un teléfono inconfundible, uno que no se ve en la gama media de ningún otro fabricante. No es el motivo principal para haberse llevado uno de los Premios Xataka más disputados de este año, pero creo que sí ha sido el detalle que lo ha hecho sobresalir frente a sus rivales. Porque si el móvil, además de bueno, es diferente, pues mejor. Que ya hay demasiada uniformidad entre los smartphones.
