articles.title: Cómo programar mensajes en WhatsApp sin usar apps de terceros
articles.text:
WhatsApp sumó una función nativa para programar mensajes, sin depender de aplicaciones externas. La herramienta permite redactar un texto en cualquier momento y fijar su envío entre 10 minutos y 14 días después, tanto en chats individuales como grupales.
La novedad acerca a la app a opciones ya conocidas en plataformas de correo electrónico como Gmail y Outlook, y resuelve situaciones en las que el contenido está listo pero el horario no es el adecuado: un saludo de cumpleaños a la medianoche del país donde vive el destinatario, un recordatorio laboral o un mensaje de aliento antes de un examen, sin necesidad de permanecer pendiente del reloj.
Pasos para programar un mensaje en WhatsApp
Para activar la función, el proceso comienza en el chat individual o grupal elegido, donde se escribe el texto que se quiere enviar. Luego, en lugar de tocar el botón de enviar de forma habitual, se debe mantener presionado ese mismo botón. Ahí aparece la opción para seleccionar la fecha y hora de la entrega.
La aplicación admite un rango de programación de hasta 14 días, con un mínimo de 10 minutos de anticipación. Una vez confirmado el horario, el mensaje queda en espera dentro de la plataforma y se envía de forma automática en el momento definido por quien lo creó.
El envío de contenido de una sola vista, para fotos y videos, mantiene el mismo mecanismo de siempre y no se modifica con esta incorporación.
Chats individuales y grupos: dónde funciona la programación
La función de mensajes programados está disponible tanto para conversaciones entre dos personas como para grupos, lo que amplía su utilidad.
En el plano individual, permite preparar un saludo privado con anticipación. En comunidades, familias o equipos de trabajo, administradores o integrantes pueden dejar listos avisos para que lleguen a todos en el horario acordado.
En los grupos, en particular, la herramienta evita depender de que alguien esté conectado a una hora determinada para compartir información. Un recordatorio de reunión, una fecha límite o una convocatoria puede redactarse con anticipación y quedar previsto para el momento oportuno, sin alterar el funcionamiento habitual de la conversación.
Textos, fotos y videos: qué formatos admite la herramienta
La programación no se limita a los mensajes de texto. La función también admite fotos y videos, por lo que es posible dejar lista una felicitación acompañada de una imagen o un aviso audiovisual dirigido a familiares, compañeros o integrantes de una comunidad.
Cuando el contenido llega al destinatario, se visualiza como un mensaje corriente. No incluye ninguna marca especial que indique que fue preparado con anticipación ni exige una acción adicional de quien lo recibe.
La diferencia se concentra del lado de quien envía el mensaje, que organiza la entrega para una fecha posterior sin que eso se note del otro lado de la conversación.
Cómo revisar o eliminar un mensaje programado antes del envío
Quienes utilicen esta función pueden consultar los envíos pendientes antes de que se cumpla el horario elegido. Esa posibilidad permite controlar los mensajes ya previstos y modificar la decisión si las circunstancias cambian, por ejemplo, si una reunión se cancela o un saludo deja de tener sentido.
También es posible eliminar un mensaje programado antes de su envío. La eliminación evita que el contenido llegue al chat seleccionado, siempre que se realice antes del momento fijado.
Esta gestión de pendientes ofrece una alternativa para corregir errores o retirar información que ya no deba compartirse, sin necesidad de recurrir a herramientas externas.
Entrega garantizada aunque el teléfono esté apagado o sin batería
Uno de los aspectos que la compañía remarcó es que la entrega del mensaje no depende de que el teléfono permanezca encendido, con batería o conectado a internet en el horario previsto.
Según explicó WhatsApp, el mensaje aparecerá en el chat elegido aun si el dispositivo está apagado o se quedó sin carga en el momento en que estaba programado el envío.
La empresa señaló además que estos mensajes mantienen el cifrado de extremo a extremo que aplica a las conversaciones personales. Esto implica que el contenido permanece protegido durante todo el proceso y que terceros, incluida la propia compañía, no pueden acceder a su contenido.
Con un límite de hasta dos semanas de anticipación, la función suma una herramienta de planificación a una aplicación utilizada para conversaciones personales, grupos familiares y coordinación laboral, y permite dejar listo un mensaje apenas surge la idea para que llegue en el horario más conveniente para cada destinatario.

articles.title: Engineering Reliable Telematics from Smartphone Sensors
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Smartphone GPS, motion sensors, and vehicle interfaces can each report valid measurements that produce incorrect results when combined without accounting for timing and coordinate frames.
- Preserve raw observations and their provenance before synchronizing, transforming, or normalizing them.
- Introduce a quality gate that determines whether telemetry is suitable for a particular decision instead of forcing every observation into a definitive result.
- Design for real-world conditions, including delayed GPS updates, phone movement, background interruptions, and intermittent connectivity.
- Monitor data quality alongside conventional application and infrastructure metrics because a functioning pipeline can still produce unreliable driving events.
Why this matters: the phone is not the vehicle
A smartphone can provide a surprising amount of information about a journey, including GPS estimates location and speed, accelerometers measure motion along the device's axes, gyroscopes capture rotation, and others. A connected vehicle may expose additional signals, such as speed, engine state, or diagnostic information.
Combining these sources creates opportunities for fleet monitoring, usage-based insurance, driving-behavior analysis, trip reconstruction, and connected mobility services.
However, having more sensors does not automatically produce better telemetry.
In fact, a GPS update may arrive after a vehicle has already slowed down. A phone may rotate in its mount, changing how its accelerometer readings relate to the vehicle's movement. An application may pause collection when the operating system restricts background activity. A backend service may receive observations out of order after a device reconnects.
Each observation may look reasonable in isolation, but the problem appears when the system combines observations that do not describe the same moment, coordinate frame, or physical event.
I would approach this as an architectural problem before treating it as a sensor-processing problem. The goal is not to make every sensor perfect. It is to build a system that understands the limitations of its inputs and prevents unsuitable evidence from silently becoming a business decision.
This distinction matters because a misleading telemetry event can have consequences beyond an inaccurate chart. It may influence a driver's score, trigger a fleet alert, affect an insurance calculation, or lead an operations team to investigate an event that never happened as represented.
Who should read this, and what will they gain?
For architects, the challenge is deciding where sensor collection, normalization, quality evaluation, and event detection belong and what contracts connect those stages.
For mobile engineers, the concern is preserving useful observations despite changing device orientation, sampling gaps, intermittent connectivity, and operating-system lifecycle behavior.
For streaming and data engineers, the problem includes delayed events, out-of-order delivery, duplicate observations, and reconciling streams that operate at different sampling rates.
For product and operations teams, the question is how to distinguish a confident event from one that needs further evidence or should not be reported at all.
The practical outcome is a design approach that makes data limitations visible, keeps event logic separate from data-quality decisions, and provides evidence that can be inspected when a result is challenged.
How this architecture took shape
I arrived at this architecture by tracing the journey of a telemetry observation from the moment it is captured to the point at which an application uses it to make a decision. Rather than starting with a sensor-fusion algorithm, I considered what could go wrong at each step. A speed measurement could be delayed, two observations could represent different moments, a phone's orientation could change, or an operating system interruption could leave gaps in the collected data. Each problem affects a different part of the processing flow, but all can ultimately influence the same business decision.
This led me to identify the responsibilities that a reliable pipeline needs to address independently: preserving the original measurements, establishing their temporal relationship, interpreting them in a consistent reference frame, evaluating their quality, detecting events, and retaining the evidence behind the resulting decisions. These responsibilities form the six logical stages described below. The intent is not to prescribe a particular deployment topology, but to establish clear architectural boundaries so that uncertainty introduced at one stage does not silently propagate into the next.
Start with the architecture, not the algorithm
I prefer to separate raw measurement collection from interpretation. Requirements such as detecting harsh braking, classifying trips, or calculating a driving score should not dictate how raw observations are represented.
A practical architecture has six logical stages, as the following image shows. They do not need to be six separately deployed services, as several can run within the same mobile application. The separation into six stages matters because each stage has a distinct responsibility, failure modes, and validation requirements. In the next sections, we are going to review all these stages in detail.
Figure 1. A quality-aware mobile telematics pipeline (Source: created by the author)
1. Collect and preserve raw observations
Start by retaining the original observation before applying transformations.
A record should carry the value and its unit, source or sensor type, measurement timestamp, available arrival timestamp, and relevant metadata. Depending on the source, that metadata might include accuracy estimates, sensor sampling information, device identifiers, or the vehicle association.
Why preserve the original? Because a later transformation may be incorrect, an assumption may change, or an event may be disputed. If the system retains only its normalized output, engineers may be unable to determine whether the original observation was poor or the transformation introduced the error.
For example, suppose an application converts a GPS speed reading into a standardized unit and later combines it with vehicle speed. If an event looks implausible, the engineering team should be able to inspect the original value, its timestamp, and the conversion applied to it.
Preservation does not mean keeping every field forever, since retention, privacy, security, and storage policies still apply. It means defining which evidence is needed for diagnosis and traceability before transformations discard it.
2. Establish temporal alignment
Sensor streams do not necessarily report at the same frequency or on the same schedule. A vehicle interface may produce frequent speed updates while GPS observations arrive less often. Mobile and backend components may also introduce different buffering and delivery delays.
The first distinction I make is between measurement time and arrival time.
Measurement time describes when the observation was captured, according to its source clock. Arrival time describes when a component received it. Arrival time is useful for understanding latency, but it is not a safe substitute for measurement time when reconstructing physical events.
A stream processor that compares the latest values received from two sources can accidentally compare different moments. This becomes especially problematic during rapid acceleration, braking, or turning, when the underlying state changes quickly.
The architecture should therefore define an alignment policy. It needs to specify how observations are matched, how much temporal separation is acceptable for each use case, and what happens when the system cannot find a suitable match.
Interpolation may be appropriate for some continuous signals, but it should not be applied indiscriminately. It can create a plausible-looking value where the evidence is sparse, and it may obscure a sharp change. The system should retain whether a value was directly measured, interpolated, or otherwise estimated.
When alignment cannot be established within the required tolerance, the right result may be lower confidence or no event at all.
3. Normalize coordinate frames and measurement semantics
A measurement's value is only part of its meaning. Its unit, coordinate frame, source, and interpretation matter just as much.
A phone's accelerometer reports motion in device coordinates. Those axes are attached to the phone, not inherently to the vehicle. If the phone rotates in a mount, the relationship between the phone's axes and the vehicle's forward, lateral, and vertical directions changes.
A system that assumes the phone is always mounted in the same orientation can interpret device movement as vehicle movement. That can distort acceleration, braking, and turning estimates.
Normalization should make these assumptions explicit. It may include unit conversion, coordinate transformation, sensor calibration, and checks on the validity of orientation estimates. A transformed observation should retain enough information to identify the transformation and its assumptions.
The system must also distinguish coordinate normalization from measurement quality. A transformation can be mathematically correct but based on an uncertain orientation estimate. The result may therefore remain unsuitable for a particular event calculation.
4. Evaluate data quality before accepting a measurement
At this stage, the system asks a different question: not simply whether a value exists, but whether it is fit for the intended use.
Useful checks include freshness, timestamp alignment, missing samples, source consistency, measurement uncertainty, and the reliability of any required coordinate transformation.
These checks should not be buried inside individual event rules. A shared quality stage gives different event detectors a consistent view of the evidence and makes quality decisions easier to monitor and test.
I would use three broad outcomes:
- Accept: The observation meets the requirements for the intended calculation.
- Degrade: The observation remains useful, but the system should limit its use or communicate reduced confidence.
- Abstain: The available evidence does not support a decision that is reliable enough for the intended use.
These are not universal labels with fixed thresholds. A GPS observation might be adequate for a coarse trip map but unsuitable for calculating a short, sharp braking event. Quality must be evaluated in context.
5. Detect events using qualified evidence
Event detection should consume measurements that have already passed through the relevant quality checks.
This does not mean every event requires every sensor. A trip-start detector and a harsh-braking detector have different evidence requirements. The architecture should allow each detector to declare what it needs and how it handles missing or uncertain inputs.
Consider a braking detector that combines vehicle speed and GPS speed. If the two values refer to different moments, the detector may infer a rate of deceleration that is not supported by the underlying movement. A quality-aware design prevents the detector from treating a poor match as equivalent to aligned observations.
The detector should also distinguish the event's classification from the quality of its evidence. An event may be a candidate for further review rather than a definitive result. Keeping these concepts separate makes the system easier to tune without changing the meaning of quality checks throughout the pipeline.
6. Produce a decision with supporting evidence
The final stage produces more than an event label.
A useful event record can include the event type, event time or interval, relevant vehicle or trip association, quality status, supporting observations, and the processing-rule version. Where a confidence estimate is used, its meaning and limitations should be documented rather than treating it as a universal probability of correctness.
This information makes a decision inspectable. An engineer can trace an event to the observations that supported it, see whether any measurements were downgraded, and understand which processing logic was applied.
It also helps separate two questions that are often conflated: "What did the system decide?" and "What evidence justified that decision?"
These six stages form one continuous data path. Raw preservation protects the evidence; temporal alignment and normalization make observations comparable; the quality gate determines their suitability; event detection applies the domain logic; and the final record explains the result.
How the six stages work together
The value of this architecture comes from the boundaries between stages.
- If the phone and vehicle speed measurements disagree, temporal alignment checks whether they describe comparable moments.
- If a phone rotates, normalization identifies that the relationship between device axes and vehicle axes has changed.
- If the available evidence remains insufficient, the quality gate prevents the uncertainty from disappearing.
- The event detector uses only evidence that meets the requirements for its task.
- The final output retains enough provenance and quality information to support investigation and improvement.
This is deliberately more than a sensor-fusion algorithm. It is a contract for how imperfect physical observations become software decisions.
The principle is straightforward: preserve what was measured, establish what it means, evaluate whether it is fit for use, and only then act on it.
Real-world example 1: The phantom braking event
Imagine a fleet operator whose mobile application scores driving behavior. Drivers receive alerts for harsh braking, and fleet managers use the events to identify potentially risky patterns.
One morning, a driver approaches a traffic light and brakes normally. The smartphone collects GPS-derived speed while the vehicle interface reports speed independently. The backend later records a harsh-braking event.
The driver disputes the alert. The vehicle did slow down, but not as abruptly as the application claims.
The engineering team examines the processing flow and discovers that the phone and vehicle streams were paired by arrival order. GPS updates were less frequent, and one observation represented an earlier point in the journey. During deceleration, the system compared that older speed estimate with a more recent vehicle measurement.
The discrepancy looked like physical behavior. Part of it was actually a timing problem.
The pipeline had accepted both values because they were syntactically valid. It had no mechanism to establish whether they were temporally comparable.
Figure 2. How a timing mismatch can create a misleading event (Source: created by the author)
What changes?
The team introduces a temporal-alignment stage before event detection. Each observation retains its measurement timestamp, while arrival time is tracked separately. The pipeline evaluates the freshness of each observation and avoids comparing streams when timing uncertainty exceeds the application's defined tolerance.
The detector also stops treating every speed discrepancy as equivalent. When the measurements are not sufficiently aligned, it lowers confidence or abstains from generating a definitive event.
The team adds monitoring for timestamp offsets, stale observations, alignment failures, and event reclassification. These metrics help distinguish a change in driving behavior from a change in data quality.
This approach does not guarantee that every braking event will be classified correctly. It gives engineers a way to identify a measurement-comparison problem before treating it as driver behavior.
The same pattern applies to fleet diagnostics, trip reconstruction, usage-based insurance, and connected-vehicle analytics.
The lesson: before interpreting disagreement between sensors as physical behavior, establish whether the measurements are temporally comparable.
Coordinate frames: accurate measurements can still mean the wrong thing
Time alignment does not solve the second major problem: orientation.
An accelerometer measures along the device's axes. A vehicle-relative interpretation assumes that the system knows how those axes relate to the vehicle. If the phone rotates, that relationship changes.
The gyroscope can help estimate rotation, and sensor-fusion algorithms can estimate orientation. Neither eliminates uncertainty automatically. Estimates may drift, the initial orientation may be unknown, and the phone can move independently of the vehicle.
A field named longitudinalAcceleration can therefore be misleading if it was calculated from device-relative measurements while the phone's orientation was uncertain.
The architecture should distinguish raw device-frame measurements from transformed estimates and preserve the assumptions behind each transformation.
Real-world example 2: The phone moves, but the vehicle does not turn
Consider a mobile telematics application that detects cornering and sudden lateral movement using the phone's accelerometer and gyroscope.
A driver starts a journey with the phone secured in a horizontal dashboard mount. The application estimates orientation and interprets motion relative to the vehicle. Later, the mount loosens on a rough road, and the phone rotates. The driver continues straight.
The application detects apparent lateral movement and records an aggressive-turning event.
The sensor values changed, but the physical interpretation was wrong. The device's orientation changed, so the relationship between its axes and the vehicle's direction of travel was no longer the same.
This problem is easy to miss when testing only with a phone mounted in a fixed position. The algorithm may perform well in a controlled setup and fail when users reposition the phone, adjust the mount, or carry it during a trip.
Figure 3. The device frame is not automatically the vehicle frame (Source: created by the author)
What changes?
The team makes orientation confidence an explicit input to event detection. Raw accelerometer and gyroscope observations are preserved, while transformed measurements carry metadata describing the estimated reference frame and the confidence in that transformation.
The detector no longer assumes that one phone orientation remains valid for the entire journey. It monitors orientation changes and identifies periods when the relationship between the device and vehicle is uncertain.
When orientation is reliable, the application can use transformed measurements according to its validated detection policy. When confidence falls, it can rely on other trustworthy evidence, reduce the confidence of the event, or abstain from making a definitive classification.
The team tests deliberate phone rotations, loose mounts, different mounting positions, and periods when orientation cannot be estimated reliably. It measures false positives and false negatives against a defined reference rather than assuming that a more sophisticated algorithm automatically improves accuracy.
This also improves the user experience. Instead of penalizing a driver for an uncertain observation, the application can indicate that it could not classify the event reliably.
The lesson: sensor accuracy and interpretation accuracy are different things. A sensor can report its measurement correctly while the application assigns that measurement the wrong physical meaning.
The same principle applies to phone-based activity recognition, wearable devices, robotics, and industrial IoT.
The quality gate: a contract between sensors and business logic
The quality gate is the fourth stage in the architecture, but its responsibility extends beyond checking whether sensor values look reasonable. It determines whether the available measurements are reliable enough for the specific decision an application intends to make.
The preceding stages preserve observations, establish temporal relationships, and normalize their measurement semantics. However, even after these steps, the resulting measurements may still contain uncertainty, missing samples, or inconsistencies. Without an explicit quality evaluation, individual event detectors must handle these conditions independently, often using different assumptions and fallback rules. This can lead to inconsistent decisions across the application.
I consider the quality gate a contract between the telemetry pipeline and the business logic that consumes its output. It makes the limitations of the available evidence explicit and defines what downstream components are permitted to do with it.
This section explores three aspects of that contract: why measurement quality must be evaluated in the context of the intended decision, how the system should distinguish between accepting, degrading, and abstaining from a result, and why abstention should be treated as a legitimate outcome rather than a processing failure.
Quality depends on the decision
Suppose a fleet application supports two functions: displaying the approximate route of a trip and identifying a short, aggressive braking maneuver.
The route display may tolerate a less frequent location update. The braking detector needs evidence that is sufficiently aligned in time and suitable for estimating a rapid change in speed.
Using the same universal threshold for both functions can be unnecessarily restrictive for one and dangerously permissive for the other.
Instead, each consumer should declare its requirements. The quality gate evaluates the observation against those requirements and communicates the outcome.
This approach also makes product trade-offs explicit. If a team wants more events at the expense of accepting weaker evidence, that decision becomes a documented policy choice that can be evaluated—not an accidental consequence of a permissive fallback in a detector.
Abstention is a valid result
Engineering teams often focus on maximizing the number of events detected. But a system that always returns an answer can create a false sense of certainty.
Abstention is useful when the evidence does not support the intended decision. It should not be treated as an exception that disappears into a log file.
The system should record why it abstained, whether additional data could resolve the uncertainty, and whether the decision needs to be revisited. For some use cases, waiting briefly for a delayed observation is reasonable. For others, the system may need to return an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome.
This is especially important when events influence human decisions, scores, or downstream automation. A clearly identified lack of evidence is often more useful than a precise-looking result that cannot be defended.
Make data quality observable
A quality-aware architecture is only as good as the team's ability to see it working. If the system records only the number of events generated, it becomes difficult to distinguish a genuine change in driving behavior from a change in sensor availability, application lifecycle, or processing logic.
I would monitor the quality pipeline alongside the business outcomes.
Useful operational signals include:
- Freshness: How old are observations when a consumer uses them?
- Temporal alignment: How far apart are measurements paired for the same calculation?
- Sampling gaps: How often do expected observations go missing, and how long do gaps last?
- Quality outcomes: What proportion of observations are accepted, degraded, or rejected, and for what reasons?
- Orientation confidence: How often does an orientation-dependent calculation lack a sufficiently reliable transformation?
- Event stability: How often are candidate events revised or reclassified after delayed observations arrive?
- Processing latency: How long does it take from measurement to event decision, separately from the measurement's age?
- Provenance completeness: Can an event be traced to its supporting observations and processing-rule version?
These measurements should be segmented where useful by device type, operating-system version, sensor source, application version, and collection conditions. Otherwise, a system-wide average may conceal a failure affecting a particular group of devices.
I would also connect quality metrics to event outcomes. If the number of harsh-braking events suddenly rises, the team should be able to investigate whether driving behavior changed, timestamp skew increased, or a new application version altered sampling behavior.
This requires a distinction between technical metrics and business metrics. Event counts and driver scores tell us what the application concluded. Freshness, alignment, and rejection metrics help explain whether the evidence behind those conclusions changed.
Observability should support investigation, not just dashboards. Logs and event records need enough structured context to reconstruct a decision while respecting data-retention and privacy requirements.
Account for the mobile operating system
A smartphone sensor pipeline does not run in a perfectly controlled environment. Applications can move into the background, devices can enter power-saving modes, connectivity can disappear, and operating systems can constrain background execution.
The architecture should not assume that a requested sampling rate guarantees a continuous stream.
On the device, collection code should handle sensor unavailability, sampling gaps, lifecycle transitions, and local buffering. When connectivity returns, queued observations may arrive in a burst or out of order. The backend should therefore apply its temporal-alignment and duplicate-handling policies even when the data originated from a single phone.
The system should preserve the distinction between the time an observation was measured and the time it was uploaded. It should also make gaps visible rather than filling them silently with fabricated continuity.
Offline operation introduces another design decision: how much data to buffer and for how long. That depends on the product's latency, privacy, storage, and battery constraints. Not every observation needs to be retained indefinitely, but the policy should be deliberate.
These concerns are not separate from sensor reliability. They determine whether the system has enough timely evidence to make a defensible decision.
Where to start: a practical implementation plan
I would not attempt to perfect every sensor or event detector at once. I would start with one high-impact event and establish a reliable path through the architecture.
- Preserve the evidence. Confirm that raw values, units, source identifiers, measurement timestamps, arrival timestamps, and relevant metadata are captured before transformation.
- Define the temporal contract. Document how observations are aligned, how stale data is handled, and what happens when a required measurement is missing or late.
- Make coordinate assumptions explicit. Identify which calculations depend on phone orientation, how transformations are established, and how uncertainty affects downstream use.
- Introduce a quality contract. Define accept, degrade, and abstain outcomes for one event type. Record reason codes so that quality failures can be distinguished from event-rule failures.
- Validate failure scenarios. Test delayed, missing, duplicated, out-of-order, and contradictory observations. Test phone rotations and changes in sensor availability, not only normal journeys.
- Instrument the pipeline. Track timestamp skew, data freshness, sampling gaps, quality outcomes, event revisions, and end-to-end latency.
- Expand incrementally. Once the chosen event has a defensible processing path, apply the same architectural contracts to other event types, adapting the quality requirements to each use case.
The goal is not to add complexity for its own sake. It is to discover where the system's assumptions are hidden and make them explicit before those assumptions affect a business decision.
What this architecture does not solve
A quality-aware architecture makes sensor limitations and processing uncertainty explicit, but it does not eliminate them. Architects and developers should consider several limitations when applying this model.
It cannot recover missing evidence
The architecture can identify missing samples, stale observations, and unreliable measurements, but it cannot reconstruct physical events when evidence was never captured. Interpolation and estimation may help, but introduce assumptions and should not be treated as direct measurements. When evidence is insufficient, the system should communicate that limitation rather than manufacture continuity.
It does not replace algorithm validation
The six stages define architectural responsibilities, not specific sensor-fusion, calibration, or event-detection algorithms. Developers must validate these techniques against appropriate reference measurements and real-world conditions. A well-structured pipeline cannot compensate for an inaccurate orientation estimate or an incorrectly designed detection algorithm.
Quality thresholds are not universal
Freshness, timestamp tolerance, measurement uncertainty, and orientation confidence must be evaluated against the intended decision. Requirements for displaying a trip route differ from those for detecting harsh braking. Thresholds should be validated for each use case, and confidence scores should not be treated as universal probabilities of correctness.
Operational trade-offs remain
Background execution restrictions, battery consumption, connectivity, device diversity, and privacy influence what can be collected and processed. Teams must balance these constraints with evidence requirements and processing latency. They must also define how uncertain outcomes and abstentions are communicated and when additional data or manual review is appropriate.
Ultimately, this architecture is a framework for managing uncertainty, not a guarantee of perfect telemetry. Its effectiveness depends on sensor quality, validated algorithms, appropriate quality requirements, and continuous testing under real-world conditions.
Conclusion: reliability belongs to the pipeline
Smartphones make telematics more accessible by combining location, motion sensors, computing power, and connectivity in a single device. But the convenience comes with a trade-off: device placement varies, sampling behavior is managed by the mobile platform, and measurements have different timing and coordinate semantics.
The architectural response is to separate observation from interpretation. Preserve what the phone measured. Establish when and in what frame it was measured. Evaluate whether the evidence is suitable for the decision. Only then should business logic act on the result.
The phantom braking scenario shows why measurements from different sources must be temporally comparable. The rotated-phone scenario shows why device orientation must be treated as a variable rather than an assumption. Both demonstrate why a technically healthy pipeline can still produce an unreliable conclusion.
The distinction is simple: collecting telemetry produces data. Engineering reliable telemetry produces evidence that downstream systems can evaluate, qualify, and use responsibly.

articles.title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
articles.text:
AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  University of Plymouth
- Summary:
  Scientists have developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a major study involving nearly 70,000 patients. By revealing subtle patterns that conventional screening misses, the technology could help doctors detect cancer earlier and spare patients unnecessary invasive procedures.
- Share:
Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.
Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.
The new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.
AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records
Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.
Confirming bladder cancer currently requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.
To explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.
The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.
AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases
The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.
The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.
Importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.
The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.
For example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.
These findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.
Another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.
Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.
A New Approach to Early Cancer Screening
Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).
This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.
For example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.
PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, said: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022."
"Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research shows that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods."
Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?
The potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.
Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.
"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.
"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved."
Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.
"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.
"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages."
More Research Needed Before Clinical Use
Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.
All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.
Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.
"It's important to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.
"But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions."
The findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.
The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.
The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

Materials provided by University of Plymouth. Original written by Mrs. Amy King. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:

Véspera da Black: Galaxy Tab S10 FE Plus 5G sai pelo menor preço que já vimos
Galaxy Tab S10 FE Plus 5G (128 GB) com tela de 13,1" e S Pen na caixa recebe desconto de 52% no Pix com cupom no Mercado Livre, a um dia da Black Friday 2026
O Galaxy Tab S10 FE Plus 5G de 128 GB está em saindo por R$ 2.564 no Pix com cupom MODOTECH no Mercado Livre. O tablet da Samsung voltado a profissionais, com tela de 13,1″ e a S Pen no kit, atinge o menor preço já publicado pelo Achados na Black Week 2026, com desconto de 52% sobre o original de R$ 5.299.
Esta oferta é o menor preço que já encontramos para o Galaxy Tab S10 FE Plus 5G 128 GB. Nas outras 10 ofertas publicadas desde março de 2026, o melhor foi R$ 2.834,10 (Amazon, 10/11/2026).
O Galaxy Tab S10 FE Plus chama a atenção para sua tela LCD de 13,1″ com taxa de 90 Hz, que oferece bastante espaço para atividades de escritório, como abrir documentos, rodar planilhas e afins, além de entregar fluidez e alto brilho e contraste.
Seu chip Exynos 1580 e os 8 GB de RAM suportam editores de texto e navegadores, mas não apps mais pesados (a Samsung afirma que ele dá conta do Adobe Photoshop, entretanto). Os 128 GB de armazenamento podem ser expandidos com cartões microSD de até 2 TB.
A suíte Galaxy AI oferece ferramentas de produtividade, como o Assistente Matemático para fazer cálculos e o Circule para Pesquisar com gestos de busca inteligente, além de outras funções de IA, como o Apagador de Objetos em fotos.
O kit inclui o tablet, uma capa protetora e a caneta S Pen, que oferece precisão ao desenhar e escrever. A bateria de 10.090 mAh do S10 FE Plus resiste a até 21 horas de vídeo, diz a fabricante, e suporta carregamento rápido de 45 W via USB-C.
A certificação IP68 confere proteção contra ambientes empoeirados e mergulhos acidentais, enquanto o kit de câmeras inclui wide traseira de 13 MP e frontal de 12 MP, que capturam documentos e sustentam videoconferências com qualidade. Ambas filmam em 4K.
O Galaxy Tab S10 FE Plus de 128 GB (R$ 2.564 no Pix com cupom MODOTECH) foi atualizado para o Android 16 e receberá updates por mais cinco anos. O tablet da Samsung possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 6E e Bluetooth 5.3.
A Black Friday 2026 rola nesta sexta-feira (27), e lojas como o Mercado Livre vão oferecer uma penca de cupons e promoções em eletrônicos com condições especiais até a Cyber Monday, na próxima segunda-feira (30).
Acompanhe os Achados do TB no Telegram ou WhatsApp e não fique de fora da festa.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

LIVE: Latest Updates
AudioEngine's latest A2 GEN3 speakers with USB-C and redesigned power amp are sale for 25% off
The AudioEngine A2+ speakers have been our go-to recommendation for years on our roundup of the best PC speakers. The newer A2 GEN3 speakers have several improvements, including Bluetooth 5.4, adding support for various aptX codecs, and a Class D amplifier, which should help the speakers run cooler. AudioEngine also swapped out the micro-USB port on the original speakers for a USB-C port.
One of the best desktop speakers we've tested, now updated with USB-C and aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC for stellar wireless connectivity up to 100 feet, these are an excellent audio upgrade for any desk.

The cabinet and drivers remain unchanged. The speakers feature a 2.75-inch woofer and 0.75-inch tweeter, and they're among the best-sounding speakers in this class. They're expensive at $300, and even during shopping events, they don't always go on sale. That's what makes the 25% discount during Black Friday so attractive.
Outside of quality raw components, the speakers include a 24-bit internal DAC, and AudioEngine stands behind the speakers with a three-year warranty. — Jake Roach
Anker’s 25,000 mAh Laptop Power Bank is almost $44 off and at an all-time low price – $91 yields a 3-port, 165W power bank with two retractable USB-C cables
If you’re always on the go with your laptop, it helps to have a power bank handy to keep your device charged without a wall outlet. Anker’s 25,000 mAh, 165W laptop power bank (model A1695) is a solid option. It’s now on sale at an all-time low of $91.19. The power bank sports an information LCD display that shows output wattage, percent left, and more.
Anker’s Laptop Power Bank is ideal for laptop users and features three 100W USB-C ports (two built-in, one retractable; the other doubles as a carry strap) and one Type-A for simultaneous charging up to 165W. It offers ultra-fast recharge speeds up to 100W with a compatible charger, plus a built-in screen to display charging information. It’s pricey, but it charges quickly and sustains its output over time in our testing.
Read moreRead less▼
Output includes two retractable Type-C cables, plus a Type-C port and a Type-A port, allowing you to charge up to four devices at once. It’s great for traveling and complies with 100Wh airline restrictions. If you’re looking for a powerful multi-port power bank, this Anker is one of the best deals for a high-quality device with a display. – Joe Shields
Trade a bit of speed for capacity with $0.10 per GB deal on a 2TB Silicon Power NVMe SSD
Given the current SSD market, it's been months since we've seen a drive at $0.10 per GB, but that's the price for this 2TB Silicon Power NVMe SSD. It's a PCIe 3.0 drive, so you're trading some speed for the price. However, it's still far faster than any SATA SSD, and many of those drives are selling for more than the cost of this one.
Perfect as a storage drive for your Steam library, this PCIe 3.0 drive can reach read/write speeds of up to 2200/1600 MB/s, respectively.
Read moreRead less▼
The drive comes with 2,200 MB/s and 1,600 MB/s sequential read/write performance. As you might expect, it's a DRAM-less SSD, instead relying on HMB and an SLC cache. It comes with an endurance rating of 1,200 TBW, which is excellent considering the price.
Although stepping down to PCIe 3.0 isn't ideal, there are a ton of applications for 2TB of storage where the slower speed won't matter much. Especially when looking at older games and media, the practical difference between this drive and even an expensive PCIe 5.0 isn't massive. — Jake Roach
Save 43% on Ugreen’s X515 USB Wall Charger - just $9.44 buys a 3-port GaN II charger; one of the most efficient chargers we tested is now on deep discount
UGreen’s X515 USB Wall Charger is only $9.44, a solid 43% (over $7) off the list price. We reviewed this charger and loved how cool it ran during our testing, as well as its efficiency. The small charger has two Type-C and one Type-A port for 30W total output. The X515 supports multiple charging protocols, including PD/QC 3.0, PPS, FCP, and AFC so you'll get the most out of most anything you want to charge.
The value pick in our low-wattage group is UGreen’s 3-port USB-C GaN II charger (X515). It's an affordable, high-quality option that supports charging multiple devices at once. It was among the most efficient chargers we tested, ran cooler than most of the competition, and was still compact enough for travel.
Read moreRead less▼
We named the X515 our low-wattage value pick in our Best Chargers article, beating several comparables. Overall, it’s a solid choice for anyone who needs a high-quality multi-port USB wall charger. And being well over 40% off makes this a steal for its class. – Joe Shields
SanDisk’s lightning-fast Optimus GX Pro 8100 2TB NVMe SSD is 21% off and $0.18 cents per GB – $349 for a PCIe 5.0 M.2 SSD is about as good as it gets for Black Friday
SanDisk’s WD Black SN8100 clone, the 2TB Optimus GX Pro 8100 PCIe 5.0 SSD, is on sale for almost $95 off its typical price and at an all-time low, according to Amazon. For $349, you can get one of the faster 2TB drives. At less than $ 0.18 per GB, it’s one of the cheapest 2TB PCIe 5.0 drives available right now. The drive reaches speeds up to 14,900/14,000 MB/s (read/writes), nearly saturating PCIe 5.0 bandwidth.
All-time low price.
Expand your internal storage with Sandisk's 2TB Optimus GX Pro 8100 PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSD. This speedy drive offers 14,900/14,000 r/w speeds and has a 5-year warranty.
Read moreRead less▼
Whether you use it as your primary OS drive or to store your most frequently accessed games, the SanDisk Optimus GX Pro 8100 2TB is an excellent option for a new PC or even upgrading your current storage. At an all-time low price of $349.99 (less than $0.18 per GB), it’s not only fast (faster than the Samsung 9100 Pro), but the price is right, too. – Joe Shields
Add extra gigabit Ethernet devices to your network with this $7.99 TP-Link switch
It's all about speed. If you're streaming at 4K, or playing games online where latency can kill you before your opponents can, then you need fast networking. This TP-Link 5-port switch, down to just $7.99, can unlock an extra four gigabit Ethernet ports to your network for your PC, laptop, game consoles, and more.
All you need to do to use this unmanaged switch is to switch it on and hook it up to your router using one of the ports. If you're stuck with slow Wi-Fi, especially in a congested area, there isn't a better alternative. You'll be able to max out your internet connection's bandwidth with a faster wired network this way.
The TP-Link Litewave 5-Port Gigabit Ethernet Switch LS1005G provides four additional Ethernet ports, delivering reliable, high-speed wired internet for your gaming PC, NAS, console, TV, and other connected devices. Another popular Tom's Hardware recommendation and one that several of us own ourselves.
Read moreRead less▼
This is a plug-and-play option that doesn't need configuring, so it's perfect for a beginner and a pro. If you're struggling with lag or slow connectivity on your local network, then this $8 switch (along with some Ethernet cables) is an easy solution, and at a great price. — Ben Stockton
Just $45 for a HyperX gaming mic with a built-in stand
HP's HyperX gaming brand is known for its good quality peripherals, including gaming mics, which are easy to use and usually sound great. Right now, the HyperX SoloCast 2 is on sale, and it's down to just $44.98.
This USB condenser mic has just one polar pattern (cardioid); it's designed to pick up just one person's voice in front of it. It's well built, made of a solid black cylinder with a metal grille, weighing almost 13 ounces (365.7g). Unlike most mics, this has a built-in stand, which you can tilt back by around 40 degrees to angle it right at your face. It's backed with rubber at the bottom, too, so it won't slip around, with mounting points if you want to add it to a boom arm.
This 14mm electret condenser capsule mic features an integrated desktop stand that tilts the mic upward 40 degrees (there's a mounting point on the bottom of the stand, in case you do want to mount it on a boom arm). It has a cardioid polar pattern and sounds pretty good out of the box, and it features HyperX's signature tap-to-mute button on the top.
Read moreRead less▼

View Original
View Original

There's a USB-C port on the back, with a large tap-to-mute button on top for easy access, along with a red indicator light to let you know when you're muted. It records at a high-res 24-bit, 96 kHz bit-depth and sample rate, sounding very good out of the box. There's also a built-in internal shock mount and pop filter, although it's better mounted rather than sitting on your desk.
This HyperX mic is simple and a good starter option for a gamer or office worker, and thanks to the $44.98 sale price, it's cheaper than ever. You can check out our HyperX SoloCast 2 review to learn more. — Ben Stockton
Treat yourself to VR with the Meta Quest 3S, now under $300 with a bonus $15 promo card
Want to try out VR? Then Meta's budget-friendly Meta Quest 3S should enter your checkout. Thanks to Black Friday, it's on sale for just $297.49 right now at Newegg, a 15% price drop compared to its usual price. You're also scoring a $15 gift card that you can use to put towards another Newegg purchase.
The Meta Quest 3S is the most affordable VR headset from Meta. Despite that, it still comes with the same CPU, RAM, and base storage as the most expensive Meta Quest 3, while also offering a slightly better battery life.
Read moreRead less▼
The Meta Quest 3S is a completely wireless experience, so there aren't any cables or cords to worry about here, and you don't need a PC to power it. It's got a smaller battery compared to the Meta Quest 3, but this VR headset should still last for 2.5 hours with continuous use.
The controllers, meanwhile, are powered by a single alkaline AA battery each. It's probably worth keeping a few extra rechargeable lithium-ion batteries close at hand, though, so you don't get cut off mid-way through a game. The Meta Quest 3S would make for a great gift this holiday season, for yourself or for a loved one, especially with that 15% discount on top. — Ben Stockton
Edifier's compact M60 PC speakers are down to $149.99, back at their lowest price
Another Black Friday deal is here for those audiophiles needing an upgrade to their desk audio setup. These Edifier M60 PC speakers are back down to $149.99 on Amazon right now. That's a $50 off the retail price and it brings it back down to record lows, a price we last saw during Amazon's October sale.
The Edifier M60 speakers come with 3-inch mid-low drivers and 1-inch tweeters, and they're relatively compact, measuring just 6.6 inches (168mm) high by 3.9 inches (100mm) wide. They come with a pair of aluminum speaker stands that angle the speakers up by 15 degrees, pointing them directly toward your ears when they're placed at a desk.
This pair of compact desktop stereo speakers features USB-C, AUX, and Bluetooth 5.3 connectivity, as well as touch controls and a built-in DSP. And they're on sale for their lowest price ever.
Read moreRead less▼
You can connect in a few different ways with the M60s, including by USB-C or traditional aux inputs, as well as by using Bluetooth 5.3. If you use Bluetooth, you can stream high-res audio (24-bit / 96 kHz) from mobile devices running Android 8 or later, too.
The speakers have a built-in DSP and touch controls that'll light up when you move your hand over them. With a total output power of 66W RMS, these aren't the most powerful PC speakers in the world, but they'll be a massive step up over listening through your laptop (or, worse, monitor's) tinny speakers. — Ben Stockton
This is the cheapest AMD Radeon RX 9070 GRE graphics card that you can buy right now
There haven't been a huge amount of GPU deals during this Black Friday sales event, so this is a rare one. For $619, you can pick up this PowerColor RX 9070 GRE. It's the cheapest you'll find this GPU and, more importantly, it's a solid mid-tier performer for gaming at 1080p and 1440p at a far better price than rival GPUs like the RTX 5060 Ti.
This Radeon RX 9070 GRE is delivering great 1080p and 1440p gaming performance at a low price in today's market, giving you access to AMD's high-quality FSR 4 upscaler for a performance boost when you need it.
Read moreRead less▼
Our GPU hierarchy tests saw the RX 9070 GRE hit 90 FPS on average during all of our raster and ray tracing tests at 1080p, while also reaching 60 FPS at 1440p. Given the cost of this card, that's a really solid performance, especially as you might pay hundreds of dollars more for a rival Nvidia card to match it.
The 9070 GRE is an even better performer for pure raster gaming, hitting 120 FPS at 1080p and 90 FPS at 1440p, and that's before you even consider AMD's FSR 4 upscaling tech. If you want a quick, cheap and well-performing GPU upgrade for Black Friday, this PowerColor Reaper card might be one of the best ways to do it.
Delete dust and grime from your PC case with the Wolfbox MF50 for under $30
Dust: the enemy of all PCs. Dust is the perennial problem for PC owners, and once it builds up in your PC, it can cause it to overheat. Cleaning your rig regularly is the best course of action but, rather than rely on compressed air cans, you can invest in a compressed air duster, like this discounted Wolfbox MF50 for just $29.06, a new record low price for Black Friday.
An electric air duster, providing you with your own infinite supply of compressed air.
Read moreRead less▼
With this, you can banish the cans of compressed air and instead delete dust bunnies from your PC, along with any food or grime from your keyboard, along with any other areas of dirt collection on your desk. This portable and economical tool will keep your tech clean and tidy.
You can charge it over USB C in just 3.5 hours. It has a "turbo" fan that can reach speeds of up to 110,000 RPM, which provides up to four hours of use at its lowest setting. The MP50 has simple push controls, but all you really need to do is point and fire. There are four nozzles that'll help you control the airflow during a clean, too. — Ben Stockton
Save $85 on this top Razer Iskur V2 X gaming chair
One of our favorite budget gaming chairs is now at an even better price for Black Friday. You can pick up the Razer Iskur V2 X for just $214.99 right now, a price drop of $85 compared to its usual list price.
The budget-friendly alternative to the Iskur V2, the Razer Iskur V2 X is a no-frills alternative that drives the price down by removing some of the adjustability options. That said, this chair still comes with built-in lumbar support, 2D armrests, and a 152-degree recline.
Read moreRead less▼
As our Razer Iskur V2 X review explains, this is the slightly less luxurious version of the OG Iskur V2. That does mean you have to accept a few compromises, but it's otherwise the same high-quality construction that we saw when we reviewed the original.
You're getting significant support on the base and back, high-density foam for the seat cushion, and adjustable 2D armrests here. Grab this steal of a Razer gaming chair at this price while you can. -- Ben Stockton
This $55 130W portable battery from Ugreen with a 20,000 mAh battery is at a record-low price
If you're traveling, you'll want a beefy portable power bank to fall back on to keep all of your devices charged. That's where this Ugreen Nexode 20,000 mAh power bank comes into play. It's on sale right now for $54.99, a new record low price that knocks $35 off the list price.
The UGREEN Nexode 20000 mAh power bank supports up to 130W of combined power output and features two USB-C and one USB-A port.
Read moreRead less▼
This power bank supports up to 100W of total power output across its two USB-C ports, but there's also a USB-A port for legacy devices that need charging. However, the different ports do have different max power levels: USB-C port 1 will give you 100W, while USB-C port 2 is capped at 65W, with the USB-A port at 22.5W max. According to Ugreen, this power bank can recharge a 13-inch MacBook Air up to 1.3 times if it's fully charged, or it can recharge an iPhone 16 Pro up to 3.7 times.
This Nexode bank also comes with a LCD display that'll tell you the current charge level of the battery, along with power output levels and the time remaining until the battery is discharged (or fully charged if it's charging). $54.99 for peace of mind while you're traveling isn't a bad option. — Ben Stockton
Protect your PC from outages with this CyberPower UPS for under $100
Power outages aren't fun, but they're especially not fun for your gaming PC. An outage can cause everything from lost data to electrical damage, but not if you buy this CyberPower UPS. It's on sale for $99.95 right now, a 29% price drop, bringing it down to a price we've not seen since 2023, according to Camelcamelcamel's price data.
This 900 V / 500 W battery backup protects up to six devices from a power outage, with a further six outlets offering surge protection. It has two USB charging ports.
Read moreRead less▼
This UPS battery pack is rated for 900 VA / 500 W and comes with 12 outlets. Six of them include both the battery backup protection, meaning you'll continue to have power after your electricity goes out, with an additional six offering just surge protection.
The pack also has spaced-out outlets for bigger plugs, along with two USB ports for charging. It has a three year warranty, along with a $125,000 guarantee to protect any devices you connect up to it. — Ben Stockton
Save $100 on this Wi-Fi 7 router from TP-Link with five 2.5Gb Ethernet ports
Struggling with bad Wi-Fi? You need a router upgrade, and this TP-Link Archer BE550 for $149.99 is the answer, with a $100 saving to sink your teeth into. You're getting a ri-band Wi-Fi 7 router, able to provide up to 2,000 square feet of coverage, and fully expandable with EasyMesh-compatible devices.
You're able to get a combined maximum theoretical speed of 9.3 Gbps, split across the 6 GHz band for Wi-Fi 7, along with 5 and 2.4 GHz. If you're using a recent-enough device, Multi-Link Operation (or MLO) means you're able to use the different bands, like 5 GHz and 6 GHz, simultaneously for faster speeds and greater reliability.
The TP-Link Archer BE550 router packs six antennas, unlocking Wi-Fi 7 support for your network, with five 2.5 Gb Ethernet ports to help you future-proof your home network.
Read moreRead less▼
There are five 2.5 Gb Ethernet ports included in this BE550. One is the WAN port, so you'll use it to hook it up to your internet connection, along with four others that'll work for local devices like your gaming PC.
This router has everything you'd expect from a modern, mainstream Wi-Fi 7 router. It's got a USB port, too, that you can use for a quick-and-easy NAS solution using an external hard drive. Support for a mesh-style network, with per-device Quality of Service controls, mean you can set up priority for traffic for certain devices on a busy network, too. — Ben Stockton
Grab 16TB of shuckable storage at $0.02 per GB in this Newegg deal
Yes, AI has consumed the storage market, and hard drives have become pretty expensive these days, making it tough to be a humble data hoarder. While we've seen better storage deals in previous years, this $399.99 sale price for a 16TB Seagate Expansion external HDD is a good price in the current market.
The Seagate Expansion Desktop drive is a 16TB HDD that connects via USB 3.0. It's formatted to ExFAT by default, allowing it to work with virtually platform out of the box.
Read moreRead less▼
You can expect to pay hundreds of dollars more than this right now for a 16TB hard drive. Compare and contrast: for $399.99, this drive comes in at $0.02 per GB, which is a pretty sizable discount. Seagate doesn't disclose what model of drive it uses here, but these drives are typically shuckable.
That means that, if you want to break the 3.5-inch hard drive out of this enclosure, you can use it in your PC internally using SATA. This will void the warranty but it could be a good option if you need a lot of storage for your media files. — Ben Stockton
Apple's M5 Macbook Air is $400 off for 1TB of storage
We've seen the price rises hit Apple's MacBook range, but Amazon has cut its prices back for Black Friday. A good option for buyers looking for an upgrade right now is the MacBook Air with the M5 chip. Earlier, we brought you the $999 512GB version; now the 1TB version is $400 off.
This is a go-to everyday laptop with premium build quality, a good trackpad, and solid battery life. It's a no-brainer for anyone looking for a step up from the MacBook Neo, with a bit more computing heft for everyday tasks, as long as you can handle the display's notch.
The M5 MacBook Air offers 1TB of storage, a 13-inch Retina display, and a 10-core CPU and 8-Core GPU with 16GB of unified memory that can take on pretty much all everyday tasks with ease.

This model scored highly in our MacBook Air M5 review earlier in the year, and its great value was one of the big reasons why. At under $1,200, that value prospect is even better. You've got frills like MagSafe charging, high-quality speakers and a comfortable keyboard and trackpad to work with, too. This is a laptop that'll suit most people, and for $1,199, it's $400 less than what it cost just a few months ago. — Ben Stockton
Treat yourself to Logitech's G Pro X Superlight 2 for a cool $69
There's an ultra-light gaming mouse in your future, if you want it. Logitech's award-winning, ultra-light G Pro X Superlight 2 is on sale right now for just $69, down from $139.99. This near half-price saving unlocks a pseudo-ambidextrous wireless gaming mouse that weighs just 2.12 ounces (60g) and sports the company's Hero 2 optical sensor.
Logitech's ultralight 60g wireless mouse features a pseudo-ambidextrous symmetrical shape and sports the brand's Hero 2 optical sensor and Lightforce hybrid optical/mechanical switches.

The G Pro X Superlight 2 is ultra sensitive, up to 32,000 DPI, with a maximum speed of 500 IPS, and can handle up to 40 G's of force. It has a lightweight plastic shell with a smooth, soft-touch finish, and comes with five programmable buttons for macros or shortcuts.
The primary buttons use Logitech's Lightforce hybrid mechanical/optical switches, which are tactile and clicky (and a little loud). You can check out our Logitech G Pro X Superlight 2 review if you're still unsure, but either way, $69 is a bargain for a no-nonsense mouse for competitive gaming. — Ben Stockton
Upgrade your Mac Mini with a Ugreen dock for your peripherals for less than $50
If you've got a Mac Mini, or you're treating yourself to one over Black Friday, you can expand it pretty easily using a docking station. This Ugreen model is on sale for $49.99 right now, a 21% saving compared to its usual price.
This Ugreen dock has 11 different ports, as well as an SD card reader and room for an NVMe M.2 SSD.
Read moreRead less▼
This dock sits below the Mac Mini, connecting to its high-speed Thunderbolt port. It has several ports, including five USB-A 3.2 ports (rated for a mix of 10 and 5 Gbps), as well as two USB-C 3.2 (10 Gbps) and an SD card reader. It's also an enclosure for an additional M.2 NVMe SSD, giving your Mac Mini a quick and easy storage boost, although you'll need to supply your own drive.
This Ugreen dock supports recent-gen Mac Minis with M6, M5 Pro, and M4 chips. — Ben Stockton
Save $50 on Logitech’s 5.1 surround sound speaker setup for your PC
Regularly priced at $449.99, Logitech’s Z906 5.1 surround sound system has had $50 knocked off the price, making the 1000W system now only $399.99. This is the lowest price in a while, but nothing near its all-time low of 2017. This model of speakers has been around for a long time now, but with few alternative 5.1 surround sound setups on the market, they still prove to be a popular choice.
Experience full surround sound on your PC when playing games or watching movies. This THX-certified system features a whopping 1000W of peak power output or 500W RMS. Five speakers, a subwoofer, a control box, and a remote control are all part of the package.
Read moreRead less▼
This 5.1 surround-sound set of speakers from Logitech contains 5 speakers plus a subwoofer and control box. Highlights of this setup include an impressive 1000W peak power and 500W RMS for room-filling sound, THX certification for the best soundstage, which is perfect for movie night, and a wireless remote control to easily changing volumes and channels when sat away from the PC and control box.
You can connect up to 6 devices at once and have individual control of each speaker via the control box to optimise sound. Make sure to position the five satellite speakers around your room for full immersion in whatever media you’re enjoying.
The closest PC surround sound speaker setup to this is the Arena 9 from SteelSeries, and although and very good set of speakers, the current price tag is $679.99 direct from SteelSeries, making the Logitech Z906 and very attractive proposition at just $399.99. — Stewart Bendle
Pick up a handy Elgato Stream Deck MK.2 with 27% off at Amazon
While the Elgato Stream Deck MK.2 might, at first, appear to be a tool used for streamers and content creators, the customizable nature of the macropad makes it incredibly useful for anyone who sits and works at their desk every day. With configurable buttons and macros, including widespread community support, you can expect to configure heaps of plugins, assign hotkeys, and more across the 15-key keypad.
Built for streamers and content creators, the Elgato Stream Deck MK.2 is a purpose-built macro pad offering 15 LCD keys and widespread software support for a slew of additional plugins.
Read moreRead less▼
We reviewed the Stream Deck MK.2 when it was released in 2021, and called out how well it managed to streamline the process of streaming, thanks to the LCD keypad, USB-C connectivity, revised angle, and customizable plates. For anyone doing serious work at a desk, this is an ideal gift to add to their setup, even if they don't do any streaming or content creation. — Sayem Ahmed
20% off this GameSir wireless controller for PC gaming, back at its lowest-ever price
The GameSir Cyclone 2 is a wireless controller with TMR joysticks and micro-trigger buttons, and you can save 20% off it for Cyber Monday.
Read moreRead less▼
Under the hood, you're getting a very premium experience for less than $45. The silky TMR joysticks have the durability of Hall Effect sticks, and GameSir uses micro switches for the face buttons and D-pad, giving you a tactile feedback with each input.
In addition, there are two buttons on the back that you can set up for custom macros or commands, and it lets you hook it up to your devices using either the 2.4 GHz adapter or Bluetooth. This is a no-nonsense gamepad for your PC or laptop and, thanks to that sale price, one that makes it a more affordable option for gamers. — Ben Stockton
The GameSir Cyclone 2 is a top quality controller for gamers. It's got a layout that's true to the standard Xbox gamepad, so it won't be a difficult one to adjust to. More importantly, though, is the price: it's down to $44.79, back at its record lowest on Amazon.

A hugely powerful RTX 5090 OLED gaming laptop from Lenovo is on sale at B&H Photo. You can score a Lenovo Legion Pro 7i for $3,999.99, down from $5,299.99, for as long as the stock holds out.
The model we're looking at here includes a 24-core Core Ultra 9 290HX CPU and a 175W RTX 5090 laptop GPU with 24GB of VRAM. That's not as beefy as the RTX 5090 on a desktop PC but, this is a laptop, so it can't quite reach those kinds of power demands.
Lenovo's Legion Pro 7i boasts a 24-core Core Ultra 9 290HX CPU and 175W RTX 5090 GPU with 24GB of VRAM. This is a high spec laptop for gaming that'll handle anything you can throw at it.

Otherwise, this top-end system comes with 32GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD. More importantly, though, is that 16-inch OLED display, offering up 1600p gameplay at 240 Hz, with Nvidia G-Sync support to stop any screen tearing. You've got a high spec rig here with peformance on the top end of what you're able to achieve on laptop, and the $1,300 discount makes it all that sweeter.
You'll need to be quick, though. Stock is low on this one, so don't expect it to hold out forever. — Ben Stockton

Ever needed to duplicate a hard drive for a friend, family member, or for yourself as a quick backup? I've done this before to copy my main Windows installation drive over to a bigger one, for instance. Doing it manually is hard, but with this Rosewill M.2 cloner, you don't have to worry. This is one of those back-of-the-cupboard tools that you'll want in your arsenal, because you'll hate yourself when you don't. It's also down to a record low price of $32.29 right now.
This M.2 SSD cloner works with NVMe and AHCI drives (Key M), and lets you easily duplicate boot or storage drives with the press of a button. Note that it does not work with older SATA-based M.2 (Key B) drives.
Read moreRead less▼
Tom's Hardware staffers have used this drive duplicator before. You just need to plug it in, pop in your old M.2 drive into the left slot, place the new drive in the right slot, press the button, and wait for the magic to happen. You can also plug the whole thing into a PC and use software to duplicate your drive, which you might want to do if you're resizing partitions and going from a smaller to larger drive.
The $32.29 sale price makes this Rosewill M.2 cloner an easy buy. You won't always need it, but when you do, you won't be without out. It can take a tough storage situation and turn it into a 15-minute quick fix. — Ben Stockton
UGREEN Nexode 20000 mAh power bank drops to $55 — 130W portable battery discounted 39%
When I travel, I like to carry around a relatively beefy portable power bank with me to keep my devices charged. To that end, UGREEN's Nexode 20000 mAh power bank is more than up to the task of serving as a mainstay in your travel bag. It usually retails for $89.99, but is on sale right now for $54.99.
The UGREEN Nexode 20000 mAh power bank supports up to 130W of combined power output and features two USB-C and one USB-A port.

The power bank supports up to 100W of total power output between its two USB-C ports. USB-C1 supports up to 100W output, while USB-C2 outputs up to 30W. Besides its two USB-C ports, there's also a single USB-A port.

This Hoto 24-in-1 precision screwdriver with 24 different bits is the perfect addition to a hobbyist or 3D printer's toolkit.

The TL-SG108S-M2 offers 40 Gbps of switching capacity and supports devices at 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, or 2.5 Gbps speeds.
