articles.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
articles.text:
AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
Using AI to make bionic vision smarter and more precise, scientists are bringing the possibility of restoring sight to people with blindness one step closer to reality.
- Date:
  November 12, 2026
- Source:
  University of California - Santa Barbara
- Summary:
  Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.
The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.
Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.
"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."
How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes
For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.
Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.
The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.
Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."
The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.
Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man
An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.
At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.
When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.
Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.
To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.
Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.
AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise
When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.
Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.
This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.
"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."
The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.
Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person
A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.
This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.
The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.
Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.
The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.
By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.
"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."
A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight
The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."
The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.
Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.
Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Santa Barbara. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Pehuén Moure, Jacob Granley, Fabrizio Grani, Leili Soo, Antonio Lozano, Rocío López-Peco, Adrián Villamarín-Ortiz, Cristina Soto-Sánchez, Shih-Chii Liu, Michael Beyeler, Eduardo Fernández. Deep learning-based control of electrically evoked activity in human visual cortex. Neuron, 2026; DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.07.006

articles.title: Tirar una tostada un poco quemada por miedo al cáncer es un gesto muy común. La evidencia dice que puedes dejar de hacerlo
articles.text:
Hay muchos mensajes en torno a la alimentación que hemos ido escuchando a lo largo de los años, como por ejemplo que comer algo que está un poco quemado puede provocar cáncer. Esto ha hecho que, por ejemplo, cuando tomamos una tostada y se quema un poco más de la cuenta, decidamos tirarla para empezar de cero o raspar sobre el fregadero para minimizar ese "riesgo". Pero... ¿Es verdad?
Podemos estar tranquilos. La respuesta corta a esta pregunta es "no", puesto que no hay pruebas sólidas de que comer pan o alimentos en general que estén un poco quemados aumente el riesgo de provocar cáncer en seres humanos.
¿De dónde viene? Este mensaje nos llega a raíz de experimentos que se hicieron con animales a los que se les expuso a alimentos muy quemados durante mucho tiempo. Pero cuando los epidemiólogos buscan este mismo efecto cancerígeno en una muestra humana muy amplia, el rastro prácticamente desaparece. Lo que sí es cierto es que los organismos europeos siguen recomendando no pasarse con el tostado por un principio básico de precaución.
Lo que hay detrás. La protagonista de esta historia se llama acrilamida, un compuesto químico que se forma de manera natural cuando alimentos ricos en almidón, como el pan, las patatas o las galletas, se cocinan a altas temperaturas al freírlos, hornearlos o tostarlos.
Curiosamente, la acrilamida ya tenía mala fama antes de que nadie supiera que estaba en nuestro desayuno. En 1994, la Agencia Internacional para la Investigación del Cáncer la clasificó dentro del grupo 2A como "probable carcinógeno para los humanos". Sin embargo, aquella evaluación se basó en exposiciones industriales y en estudios con animales, ocho años antes de que un grupo de investigadores suecos descubriera en 2002 que la sustancia se generaba de forma cotidiana en la cocina.
No es muy peligroso. Son muchos los trabajos que han surgido llamando a la calma, como por ejemplo uno de 2015 que analizó 32 estudios sobre 14 tipos de cáncer distintos. Y al final no se encontró asociación relevante para la gran mayoría de tumores, dejando apenas una señal estadística límite en cáncer de riñón y, exclusivamente en mujeres no fumadoras, en endometrio y ovario. Pero años después, un segundo estudio descartó cualquier relación entre la acrilamida de la dieta y el cáncer de riñón.
Y si teníamos alguna duda, un trabajo publicado en 2022 reunió 16 estudios con más de 1,15 millones de personas seguidas durante una mediana de casi 15 años. El resultado apuntó a que no había asociación con ningún cáncer no ginecológico, con la única excepción del cáncer de pulmón en fumadores. Algo que tiene sentido, porque el tabaco contiene una gran cantidad de acrilamida y decenas de carcinógenos que distorsionan cualquier efecto de la dieta.
Se advierte. Como hemos dicho antes, pese a que ahora mismo tenemos artículos publicados de la seguridad de esta molécula, las autoridades europeas siguen siendo muy cautas. Esto se debe sobre todo al mecanismo biológico, puesto que en la evaluación que hizo en 2015 la EFSA se reconoció que las pruebas en humanos eran limitadas y no concluyentes, pero subrayó que en animales la acrilamida son carcinógenos.
Esto hace que, cuando hay un mínimo riesgo de que un compuesto sea un carcinógeno, no se pueda recomendar una "ingesta diaria tolerable". Y esto se suma también a las preocupaciones que hay sobre los estudios poblacionales, ya que es bastante complicado medir lo que comemos para tener una gran exactitud.
Hay que ver lo que se quema. En el día a día se suele meter toda la comida quemada en el mismo saco, pero la realidad es que no es igual. Y es que cuando quemamos una tostada o unas patatas, el compuesto protagonista es la acrilamida, pero cuando se cocina carne o pescado a temperaturas muy altas directamente sobre la llama o en una sartén muy caliente, se forman otras familias químicas como aminas heterocíclicas.
Según detalla el Instituto Nacional del Cáncer, estas sustancias también provocan daños en el ADN y tumores en modelos animales, aunque en aquellos ensayos se administraron dosis equivalentes a miles de veces lo que una persona consumiría en una dieta normal. Al igual que ocurre con la acrilamida, los estudios poblacionales en humanos tampoco han logrado establecer hasta la fecha un vínculo definitivo entre el consumo habitual de aminas heterocíclicas y el desarrollo de cáncer.

articles.title: Microsoft alertó que hackers de China y Corea del Norte automatizaron ataques cibernéticos
articles.text:
Microsoft reveló que grupos de hackers respaldados por los gobiernos de China y Corea del Norte usan ARTEX, un programa de inteligencia artificial que automatiza ataques informáticos y puede pasar de explorar una red a tener acceso persistente y con privilegios en cuestión de minutos, según su equipo de inteligencia de amenazas.
ARTEX salió en julio de 2026 como programa de código abierto, es decir, con el código disponible para cualquiera. Fue concebido para pruebas de intrusión autorizadas, aquellas que las empresas encargan para descubrir sus propias fallas, pero Microsoft detectó que también lo adoptaron atacantes reales.
Microsoft nombró a seis grupos que integraron ARTEX a sus herramientas: Salt Typhoon y Crystal Typhoon, que The Register identificó como chinos; Onyx Sleet y Pearl Sleet, norcoreanos; Storm-0940 y Storm-3358, un grupo con motivación económica. Según ese medio, Storm-0940 está alineado con el Estado chino y Storm-3358 opera desde Camboya.
Cómo funciona un ataque que se maneja solo con IA
Según Microsoft, quien opera ARTEX define el alcance y los objetivos. Después, varios agentes de IA, es decir, asistentes que ejecutan tareas por su cuenta, planifican cada etapa, usan herramientas de ataque, registran los sistemas descubiertos y redactan al final un reporte con cada falla confirmada.
El programa puede conectarse a casi cualquier modelo de lenguaje, incluidos modelos de código abierto o versiones modificadas para quitarles las protecciones. Por eso, advirtió Microsoft, su actividad no queda limitada por los controles de seguridad de un solo proveedor ni es visible en la telemetría de una sola empresa.
ARTEX no inventa técnicas nuevas. Usa herramientas y métodos de intrusión ya conocidos, como la búsqueda de contraseñas débiles, la explotación de fallas en sitios web y la lectura de claves guardadas en archivos de configuración. Lo que cambia es la velocidad: tras vulnerar un sistema, el programa envía de inmediato más agentes a la siguiente etapa.
En la nube, añadió la compañía, los agentes pueden mapear permisos, agregar credenciales para mantener el acceso y asignarse funciones con privilegios elevados.
Campañas ya documentadas y un programa con dueño chino
En las últimas semanas, Microsoft publicó informes sobre varias campañas con ARTEX: búsqueda de claves expuestas en repositorios públicos de código, ataques a la cadena de suministro de software y rastreo de sistemas conectados a internet. The Register recordó que Storm-0940 lo usó en el ataque a ConnectWise, con intentos de inicio de sesión en más de 2.250 cuentas empresariales de Microsoft 365.
El mismo medio mencionó ataques a entidades financieras de Corea del Sur y de India, y señaló que algunas campañas llegaron a acceso con privilegios en menos de tres horas. Esos casos provienen de The Register, no del informe de Microsoft.
El origen del programa es chino. Según Microsoft, el usuario de GitHub Autumn-27 publicó el código en julio con una interfaz en idioma chino y su autor original lo retiró en octubre. Otros desarrolladores ya habían copiado el proyecto, y esas versiones siguen circulando en varios idiomas.
En noviembre, la empresa china de ciberseguridad ThreatBook reclamó la propiedad de ARTEX y empezó a ofrecer acceso comercial a una versión llamada “ARTEX Pro”.
Qué recomienda Microsoft a las organizaciones
La señal más confiable para detectar el programa es su comportamiento: ráfagas de muchas solicitudes distintas en poco tiempo y reintentos de variantes de una misma técnica a velocidad de máquina. Los atacantes cambian con frecuencia datos como la dirección IP o el identificador del navegador, de modo que bloquear esos indicadores no basta.
Microsoft recomienda reducir la exposición de sistemas a internet, proteger credenciales y claves, limitar los caminos de movimiento lateral dentro de la red y activar la interrupción automática de ataques en su plataforma Defender XDR. También sugiere señuelos y sistemas trampa para desviar a los agentes hacia objetivos sin valor.
The Register añadió que el Centro Nacional de Ciberseguridad del Reino Unido emitió esta semana una advertencia sobre este tipo de herramientas ofensivas con IA. Según el centro, su fortaleza es la rapidez y su bajo costo, pero generan mucho ruido en los registros de red, lo que facilita detectarlas.

articles.title: The Best Gaming Monitors: Late 2026 Update
articles.text:
Choosing the best gaming monitor has become considerably more interesting in 2026. OLED prices have continued to fall, newer generations of WOLED and QD-OLED panels have brought meaningful improvements to image quality, and there are some genuinely exciting new display formats at the high end. Even budget LCDs are offering a level of performance and features that would have been difficult to find at these prices a couple of years ago, and that's the way it should be.
For our latest gaming monitor buying guide, we've refreshed our recommendations across 8 categories, from flagship 5K2K ultrawides and premium 4K OLEDs to affordable 1440p displays, mini-LED LCDs, and ultra-high-refresh-rate monitors for competitive gaming. We're also introducing a new category for high-resolution monitors that are particularly well suited to a combination of gaming and productivity.
As always, our recommendations are based on extensive hands-on testing, rather than simply comparing spec sheets. Nearly every monitor featured here has been thoroughly reviewed either on TechSpot or over at Monitors Unboxed, with a few recommendations based on closely related models and familiar panel technology. Our dedicated reviews and more specialized buying guides provide a deeper look at the performance of each display.
Whether you're spending $150 or more than $1,000, there are some excellent options available right now. Here's what we'd buy.
The Ultimate Gaming Monitor
Dell Alienware AW3926QW
For the past few updates, we've recommended that flagship monitor buyers purchase a nice, high-end 32-inch 4K OLED. Those are still great products, but a new category in 2026 has taken over this position at the top of the market. In our opinion, the best gaming monitor format right now is the 39-inch 5K2K ultrawide. If you're going to spend over $1,000 on a display, this is where we'd be spending that money.
A 39-inch 5K2K display, with a resolution of 5120x2160 and a 21:9 aspect ratio, is a large, immersive format for gaming. It's the same height as a 32-inch 4K 16:9 monitor, but with an additional 20cm of width, enveloping substantially more of your field of view. The latest models released in 2026 include crucial upgrades that mean they no longer lag behind other high-end panel types. They're finally in a position where we can wholeheartedly recommend them.
The best 39-inch 5K2K OLED monitor is the Dell Alienware AW3926QW, which has just hit a new all-time low price of $1,000. Even at its regular $1,100 MSRP, we think this display is a great buy. It uses a Tandem WOLED panel with an RGB Stripe subpixel layout, has a beautiful glossy finish that preserves deep blacks, and performs really well across most areas. It's actually the monitor I personally use for gaming, and I've gone into considerable detail about why I made that decision in a separate feature.
In our opinion, the best gaming monitor format right now is the 39-inch 5K2K ultrawide. If you're going to spend over $1,000 on a display, this is where we'd be spending that money. It's the same height as a 32-inch 4K 16:9 monitor, but with an additional 20cm of width, enveloping substantially more of your field of view.
The 5K2K resolution is a big upgrade over previous ultrawides of this size, as this level of pixel density is necessary to produce a crisp image on such a huge screen. It uses a pleasant 1500R curve, rather than the overly aggressive 800R curvature found on some competing monitors, and the OLED technology is current-generation Tandem WOLED, the latest from LG Display.
It offers great HDR performance, including decent peak brightness, vibrant colors, true zero-level blacks, and amazing contrast. Dell has also done a wonderful job of calibrating the screen, even offering several useful HDR modes.
As with all products, there are some drawbacks, the main one being its 165Hz refresh rate. We'd have loved to see this monitor offer 240Hz, but currently no 5K2K ultrawide does. Still, as this monitor is designed primarily for immersive single-player experiences, 165Hz is sufficient.
Some aspects of performance are less impressive than we'd have liked, such as panel dimming and uniformity, which you can learn more about in our full review. But these drawbacks aren't significant enough to stop us from recommending the AW3926QW, especially considering its outstanding value at the standard $1,100 asking price.
LG 39GX950B
The other main option at this size is the LG 39GX950B, though the panel itself is different, with LG opting for the RGWB subpixel version and a matte screen coating.
The LG model is still a great monitor, but we don't think it performs as well as the Dell overall, and it's more expensive. Unless you specifically want a feature the LG offers, we'd just get the AW3926QW. Make sure to update the firmware if you do end up purchasing one, though, as the latest version includes some crucial fixes.
Best Premium 4K Gaming Monitor
Gigabyte Aorus FO32U24G | Asus ROG XG32UQWMS
If you're after a high-end gaming monitor in the $700 to $900 range, or simply don't want a massive 39-inch ultrawide, this is where we think a 32-inch 4K 240Hz OLED makes sense. These are fantastic displays, offering a large screen size, high resolution and refresh rate, plus all the latest benefits of OLED technology.
There are so many 32-inch 4K OLED panel options right now, including WOLED and QD-OLED variants spanning several generations of each technology. No option is perfect, as both WOLED and QD-OLED have their strengths and weaknesses, but we think the best option for most people right now is a Tandem WOLED display using the RGWB subpixel layout. This is the very latest generation of the technology, found in displays that have only just hit the market.
No option is perfect, as both WOLED and QD-OLED have their strengths and weaknesses, but we think the best option for most people right now is Tandem WOLED.
This panel offers a combination of strengths that sets it apart from competing QD-OLEDs and other WOLED formats. One major advantage is the screen coating. Tandem WOLED is available with a glossy finish that does a fantastic job of preserving deep blacks across a range of lighting conditions.
Gigabyte Aorus Elite FO32U24G
Another advantage is more consistent HDR brightness across both bright and dark scenes: you won't find panel dimming here. This leads to better-looking HDR without having to constantly fiddle with the settings. You also get dual-mode functionality, offering a 1080p 480Hz configuration that increases motion clarity compared to the standard 4K 240Hz mode, making it suitable for fast-paced competitive gaming.
Aside from these competitive advantages, the WOLED RGWB panel is just fantastic, and the monitors using it are excellent. You get the usual exceptionally fast response times, great color calibration, high HDR brightness, and strong feature sets.
This 2026 panel is used in both the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS and Gigabyte Aorus Elite FO32U24G. We've tested both and found the Gigabyte model to be slightly better, but both monitors are great buys in our opinion. The Asus model has been available for as little as $700 on sale, which is an exceptionally good deal, but even its $900 MSRP is reasonable.
What about QD-OLED alternatives?
You should buy a QD-OLED instead if you don't want to deal with Tandem WOLED's biggest flaw: dark gray banding. Choosing to avoid this issue comes with a trade-off, of course, as QD-OLED has its own set of issues, including raised blacks and HDR panel dimming. But some buyers find the gray banding on WOLEDs extremely annoying, so if you think this will be a deal-breaker for you, just get a QD-OLED. We'd also recommend a QD-OLED if you want higher color brightness and a less reflective screen coating.
The other reason to get a QD-OLED is pricing. The XG32UQWMS is a great buy at $700 and one of the cheapest 32-inch 4K OLEDs on the market at that price. But it's not always available for $700, given its $900 MSRP.
Gigabyte MO32U24
In those situations, QD-OLED can be cheaper, with models like the MSI 321UPX starting at $700 and the Gigabyte MO32U24 offering a newer generation panel at $800. These are worth considering if Tandem WOLED options are too expensive in your region. As they're still 32-inch 4K 240Hz models, they offer the same motion clarity and all the usual benefits of OLED's per-pixel control.
Lastly, it's worth noting that in the first quarter of 2027, Samsung Display will be releasing a new generation of 32-inch 4K panels equipped with a 360Hz refresh rate and upgraded brightness. It could be worth waiting for these new monitors if you're planning on buying something high-end.
We expect pricing to start north of $1,000, so they might not be overly competitive with existing $800 Tandem WOLEDs or QD-OLEDs, but the specifications revealed so far are tantalizing.
Best 1440p OLED Gaming
Gigabyte MO27Q28GR
The best mid-range gaming monitors on the market right now are 1440p OLEDs, and you won't need to break the bank to get one. While we generally consider the mid-range of the monitor market to be around $500, you can now pick up some very good 1440p OLEDs for around $400, occasionally even less if you find a particularly good deal.
As with the 32-inch 4K category, at 1440p you need to choose between a WOLED or QD-OLED panel, and the pros and cons of each type are similar to what we discussed in the previous section. We've covered the differences in detail in a separate feature, but as with 32-inch 4K models, we generally believe that 1440p Tandem WOLED panels are the best overall.
The best mid-range gaming monitors on the market right now are 1440p OLEDs, and you won't need to break the bank to get one.
Our primary recommendation in this category is the Gigabyte MO27Q28GR, a 27-inch 1440p 280Hz WOLED using the latest generation of panel technology. While normally priced around $500, you can grab this display for less than $430 right now. The GR model that we'd recommend to most people uses a fantastic glossy screen coating, but you can save a small amount by going with a matte coating instead, as Gigabyte's MO27Q28G is just $400 right now. The G and GR variants are virtually identical in performance outside of the differences in screen coating.
The MO27Q28GR provides great brightness across SDR and HDR modes, typically offering a brighter experience than competing QD-OLEDs. HDR brightness is also much more consistent between different types of scenes, as there's no QD-OLED-like panel dimming. This means you get a combination of higher peak brightness in favorable conditions, and more impactful, accurate HDR in brighter scenes. It's a significant factor in why we recommend Tandem WOLED and why we prefer its HDR experience.
The Gigabyte models offer a good set of features, including black frame insertion, an anti-flicker mode, USB-C input, and a KVM switch. They also perform well in color accuracy tests and offer excellent motion clarity thanks to their 280Hz refresh rate.
Asus ROG Strix XG27AQWMG
The Asus ROG Strix XG27AQWMG is another option that performs very well, and we've seen it for just $400 when on sale. However, its standard price of $650 is higher than the Gigabyte models. It's not significantly better, so we'd get whichever model is cheaper.
More affordable 1440p QD-OLEDs
Again, 1440p QD-OLEDs are a suitable alternative in this category if you don't like the idea of dark gray banding, want higher color brightness or lower reflectivity, or simply want to save some money. In some regions, the price difference is substantially in favor of QD-OLED, so be sure to check the full range of options available to you.
Dell Alienware AW2725D
We can comfortably recommend the Dell Alienware AW2725D at just $350. This is a 27-inch 1440p 280Hz QD-OLED model that uses the full-brightness panel from Samsung Display.
Usually in this price range we only see the limited-brightness QD-OLED Edge panels, which are a bit of a trap as they only offer 400 nits of HDR brightness instead of 1,000 nits. But at least right now, the AW2725D is $350, which is an absolute steal and an all-time low price.
The AW2725D is one of our favorite models to use the 280Hz panel, and it recently performed well in our budget 1440p QD-OLED roundup. It offers solid calibration, a good refresh rate, strong HDR brightness, and a great design.
Even with the Alienware at just $350, we'd still lean toward Tandem WOLED at $400 to $430, as we think those panels are better overall. But this is an amazing bang-for-your-buck product if you can't quite stretch your budget that far or would be annoyed by dark gray banding.
Gigabyte MO27Q2A
One alternative to the AW2725D that has consistently been available at a great price over the last few months is the Gigabyte MO27Q2A, which uses the same 1440p 280Hz QD-OLED panel. While we haven't tested this specific model, we're familiar with how the panel performs and have been impressed with the quality of Gigabyte's recent displays, so we're comfortable recommending it.
For really budget-conscious shoppers who can't justify spending $350 or $400 on a gaming monitor, this is where the limited-brightness QD-OLED panels make more sense. We'd want a decent discount, though. Right now, with the AW2725D at $350, it's hard to justify saving just $50 to grab a 240Hz model that doesn't properly display HDR content.
The Gigabyte GO27Q24A, for example, is a great choice among displays that use the limited-brightness panel, but at $300 we'd just spend the extra $50 to grab the 280Hz Alienware.
Alienware AW2726DM
The Alienware AW2726DM is approaching the sort of price range where it makes sense to grab a dirt-cheap QD-OLED, as it's currently available at an all-time low of $280. However, these discounts may not last, so as a general rule, we'd want to see at least a 20% price gap between limited-brightness and full-brightness models. You can learn about several other options in our recent budget QD-OLED roundup.
Best 4K Mini-LED Gaming Monitor
MSI 274URDFW E16M | Koorui S2741LM
Something we regularly hear from a subset of our readers is that they want to spend $300 to $500 on a monitor capable of gaming, but for one reason or another don't want to purchase an OLED. And there are several valid reasons for that.
If you do a lot of productivity work on your display, the prospect of OLED burn-in over time is not ideal. You may want a higher resolution than 1440p, but can't justify spending at least $600 on a 27-inch 4K OLED. Or maybe you want to enjoy HDR gaming with a ton of brightness and punch, in which case a mini-LED LCD is a great option.
If you're after a mid-range LCD monitor priced between $300 and $500, we'd generally recommend a 27-inch 4K mini-LED LCD. You can also purchase 1440p displays with refresh rates of 300Hz or higher in this category, but on balance, we think 4K mini-LED makes the most sense, especially if you're looking for a hybrid gaming and productivity display.
MSI MPG 274URDFW E16M
Late last year, we tested several 27-inch 4K mini-LED LCDs in a dedicated roundup and found that all of them were great buys, with a variety of strengths depending on the product in question. It's well worth checking out that roundup for more details, but in short, right now we'd be looking at either the MSI MPG 274URDFW E16M or the Koorui S2741LM, both of which are available for $400. The MSI's regular price is on the higher end, normally around $500, but at $400 it's a much better buy.
Both models use a 27-inch 4K IPS LCD panel with a 160Hz refresh rate and a 1,152-zone mini-LED backlight. With full-array local dimming, these 4K LCDs are genuinely capable of displaying HDR images properly, unlike fake HDR products that lack local dimming and are often labeled with misleading "HDR 400" specifications.
Koorui S2741LM
Having 1,152 backlight zones allows for a substantial increase in contrast over SDR monitors, with deeper blacks and decent control over individual areas of the screen, meaning bright and dark elements can be displayed at the same time. This creates the dazzling, impressive HDR effect that you're paying for. It's not simply a matter of running the screen at a higher brightness level.
Having 1,000+ backlight zones gets you the impressive HDR effect you're paying for. It's not simply a matter of running the screen at a higher brightness level. In the right circumstances, these LCDs can look remarkably similar to an OLED.
Speaking of brightness, these monitors are capable of some very impressive results, especially in brighter scenes. The Koorui achieves over 1,600 nits in real-scene tests. Along with good shadow detail and a fast dimming response, we get solid performance for HDR gaming that takes things to the next level relative to cheaper SDR products. In the right circumstances, these LCDs can look remarkably similar to an OLED.
Motion performance is pretty good across these models. They're typical fast IPS panels, with different levels of optimization depending on the model you get. The 1080p 320Hz dual mode increases motion clarity for multiplayer gaming, making these quite versatile products: HDR gaming in single-player titles, 320Hz gaming in multiplayer titles, and productivity work without the risk of burn-in.
AOC U27G4XM
The AOC U27G4XM is also an option at just $350, though we don't think it's quite as good as the MSI or Koorui models. Whether or not the $50 saving is worth it depends entirely on whether you prioritize value or performance. The AOC model performs well, so we still recommend it, but the others have stronger feature sets.
Best Affordable Gaming Monitors
Gigabyte M27Q2 QD | AOC Q27G40XMN
Good news for anyone shopping for a budget gaming monitor: we recently published a roundup looking at nine different 27-inch 1440p LCDs, all priced below $200. That's by far the best resource for exploring which entry-level option you should buy, and it goes into considerably more detail than we'll cover here. Of the options we've tested, there are two standouts.
The Gigabyte M27Q2 QD, or M27Q2 SA in some regions, is a fantastic $160 gaming monitor offering a 1440p 210Hz IPS LCD panel. It has a wider color gamut than most of its competitors and better response time tuning, including variable overdrive and a single overdrive mode experience. It also has a height-adjustable stand with excellent overall build quality, both USB-C and a KVM switch, which are rare in this price tier, and a good set of gaming features. The only drawback is that color calibration isn't as strong as on the best models.
Other monitors priced around $160 might match the M27Q2 QD in a couple of areas, but not as a complete package. Some might have comparable response time tuning but only offer a fixed-height stand. Others might be better calibrated but have a smaller color gamut and a limited port selection.
It's the balance of performance, a strong feature set, and excellent design that makes the M27Q2 QD our go-to choice.
Best Value HDR option
The other option we highly recommend is the AOC Q27G40XMN. This is the clear winner if you want a display with HDR, and for a lot of gamers it's probably what we'd recommend overall, especially for those who primarily play single-player games. It's one of very few models at $200 that offer true HDR capabilities, thanks to a 1,152-zone backlight and brightness output approaching 1,400 nits.
AOC Q27G40XMN
There are some caveats, though. It has a fixed-height stand, which is disappointing. Response time performance is average at best, although not too bad considering it's a VA LCD panel, and viewing angles are weak relative to the IPS alternatives. But it has an amazing contrast ratio, deep blacks, and real HDR capabilities. It's definitely a product to consider if it's available in your region.
There were other models in our roundup that we found to be reasonable and could be worth considering depending on pricing in your region. These include the LG 27G610A, KTC H27T6, and Asus TUF Gaming VG27AQL5A. Check out the full roundup for more information. However, if these products are the same price or more expensive than the Gigabyte M27Q2 QD, just get the Gigabyte. It's the better monitor.
Best for Competitive Gaming
G-Sync Pulsar | MSI MAG 272QP X50
A lot of the monitors in this buying guide so far have been all-rounder picks, suitable for many use cases, or even leaning toward single-player gaming. But if you primarily play competitive multiplayer games and want to prioritize motion clarity, input latency, and speed, we have a different set of recommendations catering specifically to those characteristics.
There are essentially two ways you can go here. A G-Sync Pulsar monitor is a great choice if you want the absolute best motion clarity. The other main choice is an ultra-high-refresh-rate OLED monitor, which might be the best option if you want speed while retaining the image quality and HDR benefits of an OLED display.
G-Sync Pulsar
G-Sync Pulsar is revolutionary because it allows you to use backlight strobing and variable refresh simultaneously. If you're not familiar with backlight strobing, it's a technology that pulses the backlight on and off between refresh cycles, instead of holding the image on screen for the full cycle. This impulse-based approach significantly reduces persistence blur. When your eyes track objects across the screen, the impulse essentially performs some visual trickery, allowing your brain to perceive the object with greater clarity.
G-Sync Pulsar is flawless in how it handles variable refresh, giving you the full benefit of strobing across its supported variable refresh rate range. You no longer have to run games at a specific fixed refresh rate and disable crucial features to get the best motion clarity.
This has big benefits in games where motion clarity is important, like fast-paced shooters, racing games, and anything that requires tracking enemies, objects, or even text in motion.
In our testing earlier this year, we found that 1440p 360Hz G-Sync Pulsar displays look clearer than OLEDs at high refresh rates, and much clearer at moderate to lower refresh rates.
This makes Pulsar the clearer technology in a wide range of situations, whether you're playing lightweight games that run at really high frame rates or typically play at, say, 120 fps. And Pulsar just works in all these situations. You enable it and away you go, with no need for further configuration.
As for specific monitors, there are four G-Sync Pulsar options on the market: the Asus ROG Strix Pulsar XG27AQNGV, MSI MPG 272QRF X36, AOC Agon Pro AG276QSG2, and Acer Predator XB273U F5. We're still working on full reviews of the Asus and MSI models, but all four use the same panel and offer the same G-Sync Pulsar functionality. The Asus and MSI models seem very solid based on what we've seen so far, and both have been available for less than $400, which is a fantastic price given that they debuted above $600 earlier this year.
Ultra-high-refresh-rate OLEDs
An alternative to G-Sync Pulsar is a high-refresh-rate OLED. This will be a better option if you'd prefer the superior image quality of an OLED panel versus an IPS LCD, want proper HDR functionality, or don't have an Nvidia GeForce GPU, as that's required for Pulsar.
If you're sensitive to the flicker of backlight strobing, you may also find OLED more comfortable to view, although OLED still exhibits a slight, rapid flicker during normal operation that causes eye strain for a tiny percentage of people.
Asus ROG Swift PG27AQWP-W
The best high-refresh-rate OLED is the Asus ROG Swift PG27AQWP-W, which uses a 27-inch 1440p 540Hz Tandem WOLED panel. This is a very similar display to the 280Hz Tandem WOLEDs we discussed in an earlier section, except with the refresh rate increased to 540Hz. It also offers a 720p 720Hz dual mode, which you might find useful in some situations, though I generally found the resolution to be too low.
While 540Hz Tandem WOLED is the best option in this category, the Asus model is extremely expensive at over $1,000. For most people, we think opting for a 500Hz QD-OLED makes a lot more sense, as they're priced closer to $500 to $600 these days.
MSI MAG 272QP X50
We'd be looking at the MSI MAG 272QP X50, and you can learn more about the available options in several of our other features, including our 500Hz monitor roundup and our dedicated 1440p and OLED buying guides.
High-refresh-rate 1080p OLEDs have also come onto the market over the last month or so, targeting hardcore competitive gamers who love the 24.5-inch display format. They're worth exploring as well, and we'll be reviewing them shortly.
Best Ultrawides: 34" and Larger
Dell Alienware AW3426DW | Alienware AW3926QW
The best ultrawide category is fairly straightforward. The ultimate choice is the Dell Alienware AW3926QW, which we already covered in the best flagship monitor section. If you're after a 39-inch ultrawide panel, that's the one to get.
But there are several other excellent options if you want a different panel size. In the 34-inch category, the best monitors right now use the latest 3440x1440 QD-OLED panel, released this year with an RGB Stripe subpixel layout and improvements to brightness and screen coating. This panel is primarily available in two versions, one with a 280Hz refresh rate and one with a 360Hz refresh rate. Our testing has shown these panels to be identical in performance outside of the refresh rate.
Naturally, the 360Hz version is better because of its higher refresh rate, making it the best overall option on the market at this size in terms of performance. But there's usually a decent price difference between the 360Hz and 280Hz models, which makes the 280Hz versions better value and ultimately the better buy in most situations.
MSI MPG 341CQR X36
For example, the MSI MPG 341CQR X36 is a great 360Hz variant that costs $900 these days. If you really want the highest refresh rate, it's the option we'd get. It's even been on sale for as little as $800, but is currently out of stock at that price. The 280Hz variants, which aren't that much slower, are available for just $650, though. The Dell Alienware AW3426DW is a monitor we've tested that offers excellent performance and recently dropped to an all-time low of $650, so that's the model we'd be looking at.
The MSI 341CQP X28 and Asus XG34WCDMS are also products to look out for. With the 280Hz models, you could potentially save over 25% by shaving a bit off the refresh rate for what is otherwise the same QD-OLED panel experience.
Going even bigger: 45-inch ultrawides
If you're interested in a larger ultrawide, our recommendation here is unchanged: the best 45-inch OLED ultrawide is still the LG 45GX950A. It has a massive 45-inch 5120x2160 WOLED panel running at 165Hz, providing an incredible level of immersion. We're not as fond of this monitor as we are of the 39-inch alternatives, as it's using slightly older panel technology and a more aggressive 800R curve.
LG 45GX950A
But it's still a decent display for those building simulator rigs or other setups that require a huge monitor.
Best 5K and 6K Monitors for Gaming and Productivity
LG 27GM950B | Samsung Odyssey G80HS
Our final category is a new addition to this buying guide: high-resolution monitors. By that we mean resolutions higher than 4K, which these days has become a fairly standard option in the premium segment.
You might be wondering why someone would even want a higher-than-4K monitor for gaming, but the primary reason actually has little to do with gaming. Higher resolutions like 5K and 6K offer greater pixel densities and more screen real estate, which is even better for productivity work. Once you get above 200 PPI on a desktop monitor, the image is remarkably crisp, with exceptionally sharp text.
High-DPI displays don't normally provide significant benefits specifically for gaming, but the latest high-resolution monitors have a few tricks up their sleeves that make them great choices as dual-use displays.
LG 27GM950B
For a start, new products released in 2026 finally offer decent refresh rates at their native resolutions. The Samsung Odyssey G80HS and LG 27GM950B are native 6K 165Hz and 5K 165Hz displays, respectively. These are refresh rates that are actually suitable for gaming and offer huge improvements in smoothness for productivity work.
Once you've upgraded from a 60Hz display to a 165Hz display, you'll never want to go back to 60Hz again, regardless of what you're doing.
Once you've upgraded from a 60Hz display to a 165Hz display, you'll never want to go back to 60Hz again, regardless of what you're doing. Most gamers probably won't want to deal with the performance costs of gaming at 5K or 6K, even if the refresh rate is 165Hz. It's a great experience in lightweight games where you can enjoy the exceptionally high resolution, but most AAA titles are difficult to run at these resolutions, especially 6K.
Samsung Odyssey G80HS
However, both models offer a 330Hz dual mode that runs at a lower resolution, purpose-built for gaming. On the 27GM950B it's 1440p 330Hz, and on the G80HS it's 3K 330Hz. Both 1440p and 3K are great resolutions for gaming and are significantly less demanding on GPU hardware. This is where these monitors become great choices for a mixture of productivity and gaming.
You can use the 5K or 6K modes in desktop applications, benefiting from the exceptionally high resolution and screen real estate, then switch to the 1440p or 3K modes for higher-performance gaming without sacrificing too much image clarity. It all works surprisingly well and finally brings high-DPI panels into the modern era of gaming monitors.
The LG 27GM950B is the 5K 165Hz option we've tested. It uses a 27-inch IPS LCD panel and has a mini-LED backlight with 2,304 zones, so it offers proper HDR functionality. It's a great option, but when we reviewed it, we found the $1,200 MSRP to be a bit high, considering some 4K OLEDs are half the price. These days, though, it's available for $800, which is much more reasonable if the combination of a 5K panel and mini-LED backlight sounds appealing.
Samsung Odyssey G80HS
The Samsung Odyssey G80HS is a 6K 165Hz model using a 32-inch IPS LCD panel. It has a similar pixel density to the 5K model, but at a larger screen size. Unfortunately, Samsung's design does not include a mini-LED backlight, which is a bit of a letdown considering the high price, but it's essentially the only 6K panel suitable for gaming right now. As with the LG, we thought its MSRP of $1,600 was far too high, but these days it will set you back just $1,100, putting it in a much better position.
We don't expect either of these monitors to be at the top of most people's lists when shopping for a gaming display. But for those who want the exceptional text clarity of a high-DPI productivity monitor without giving up the speed and responsiveness of a modern gaming display, it's great to finally see these sorts of options debut in 2026.

articles.title: Xpeng s’attaque à Porsche et Audi avec sa magnifique P7 qui arrive enfin en Europe : pourquoi on a hâte
articles.text:
Arrivé en France en 2024, Xpeng voit sa gamme européenne s’étoffer de jour en jour.
Après le lancement successif du L03 et du G9L et à quelques semaines de l’arrivée du L05, la marque chinoise profite du Salon de Canton pour confirmer l’arrivée de la P7, une berline électrique que les fans réclament depuis sa présentation en Chine.
Berline ou coupé 4 portes ?
Le nom de « Xpeng P7 » n’est pas inconnu en Europe, puisque la marque y a déjà vendu une berline de ce nom il y a quelques années, et que la P7+ est en vente en France depuis déjà plusieurs mois.
Reste que, entre la nouvelle P7 (nommée P7 Next à son lancement) et la P7+, il y a un monde, tant la nouvelle venue mise sur un design unique.
Votre production solaire dépasse votre consommation ? Stockez le surplus au lieu de le revendre à bas prix. Le SolarFlow 2400 AC+ se branche sur votre installation existante, 100 % plug-and-play, et s’amortit plus vite grâce au Black Friday.
    Pour aller plus loin
On a roulé avec la nouvelle Xpeng P7 en Chine : moins chère et bien mieux équipée qu’une Tesla
            
La signature lumineuse de la face avant, le profil de coupé 4 portes et les proportions remarquables (5,02 m de long dont 3,01 m d’empattement, 1,97 m de large et 1,43 m de haut) feront assurément tourner les têtes.
À l’intérieur, Xpeng promet que sa P7 vendue en Chine propose un coffre de 575 litres à l’arrière et 56 litres à l’avant. La planche de bord fait la part belle aux écrans (dalle centrale pivotable de 15,6 pouces, combiné conducteur, vision tête-haute, écran pour les passagers arrière), quitte à délaisser les boutons physiques.
Une arrivée en 2027, avec encore des zones d’ombre
Cette annonce n’est en soi pas une surprise, puisque des cadres de Xpeng avaient déjà évoqué l’arrivée de la P7 en Europe il y a quelques mois.
Reste que le communiqué promet que « la nouvelle P7 destinée à l’Europe bénéficiera de caractéristiques techniques spécifiquement adaptées aux marchés européens », de quoi garder le suspens sur sa fiche technique.
En Chine, la berline peut développer jusqu’à 437 kW (594 ch) et 695 Nm de couple, de quoi passer de 0 à 100 km/h en 3,7 secondes. Côté batteries, la version la plus endurante promet 820 km d’autonomie selon le cycle chinois CLTC (environ 700 km selon le cycle européen WLTP selon nos estimations), tout en pouvant se recharger de 10 à 80 % en 12 minutes – et peut-être bientôt 10,7 minutes grâce à la récente mise à jour à distance.
Enfin, ses puces Turing développées en interne lui permettront d’être compatible avec le NGP, le système de conduite semi-autonome de Xpeng et concurrent du FSD de Tesla.
    Pour aller plus loin
Lâcher les mains en ville : un an après Tesla, Xpeng vous fait tester son NGP à Paris
            
Xpeng nous donne rendez-vous début 2027 pour connaître les tarifs et les détails de cette nouvelle P7. Sachez que la P7+ oscille entre 45 990 et 53 990 euros en France avec une fiche technique plus modeste.
Comment la marque va-t-elle différencier ses deux berlines ? La P7 réussira-t-elle à se battre contre un Porsche Taycan ou une Audi A6 e-tron ? Réponse dans quelques mois.

articles.title: CRTC says Bell, Rogers, Telus violated junk fee rules
articles.text:
Amidst the chaos of Black Friday deals, the CRTC published decisions related to carriers’ junk fees and 60-day phone locking schemes.
“Following a public proceeding, the CRTC determined that some providers were in violation of the Telecommunications Act. As a result, it is requiring them to stop charging certain fees by the end of this year. These include fees for providing and setting up cellphones when signing up for a service plan,” the commission explained in a release on Friday.
“The CRTC also determined that a provider violated consumer protection measures by locking cellphones for up to 60 days. The CRTC will consider whether they should face a penalty of up to $10 million.”
While the CRTC didn’t name the carrier in its initial release, a separate document containing the full decision cites Bell as the carrier that didn’t provide unlocked phones.
Junk fees decision
Let’s start with a bit of context. The CRTC banned junk fees (like connection fees) that carriers charge when customers activate a new line back in June. However, the Big Three — Rogers, Bell, and Telus — moved quickly to introduce new fees they claimed didn’t violate the rules. The CRTC told the carriers to stop and started a review of the new fees, bringing us to today’s decision.
“Based on the record of the proceeding, the Commission finds that the cellphone handling charge from Bell Canada, the cellphone setup charge from Rogers, and the SIM and eSIM provisioning fee from TELUS are prohibited. The Commission also finds that the fees charged by Rogers and TELUS to replace broken or lost SIM cards are not prohibited, nor are the shipping fees charged by Rogers,” the commission said in its decision.
The CRTC specifically called out Bell and Rogers for their respective device handling and setup fees, and Telus for charging SIM and eSIM provisioning fees to new customers. However, the commission also acknowledges that Rogers’ hardware shipping fee, as well as SIM replacement fees, aren’t prohibited under the junk fee rules.
Further, the CRTC directed the Big Three to stop charging the prohibited fees by no later than Dec. 27, 2026. However, that deadline leaves me wondering what will happen for customers who have already had to pay the fees — such as, for example, people shopping Black Friday deals today or Boxing Day deals next month.
Elsewhere in the decision, the CRTC said that it won’t charge administrative monetary penalties (AMPs) at this time, but said it would “continue to actively monitor fees and is ready to take further enforcement action against [providers] that charge prohibited fees.”
Phone locking
The phone locking saga has been going on for some time, dating back years. It largely centres on Bell, though Telus got involved in recent months.
The CRTC banned the practice of locking phones to a network back in 2017, making it much easier (and cheaper!) for Canadians to change wireless providers. However, carriers have criticized the move, in particular claiming it has enabled more theft and fraud.
In April 2025, Bell started locking devices for up to 60 days after activation. The CRTC ordered Bell to stop the practice, but Bell continued. Then, in July 2026, Telus asked the CRTC to pause and permanently change the phone locking rules, claiming that Bell’s 60-day phone lock made its own devices more appealing targets for theft and fraud.
The CRTC issued two decisions related to phone locking. The first was for Bell, in which the commission found “that Bell Canada failed to comply with the Wireless Code” by locking devices for 60 days and is considering fining the carrier.
“The Commission is of the preliminary view that the imposition of an administrative monetary penalty (AMP) of up to $10 million may be appropriate.”
The CRTC has asked for comments on the matter, with a deadline of Jan. 15, 2027. Moreover, Bell can respond by Jan. 22, 2027.
The second decision was directed to Telus over the carrier’s request for a pause on the phone locking rules and ultimately authorization from the CRTC to lock phones for 60 days following activation.
In short, the CRTC denied Telus’ request, noting that it already granted carriers the ability to lock phones for two business days. Further, the commission said that discussions on a permanent change to phone locking rules should take place as part of its ongoing review of the consumer protection codes.
Notably, as part of that review, several carriers have already asked the CRTC to change consumer protections, including the phone locking rules. Other consumer protections carriers sought to have removed include clawbacks for sign-up benefits, roaming caps, and extended financing offers.

articles.title: Apple’s latest AirTags have dropped to just $18 a pop for Black Friday
articles.text:
If you’re tired of constantly scrounging around for your lost belongings, Apple’s second-gen AirTags are on sale for an all-time low of $18 at Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy. The handy location trackers have a list price of $29 each, but have been consistently available for around $24 since Amazon Prime Day in late June.
Apple’s latest AirTags have dropped to just $18 a pop for Black Friday
With a longer range, more precise tracking, and a louder chime, the new(er) AirTag could save you from a big headache.
The upgraded ultra-wideband chip and improved Bluetooth in the latest AirTag should provide more precise location tracking, with a range 1.5x wider than the first-gen model. The internal speaker is also 50 percent louder than the original, making it easier to find whatever item your AirTag is attached to, whether it’s buried deep in your couch cushions or at the bottom of your bag. Even without those improvements, though, AirTags are still a great option for Apple users looking for their keys or luggage, with up to a year of battery life on a single coin cell battery and compatibility with both iPhones and newer Apple Watch models.

articles.title: Xpeng humanoid robot makes 'ominous' public debut — as co-president says it will hit homes in 'one to two years'
articles.text:
Xpeng’s ‘human-like’ robot will hit homes in ‘one to two years’ — Iron humanoid combines 1,500 touch sensors with solid-state battery
We can see where those Westworld comparisons come from
- Xpeng's Iron humanoid robot just got its first public showing in China
- It will start life in retail stores in early 2027, before heading to homes
- The robot will cost as much as Xpeng's EVs, or around $18,000 / £14,000 / AU$27,000
Xpeng revealed the latest generation of its Iron humanoid robot at the company’s AI day this week, telling reporters that it could be doing household chores in “one or two years”, according to CNBC.
Taking to the stage in front of a live audience, Iron wowed crowds with its extremely natural walking gait and ability to interact with humans, including giving those in attendance a high-five or greeting them with a wave.
Brian Gu, co-president of Xpeng, has previously been open about similarities with Tesla, with any mention of Elon Musk’s company generally taken as a compliment. Alongside its EV business, it is also actively pursuing AI, autonomous driving and humanoid robots.
Gu revealed that the company hoped to train its general-purpose humanoid as a store assistant at its retail locations in the first quarter of next year, with mass production starting in January.
Speaking to Bloomberg, Gu predicted that the Iron robot could be sold to consumers in China at the average price of one of its EVs, which generally cost around 119,800 yuan (around $18,000 / £14,000 / AU$27,000) to 309,800 yuan (around $46,500 / £35,000/ AU$70,000).
It has targets to sell "tens of thousands" of its humanoid robots in 2027, which Gu described as a critical year for scaling up and commercializing the business, according to Bloomberg.
After its initial run as a store assistant, Gu hopes that the company can “start thinking about deploying into home settings”.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Analysis: Still a long road to the mainstream
Humans will naturally approach our potential robotic overlords with some degree of trepidation — and Reddit was awash with comments about how the Xpeng Iron’s glowing eyes look “ominous” and how designers clearly took inspiration from an “alien corpse”.
Referring to an image of the 'Drone Hosts' from a popular HBO sci-fi series, one Reddit commenter even went as far to say: “Literally these things in Westworld (spoiler, it does not end well for humans)”.
But Xpeng has big plans for its general-purpose robots, with targets to scale up production next year and begin selling them in large number thereafter. However, that is a lot easier said than done.
So far, Tesla’s Optimus has been met with similar levels of skepticism, with critics pointing out the reliance on teleoperation during early demonstrations.
A particularly damming video showing Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff failing to instruct Optimus to fetch him a soda resulted in tech founder Hamid Shojaee calling it "literally the worst humanoid robot demo I have seen”.
Like Tesla, Xpeng is moving away from simply producing cutting-edge electric vehicles to developing physical AI, autonomous driving and even flying vehicles.
Tellingly, Brian Gu told CNBC: “It’s much easier to be profitable for the robotics business than the autos business.”
But there’s a massive gulf between humanoids performing very specific, repetitive tasks in a manufacturing environment and the legalities of them operating freely in a domestic setting.
The internet can breathe a sigh of relief, as the latter is still likely a long way from becoming a reality. Either that, or I'll be among the first to become a robo-slave.

Leon has been navigating a world where automotive and tech collide for almost 20 years, reporting on everything from in-car entertainment to robotised manufacturing plants. Currently, EVs are the focus of his attentions, but give it a few years and it will be electric vertical take-off and landing craft. Outside of work hours, he can be found tinkering with distinctly analogue motorcycles, because electric motors are no replacement for an old Honda inline four.

articles.title: Der Sommer wird im Winter gewonnen: EcoFlow STREAM
articles.text:
Zum Black Friday bei Ecoflow den Heimspeicher fürs Frühjahr sichern
Ecoflow stellt seine Aktion unter das Motto „Der Sommer wird im Winter gewonnen“. Dahinter steckt eine einfache Rechnung: Wer den Speicher jetzt zum Aktionspreis kauft und ihn in den Wintermonaten anschließen lässt, startet mit einem betriebsbereiten System in die ertragreiche Saison und verschenkt keinen sonnigen Frühlingstag.
Welcher STREAM-Speicher passt zur Anlage?
Auf dem Papier sind beide Modelle nahezu identisch, beide haben eine Nennkapazität von 5,024 kWh. Der entscheidende Unterschied liegt darin, auf welchem Weg der Solarstrom in den Akku gelangt. Davon hängt ab, für wen sich welches Modell eignet.
Solarmodule erzeugen Gleichstrom, Haushaltsgeräte brauchen Wechselstrom. Der STREAM 5000 übernimmt beide Seiten in einem Gerät. Die Module werden direkt an den Speicher angeschlossen. Ein eingebauter Solarladeregler bestimmt, mit welcher Spannung und welchem Strom der Akku geladen wird, und ein integrierter Wechselrichter wandelt den Gleichstrom für das Hausnetz um. Ein separater Wechselrichter ist nicht nötig. Damit ist der STREAM 5000 die naheliegende Wahl für alle, die eine Solaranlage neu aufbauen.
Seine Stärke zeigt der STREAM 5000 bei der Einbindung der Module. Er bietet vier Solareingänge mit jeweils bis zu 1.250 W, zusammen also bis zu 5.000 W. Jeder Eingang hat einen eigenen MPPT-Regler (Maximum Power Point Tracking). Dieser passt Spannung und Strom laufend so an, dass die angeschlossenen Module bei den jeweiligen Lichtverhältnissen möglichst viel Leistung abgeben.
Was das in der Praxis bringt, zeigt eine Anlage mit Ost-West-Ausrichtung: Die Ostseite bekommt morgens früher Sonne, die Westseite liefert erst nachmittags ihren vollen Ertrag. Hängen beide Seiten an getrennten Eingängen, optimiert jeder Regler seine Module unabhängig. Die Ostmodule werden also nicht ausgebremst, nur weil die Westseite noch wenig liefert.
Der STREAM AC 5000 verfolgt einen anderen Ansatz. Er richtet sich an Haushalte, die bereits eine Solaranlage betreiben und sie um einen Speicher ergänzen wollen. Die Module bleiben am vorhandenen Wechselrichter, an der bestehenden Installation ändert sich in der Regel nichts; die Kompatibilität prüft eine Elektrofachkraft. Stattdessen nimmt der Speicher den Überschuss auf der Wechselstromseite aus dem Hausnetz auf und gibt die Energie später wieder ab.
Wo sich die Speicher aufstellen lassen
Die Speicher müssen nicht im Wohnraum stehen. Auch ein unbeheizter Nebenraum oder ein geschützter Platz unter einem Vordach kommt infrage. Möglich macht das die Schutzart IP65: Die Gehäuse sind staubdicht und gegen Strahlwasser geschützt.
Gerade in Garage oder Gartenhaus zählt noch ein weiteres Detail. Lithium-Akkus nehmen bei Kälte nur eingeschränkt Energie auf. Laut Datenblatt arbeiten sie zwischen -20 und 55 °C. Ecoflow gibt auf beide Modelle zehn Jahre Garantie.
Anschluss durch die Elektrofachkraft
Den Anschluss übernimmt eine qualifizierte Elektrofachkraft. Sie legt auch fest, wie viel Leistung der Speicher ins Hausnetz abgeben darf, und das ist mehr als eine Formalität. Aus der Batterie allein liefert ein einzelner STREAM 5000 bis zu 2.500 W. Kommt gleichzeitig Solarstrom hinzu oder ist eine Erweiterungsbatterie angeschlossen, sind je nach Anschluss bis zu 3.000 W AC-Ausgangsleistung möglich. Wer diese höhere Leistung im Hausnetz nutzen will, braucht laut Ecoflow eine feste Installation an einem separaten Stromkreis. An einem gemeinsamen Stromkreis sind es 800 W.
Mehr Module oder mehr Speicher?
Steht das Grundgerät, stellt sich die Frage nach dem Ausbau. Die Antwort hängt vor allem davon ab, wann im Haushalt Strom verbraucht wird.
Ecoflow bündelt den STREAM 5000 mit vier oder acht Solarmodulen à 500 W. Vier Module kommen zusammen auf 2.000 Wp, acht auf 4.000 Wp. Wp steht für Watt-Peak, also die Spitzenleistung unter Normbedingungen. Die Batterie hat in beiden Sets dieselbe Kapazität. Das größere Set lohnt sich vor allem dann, wenn tagsüber schon mehrere Geräte laufen, etwa im Homeoffice oder wenn Wasch- und Spülmaschine mittags laufen. Die zusätzlichen Module decken dann den laufenden Bedarf und liefern trotzdem häufiger genug Überschuss, um den Akku zu laden. Wie viel Mehrertrag das Set mit acht Solarmodulen tatsächlich bringt, hängt allerdings davon ab, wie gut sich alle Module ausrichten lassen und wie stark sie verschattet sind.
Für einen Zusatzakku spricht ein anderes Verbrauchsmuster: Der Speicher ist an sonnigen Tagen schon mittags voll, die Anlage speist danach vor allem ins Netz ein – und vor dem nächsten Morgen ist der Akku trotzdem leer. Dann verschiebt mehr Kapazität einen Teil des Mittagsüberschusses in die Nacht. Wer bereits eine Anlage betreibt, kann das leicht prüfen und im Monitoring die Einspeisung tagsüber mit dem Netzbezug nach Sonnenuntergang vergleichen. Sind beide Werte hoch, bringt mehr Speicher meist mehr als zusätzliche Module.
Mit einer Erweiterungsbatterie kommen beide STREAM-Modelle auf 10,048 kWh, mit zwei auf 15,072 kWh. Über das STREAM Gateway lassen sich außerdem mehrere Geräte der Serie zu einem System verbinden. Wie das funktioniert, erklärt das Ecoflow-Handbuch zur Speichererweiterung.
Was die App steuert
Gesteuert werden die Speicher über die Ecoflow-App. Sie bietet drei Betriebsarten:
- Eigenverbrauchsmodus: Solarstrom deckt zuerst den laufenden Bedarf im Haushalt.
- Eigener Zeitplan: Lade- und Entladezeiten lassen sich selbst festlegen.
- Intelligenter Modus: Er berücksichtigt den erwarteten Solarertrag, den Verbrauch und die Strompreise.
Interessant wird der intelligente Modus vor allem mit einem dynamischen Stromtarif, bei dem sich der Preis im Tagesverlauf ändert. Der Speicher kann dann in günstigen Stunden Strom aus dem Netz laden. Dafür ist ein kompatibler Smart Meter nötig.
Die Black-Friday-Angebote von Ecoflow
Die Aktion läuft bis zum 30. November 2026. Für die Aktionspreise braucht es keinen Rabattcode. Alle Angebote stehen auf der Aktionsseite von Ecoflow.

articles.title: Feds launch $50-million growth capital pilot for Atlantic Canada
articles.text:
Businesses on Canada’s East Coast are getting support to the tune of $50 million in federal funding after Ottawa launched the first Atlantic Growth Capital Pilot (AGCP).
The news: Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced the launch of the AGCP on Thursday. The AGCP is a $50-million fund that will provide repayable capital to businesses starting at $2 million. Funds are earmarked for established businesses with more than $10 million in revenue that are looking to expand production, adopt new technologies, commercialize innovation, and reach new markets.
From the source: “The Atlantic Economic Panel told us that better access to capital would help more businesses grow and keep their future in our region,” Fraser said in a statement. “We’re acting on that advice.”
The context: As Fraser noted, the AGCP is a direct response to recommendations made by the Atlantic Economic Panel, a consortium of business leaders from Atlantic Canada he convened just over a year ago in Halifax. That panel, which includes Bank of Canada lead director and CEO of Seafair Capital Anne Whelan, as well as members from Pabineau First Nation, the Halifax International Airport Authority, and McCain Foods, delivered a set of recommendations to Ottawa that called for better access to capital as a way to keep businesses headquartered in Atlantic Canada.
The AGCP will be delivered by the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, the federal government’s regional development agency for Atlantic Canada. Interested businesses can apply online from now until Dec. 11.
Final thought: Accessing capital remains a concern for companies throughout Canada’s business ecosystem, and Atlantic Canada is no more immune to those issues than anywhere else. However, Atlantic Canada’s smaller ecosystem means government funding like the AGCP often plays an outsized role when it comes to businesses looking for reliable early-stage support. Having a diversity of government funding streams to choose from in the region may mean that fewer founders will need to consider leaving the region to make those early leaps.
Feature image courtesy Sean Fraser via X.

articles.title: Freedom adds $45/200GB Black Friday plan, but with a catch
articles.text:
Freedom Mobile made a small update to its sales on the morning of Black Friday.
The carrier added another plan to its existing $35/40GB and $40/100GB offers. Customers can now get a $45/100GB plan, including 125GB of data and a 75GB data bonus, but only if they get a phone.
Along with the bonus data, the plan includes 5GB of Roam Beyond data and unlimited talk and text in Canada and 120+ destinations. The 200GB data works in Canada, the U.S., and Mexico as well.
Freedom’s other plans remain unchanged and, unfortunately, there aren’t any deals for bring-your-own-phone customers right now.

articles.title: PC lento? 5 pontos para avaliar antes de investir em um computador novo
articles.text:
Em 10 anos, o tamanho mediano de uma página da web acessada em computadores mais do que dobrou: passou de cerca de 1,4 MB em 2015 para aproximadamente 2,9 MB em 2025, segundo estudo do Web Almanac, do HTTP Archive. Navegar, abrir várias abas e alternar entre programas exigem mais da máquina do que há alguns anos.
Se o seu PC demora para ligar, trava ao abrir aplicativos ou leva tempo para carregar arquivos, o hardware ou o software pode não estar acompanhando a sua rotina. Antes de pensar em trocar tudo, vale entender o que está pesando. A Sandisk reuniu cinco dicas de João van Dinteren, Field Technical Support Engineer da empresa no Brasil, para saber quando faz sentido atualizar o armazenamento para um SSD.
“Quando um PC mais antigo ainda conta com um processador capaz e memória suficiente, atualizar seu armazenamento para um SSD pode ser uma maneira prática de melhorar sua capacidade de resposta e acompanhar essas demandas”, explica van Dinteren.
1. Comece pelo básico: mantenha sistema e programas atualizados
Antes de mexer no hardware, confira se o sistema operacional, os drivers e os aplicativos que você mais usa estão em dia. As atualizações podem corrigir problemas de desempenho, melhorar a compatibilidade e resolver falhas que afetam o funcionamento do computador.
Reiniciar o PC regularmente, principalmente depois de instalar atualizações, também garante que as mudanças sejam aplicadas corretamente. Para van Dinteren, manter o sistema e as unidades de armazenamento atualizados faz parte dos cuidados com a experiência de uso. “Ferramentas como o Sandisk Dashboard facilitam esse processo ao reunir informações relevantes e recursos de gerenciamento em um só lugar, ajudando os usuários a monitorar seu armazenamento e a tomar decisões mais conscientes sobre seus dispositivos”, afirma.
2. Libere espaço e faça backup dos arquivos
Verifique quanto armazenamento ainda está disponível e remova arquivos, aplicativos e downloads desnecessários. Isso libera espaço e mantém o sistema organizado. Arquivos grandes e conteúdos pouco usados também podem ir para outro local de armazenamento.
Antes de qualquer mudança significativa no hardware, o backup de documentos, fotos, projetos e outros dados pessoais é essencial para evitar a perda de informações. Feita essa etapa, é hora de olhar para os arquivos e o espaço que ocupam e pensar na capacidade necessária, hoje e no futuro. “Uma unidade de 256 GB ou 512 GB será suficiente, ou um SSD de 1 TB atenderá melhor às necessidades do usuário?”, questiona van Dinteren.
3. Descubra o que realmente deixa o PC lento
Se o PC continua demorando para inicializar mesmo depois dessas duas etapas, a unidade de armazenamento pode ser um dos fatores que afetam o desempenho. Os HDs tradicionais usam componentes mecânicos para ler e gravar dados, enquanto os SSDs funcionam com memória flash e não têm partes móveis. Dependendo do sistema e da carga de trabalho, trocar um HD por um SSD de alto desempenho pode reduzir o tempo de carregamento e deixar as tarefas do dia a dia mais ágeis.
Só que o armazenamento não é o único suspeito. Processador, memória RAM, programas e outros componentes também influenciam o desempenho geral. Por isso, o recomendado é confirmar se a unidade é mesmo o principal gargalo antes de investir no upgrade.
4. Verifique a compatibilidade antes de escolher um SSD
Identificada a necessidade, o próximo passo é saber quais SSDs funcionam no seu computador. Nem todos os dispositivos suportam os mesmos padrões de armazenamento, formatos físicos ou configurações.
Consulte as especificações do fabricante ou a documentação do equipamento para saber, por exemplo, se o PC aceita SSD SATA ou NVMe. Essa checagem confirma as dimensões físicas da unidade, os slots disponíveis e os requisitos de conexão, além de evitar a compra de um hardware que não possa ser instalado ou usado. Na dúvida, vale falar com o fabricante do dispositivo ou com um técnico especializado.
5. Escolha a capacidade de acordo com o seu perfil de uso
A capacidade ideal depende de como o equipamento é usado e de quanto dado você pretende guardar ao longo do tempo. Quem trabalha com arquivos grandes, edição de vídeo, jogos ou programas profissionais provavelmente tem necessidades diferentes de quem usa o computador principalmente para navegar, estudar ou trabalhar com documentos.
Avaliar o espaço que você ocupa hoje e as necessidades futuras ajuda a escolher uma capacidade adequada à rotina. A análise também evita pagar por mais espaço do que o necessário.
Vale trocar o HD por um SSD ou comprar um PC novo?
Um PC lento pode ser sinal de que a unidade de armazenamento já não acompanha o dia a dia. Depois de descobrir a origem do problema, o SSD pode ser uma alternativa prática para ganhar velocidade de resposta e prolongar a vida útil de um computador que já está em uso.
Com a combinação certa de manutenção, compatibilidade e capacidade, o upgrade ajuda a máquina a acompanhar as tarefas cotidianas. Para alguns PCs, é uma opção ao custo de trocar o equipamento inteiro, especialmente quando processador, memória e demais componentes ainda atendem ao uso diário.
