articles.title: Here are the best Black Friday deals you can grab for $30 or less
articles.text:
What can you get for $30 these days? When it comes to tech, you might be surprised. Even as gadgets get more expensive, $30 can still go a long way, especially on Black Friday. For just $8, for instance, TP-Link’s Tapo smart plug will let you control the Christmas tree lights from your phone. You can also grab a decent pair of ANC-equipped earbuds for under $20, or spend even less on a clever set of rechargeable AA batteries. And it’s not just gadgets that are on sale: you can even sign up for a year of Disney Plus and Hulu for $4.99 ($8 off) a month.
Here are the best Black Friday deals you can grab for $30 or less
From smart plugs to noise-canceling earbuds, there’s plenty of discounted tech for those on a tighter budget.
Below, we’ve rounded up the best Black Friday deals for $30 or less, from charging accessories and smart home tech to earbuds, streaming subscriptions, games, and more. Whether you’re looking for practical stocking stuffers or want to treat yourself without spending too much, these are the deals that won’t put a (huge) dent in your wallet.
Apple AirTag (second-gen)
Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.
Disney Plus, Hulu Bundle
You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.
SwitchBot Bot Rechargeable
Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.
Octobuddy Classic
Who needs magnets when you have suction cups? Octobuddy’s cheap silicone mount works with most phones to provide hands-free flexibility whenever necessary. It features 24 single-sided cups, which allow you to stick your phone to a mirror, window, or any other surface you think will provide that perfect TikTok angle.
Kodak Charmera Keychain Digital Camera
The Chamera is not a good camera, but that’s not the point. Kodak’s charming, keychain-friendly tchotchke lets you snap lo-fi memories on a whim, with an ultra-small 1.6-megapixel sensor, a built-in LED flash, and the tiniest amount of storage.
Hoto 3.6V Electric Screwdriver Kit Pro
Hoto’s rechargeable screwdriver is ideal for small repairs. It offers three torque modes, a rotational speed of up to 220RPM, and a helpful circular LED to illuminate dark spaces. The durable case also holds all 25 steel bits and an extension bar for getting into hard-to-reach places.
Zepath USB-C Li-ion AA Batteries
Rechargeable AA batteries are handy until it’s time to charge them. Most wall chargers let you refill four, maybe six, at once. Zepath’s clever solution is to ship them in an easy-to-use USB-C charging case that charges eight simultaneously. The batteries themselves are long-lasting, too.
HBO Max
An HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.
Wuben G5 rechargeable flashlight
The Wuben G5 flashlight is as small as a Zippo lighter, yet far more versatile, with a bright, rotatable light that can shine in numerous colors. It features USB-C charging and has an adjustable clip.
LifeStraw Sip
The original LifeStraw was designed for those heading into the backcountry. The new LifeStraw Sip? Not so much. The reusable steel straw is geared more toward travelers than outdoor enthusiasts, though fortunately it still manages to remove about 99.99 percent of microplastics, bacteria, and parasites from your drinking water.
Peacock
Peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you plan to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo. A Premium subscription also grants access to films from studios like Universal Pictures and DreamWorks, along with live sports and a host of Peacock Originals.
Anker 621 Magnetic Battery (MagGo)
Anker’s 621 Magnetic Battery is a slim, 5,000mAh charger that can attach magnetically to the back of any MagSafe-ready iPhone.
TP-Link Tapo Matter-Certified Smart Plug Mini
TP-Link’s Wi-Fi smart plug lets you remotely control lamps, fans, and other appliances using your phone or voice commands. It supports Matter, so it works with all major smart home platforms to set schedules and timers to automatically turn devices on or off.
Paramount Plus (monthly subscription)
Paramount Plus Premium provides access to live sports as well as movies and shows from both platforms, including Tales of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, a host of Yellowstone spinoffs, Star Trek shows, Sonic the Hedgehog 3, Twin Peaks, Dexter, and more.
Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Plus
Amazon’s last-gen Fire TV Stick 4K Plus streams in 4K and supports Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision, and Alexa Plus. It also ships with the redesigned Fire OS and, unlike more recent models, still lets you sideload Android TV apps.
CMF Buds 2A
With 12.4mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and an IP54 rating, the CMF Buds 2A offer high-end features at an affordable price. You can also customize the sound, adjust ANC levels, and find the earbuds using the Nothing X app.
Twelve South AirFly SE
Twelve South’s entry-level Bluetooth transmitter delivers up to 25 hours of continuous use and lets you connect up to two pairs of headphones to an in-flight entertainment system, making it a great travel companion no matter where you’re going.
Catan (6th Edition)
In Catan, up to four players strategically compete and trade for resources. The iconic board game ends when one player reaches 10 “victory points,” which is achieved by constructing a sprawling civilization of roads, settlements, and cities using sheep, ore, wheat, and wood.
Azul
Azul is a game in which you arrange patterned tiles in order to create the most beautiful tapestry possible. Arranging tiles in a strategic sequence will help you build your score while limiting your opponents’ ability to grow theirs.
Halo: Campaign Evolved
Halo: Campaign Evolved lets you revisit the original Halo: Combat Evolved campaign with better graphics, updated controls, and improved sound. The well-crafted remake also adds three new missions starring Master Chief and Sgt. Johnson, which take place before the main campaign. Read our review.
Anker 140W 2-in-1 USB-C to USB-C Cable
No one should have to deal with a rat’s nest behind their desk when devices like Anker’s 2-in-1 USB-C cable exist. The handy USB-C cable splits at the end, giving you the ability to charge up to two devices from a single port. That means you can split power between a phone and tablet or juice a 16-inch MacBook Pro to 50 percent in just 20 minutes using a single port.
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered
The Witcher 3 lets you explore the war-torn Northern Kingdoms as Geralt of Rivia while preparing to face the mysterious Wild Hunt. The recent remaster adds improved visuals, smoother combat, and better movement, cementing the game’s status as one of the best RPGs of all time.
Iniu P55-E2 Power Bank (10,000mAh)
Iniu’s P55-E2 Power Bank is an ultra-slim three-port USB charger that’s capable of fully recharging an iPhone 16 twice. It supports charging speeds of up to 45W via a USB-C port, which can deliver fast recharging for a range of gadgets.
Glocusent Bookmark Style Reading Light
Glocusent’s clip-in reading light features five brightness levels and multiple color temperature settings, ranging from a soft, warm glow that’s great for late-night reading to a brighter light that’s perfect for daytime use. The slim USB light easily slips into your pocket, too, so you can read anywhere, from a cozy bed to a dimly lit train.
LIFX Everyday Smart Light Bulbs (two-pack)
LIFX’s dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connectivity, simple setup, and Matter compatibility, so they work with any major smart home platform. The company is currently trialing a Thread beta that will bring the option to add Thread connectivity to all its Matter devices.
ChomChom Roller Pet Hair Remover
The ChomChom is a reusable roller that works great for removing unwanted pet hair from furniture, allowing you to skip lint rollers, vacuuming, and other cleaning tools in a pinch.
Apple TV (six-month subscription)
Apple TV offers ad-free streaming of original shows and movies, including shows like Severance, Silo, Slow Horses, and Pluribus. The service also features a rotating selection of films, along with live Formula 1 races and Major League Soccer matches.
Anker Zolo Magnetic Wireless Charger
Anker’s Qi2 charging pads support wireless charging speeds of up to 15W, and their 5-foot cable shouldn’t feel constricting if you need to move the charger around.
Blink Mini 2K Plus
Blink’s Mini 2K Plus is a small plug-in security camera that lets you monitor your home or pets with 2K video, motion detection, and color night vision. It also offers two-way audio, a built-in siren, and Alexa support; however, some features, including person and vehicle detection, require a Blink subscription.
Loop Quiet 2 earplugs
Attending a live concert? You can protect your hearing with Loop’s Quiet 2 earplugs. They pack up to 24dB (SNR) of noise reduction and come with four eartip sizes, allowing them to accommodate a range of ear shapes.
Crunchyroll
Crunchyroll is an anime-centric streaming service that offers ad-free access to shows like One Piece, Jujutsu Kaisen, The Apothecary Diaries, and Black Clover, with new episodes available shortly after they air in Japan.
Logitech Pop Mouse
Logitech’s Pop is a cute, simple wireless mouse with an ambidextrous design and the ability to switch between up to three devices. It supports customization through the Logi Options Plus app and can last for several months on a single charge.
Logitech G502 Hero
Logitech’s G502 Hero has most of the same features as one of our top choices among gaming mice, the G502 Lightspeed, except it’s wired. If you’re okay with that, this is an excellent mouse that you can usually find for $50 or less.
Ugreen Nexode 240W USB-C Cable with Digital Display
The proliferation of miniature screens continues with Ugreen’s latest Nexode USB-C Cable, which features a full-color LCD screen on one end that displays current power draw (up to 240W). It also supports 480Mbps data transfer speeds and, unlike similar power meter-equipped cables, lets you turn off the screen when needed.
Tile Pro
The Tile Pro is the company’s loudest Bluetooth tracker, one that benefits from a 500-foot range. It also features a user-replaceable battery, unlike some other Tiles, and works with both iOS and Android devices.
Anker Nano Travel Adapter (5-in-1, 20W)
Anker’s jack-of-all-trades travel adapter packs enough ports to refill your devices during some downtime. It features one AC outlet, two USB-C ports (one tops out at 20W), and two USB-A ports. It’s not the fastest wall charger, but it’s a solid choice when you can find it at a discount.
Kobo Remote
The Kobo Remote lets you turn pages on a compatible Kobo e-reader with the click of a button, so you can keep reading without reaching for the screen. It connects directly over Bluetooth and features a curved, handheld design that doesn’t require clipping anything onto your e-reader.
Ring Indoor Cam (second-gen)
The second-gen Ring Indoor Cam lets you keep an eye on your place in 1080p, with support for motion detection alerts, a live feed, and color night vision.
Workpro EDC Folding Utility Knife
Workpro’s EDC is a lightweight folding utility knife with a side-mounted button that lets you flick it open and closed with one hand. It uses standard utility blades, which you can easily replace using a spring-loaded plate, making it handy for breaking down cardboard boxes and other tasks.
Lamicall’s cord organizers use magnetic clasps to keep cables in place, preventing them from slipping behind desks, shelves, and other furniture when unplugged.
Nalgene Narrow Mouth water bottle (16-ounce)
Nalgene’s lightweight, 16-ounce water bottle features a narrow opening for sipping, a leakproof lid, and a slim design that fits in cup holders. It’s made from durable, BPA- and BPS-free plastic, with measurement markings along the side and dishwasher-safe construction.
Fanttik S1 Electric Screwdriver
This tiny cordless driver comes with five double-ended bits for most basic around-the-house projects and Ikea-level builds.

articles.title: This ER Doctor Became a Hospital’s First Clinical AI Engineer
articles.text:
When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job.
At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context.
Dinesh Rai
Employer:
Boston Children’s Hospital
Occupation:
Clinical AI Engineer
Education:
Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine
It was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology.
Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job.
When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein, chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s.
Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Now, better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems—and determining whether its answers can be trusted. Brownstein says the questions they focus on these days have shifted: “How do you embed these tools in your day-to-day operations? How do you build agents to manage literally everything that you do?”
For Rai, that has meant embracing a job broader than the role that brought him to Boston. “I’m more like a clinical AI engineer now,” he says.
Between medicine and engineering
Rai originally studied business as an undergraduate and began teaching himself to code in 2014 (the same year he entered medical school), as neural networks and image recognition were starting to attract wider attention. He kept building software while training as a doctor. In medical school, for instance, he created a platform called Academius for students to track residency interviews and assemble their rank lists.
For Rai, the appeal of coding was its scale. In emergency medicine, he could make a direct difference for the individual patient in front of him. Software offered the possibility of building something that thousands of clinicians might use for many more patients.
His 2021–22 informatics fellowship made the possibility of doing that full-time feel real. In 2022, Rai took a job at Pieces, a health care AI company, where he led work to bring LLM-based medical summarization into clinical use.
That meant taking a break from practicing medicine altogether. “Stepping away was definitely a hard decision,” Rai says. But he wanted to give the technology work his full attention. He has since reactivated his medical license and hopes to return to clinical practice in some capacity within the next year.
At Boston Children’s, roughly half his day now looks like an engineer’s: working with developers, writing code, and advancing projects from the technical side. The other half is spent with clinicians, figuring out what they actually need. That combination has become the point of the job.
Uncovering “clinical doppelgangers”
One project, called clinical doppelgangers, is designed to help doctors treating complicated patients find similar cases buried in the hospital’s historical data. Medical guidelines are generally based on large populations, but at a hospital that handles rare and complex diseases, an individual child may not fit neatly into the populations represented in published studies.
The system is being developed to let clinicians identify previous patients with relevant similarities, examine their trajectories, and see how different interventions turned out. It is not meant to replace randomized clinical trials. Instead, it could provide another source of evidence when a physician is facing a case for which the published literature offers little guidance.
Projects like that require more than knowing how to ask an LLM the right question. They require understanding what hospital data means, how a clinician will use an answer, and how an AI system can go wrong.
Rai recently encountered some of those challenges while working on another project with a clinical team and a development team. They were deciding how much of a patient’s medical record to give an AI model when asking it to identify findings relevant to a particular clinical outcome.
Better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems.
Both groups initially favored giving the model access to more information, but for different reasons. The developers assumed any data point could be useful. The clinicians assumed the model would recognize irrelevant findings and ignore them.
Rai saw a problem with both assumptions. Clinically, an abnormal lab result or vital sign is not necessarily relevant to the question being asked. And from a technical perspective, an LLM cannot be counted on to recognize that irrelevance. If the system asks the model whether a given abnormality matters, it may construct a plausible explanation for why it does, even when the record does not support the connection.
“That’s where the dual perspective has been valuable,” Rai says, “not just translating between teams, but recognizing when an approach that looks reasonable from either perspective rests on assumptions we shouldn’t make.”
After the prompt
In medicine, the challenges surrounding the prompt are now more important than polishing the prompt itself. Is the model’s output consistent with the underlying data? How should its results be evaluated? Will the clinician using it be able to recognize a mistake?
That also means listening to clinicians’ experience. For the platform Rai’s team built to draft clinical notes, the clinicians who would go on to use the tool reviewed a batch of generated notes before anything was finalized. Someone who had cared for a complicated patient in the cardiac intensive care unit for weeks would catch an error far more easily than someone skimming the chart afterward, Rai says.
Although AI adoption in medicine is surging, some health care professionals still have concerns about its use. “I think some skepticism is healthy, and we don’t try to talk people out of it,” he says. The team told clinicians up front that it was a generative AI tool meant to support their judgment, not replace their own review of the chart. “People trust it more when they’ve seen its mistakes than when we just tell them it’s good.”
An evolving career
The evolution of Rai’s role reflects how quickly AI-focused jobs can change, so Rai is wary of telling people interested in careers like his to master any particular tool. For people who want hands-on engineering jobs, fundamental programming skills still matter. Some understanding of machine learning is useful, as is experience building and testing systems. But not every clinician who wants to work with AI needs to become a database architect or take a deep dive into algorithms.
What Rai considers indispensable is domain knowledge. In the medical field, that means understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created, what that data actually represents, and where care breaks down.
That may be the more durable lesson from a career that briefly carried one of AI’s buzziest job titles.
“The value isn’t just knowing how to get an answer from a model,” Rai says. “It’s knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer we’re asking it to give.”

articles.title: SAP Confirms Cyberattack, Source Code Reportedly Compromised
articles.text:
Enterprise software giant SAP has confirmed it is investigating a cybersecurity incident following reports that threat actors targeted its development infrastructure.
German publication Der Spiegel [paywalled] broke the news on Thursday, citing SAP insiders and an internal notification sent to employees.
SAP told SecurityWeek that it had detected suspicious activity and implemented measures to protect customers and secure its services. The German company did not disclose details of the attack.
“Based on our investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data,” SAP told SecurityWeek.
German news agency DPA reviewed internal SAP communications that revealed the suspicious activity had been identified within GitHub.
According to an insider cited by Der Spiegel, the hackers obtained SAP employees’ authentication tokens, enabling them to copy and alter source code stored on GitHub.
SAP publishes developer tools, sample applications, and open source projects on GitHub. It’s unclear whether the threat actor accessed any proprietary code.
Separately, Handelsblatt reported that SAP’s emergency security measures have affected numerous teams. The software giant has reportedly replaced signing keys, limited access to GitHub, and suspended automated development operations.
None of the reports indicate that tampered code was incorporated into software delivered to SAP customers.
Sources cited by Der Spiegel suggested that the attack may have been assisted by AI. While AI involvement has not been confirmed, several major organizations, including the European Commission, have recently disclosed AI-assisted cyberattacks.
In late October, the Gentlemen ransomware group listed SAP on its leak website, pointing to the company’s Latin American operations. File listings reviewed by SecurityWeek suggest the hackers obtained SAP-related software and source code, but it is unclear whether SAP itself or a third party was compromised. The two incidents do not appear to be connected.

articles.title: Simulation zeigt: Warum wir an der perfekten Stelle der Milchstraße leben
articles.text:
Glücksfall Erde: Warum sie den sichersten Platz im All besitzt
Unser Sonnensystem befindet sich in einer Region des Universums, in der biologisches Leben selten von zerstörerischer Strahlung bedroht wird. Zu diesem Ergebnis kommt ein Team von Astrophysiker:innen, wie in einer im britischen Wissenschaftsmagazin Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society veröffentlichten Studie zu lesen ist.
Die untersuchten Daten zeigen, dass die Milchstraße ihre unruhigste Phase der Sternentstehung hinter sich gelassen hat. Galaxien dieser Größenordnung und in diesem Entwicklungsstadium bieten die stabilsten Voraussetzungen, um Planeten vor energiereicher Strahlung zu bewahren.
EAGLE-Projekt: Wie Supercomputer die Geschichte unseres Sonnensystems entschlüsseln
Für die Analyse griffen die Wissenschaftler:innen auf das Eagle-Projekt zurück, das an der University of Durham im nordenglischen Durham beheimatet ist. Die Simulation kalkuliert die Ausdehnung des Raums, die Wirkung der Gravitation sowie das Verhalten von Gas, Sternen und Schwarzen Löchern.
Auf diese Weise entsteht ein mathematisches Modell, das die galaktische Evolution über Hunderte Millionen Lichtjahre nachzeichnet. Die Untersuchung beschränkt sich dabei nicht auf den bekannten Sicherheitsabstand eines Planeten zu seinem Heimatstern, der flüssiges Wasser ermöglicht. Die Analyse zielt auf das übergeordnete System: die galaktische habitable Zone.
Milchstraße: Die Parameter der sicheren Zone
Ein Sternensystem in dieser Zone darf dem dichten galaktischen Zentrum nicht zu nahe kommen, aber auch nicht zu weit außen am Rand kreisen. Am Rand fehlen die schweren Elemente, die in der Astronomie als Metalle bezeichnet werden und erst im Inneren früherer Sterne entstehen. Ohne diese Grundstoffe können sich keine festen Gesteinskrusten oder Ozeane bilden.
Ein Übermaß an diesen Elementen birgt jedoch andere Gefahren für entstehendes Leben. Astronomische Beobachtungen zeigen, dass in chemisch zu stark angereicherten Umgebungen bevorzugt riesige Gasplaneten entstehen. Diese Himmelskörper wandern im Laufe der Zeit nach innen, wirken wie ein Schneepflug auf benachbarte Gesteinswelten und stürzen sie ins Zentralgestirn.
Kosmische Katastrophen: Warum Supernovae uns bisher nicht trafen
Die Modellierung sucht folglich nach Regionen, die eine ausgeglichene chemische Balance aufweisen. Zusätzlich berechnete das System fünf astrophysikalische Gefahrenquellen.
Dabei unterscheidet das Modell zwischen Ereignissen, die vorhandenes Leben auslöschen, aber eine spätere Erholung zulassen, und dauerhafter Zerstörung. Bei letzterer reißt die Strahlung dem Planeten die Atmosphäre weg oder verdampft die Meere vollständig.
Im frühen Universum bildeten Kernkollaps-Supernovae die größte Gefahr, also das explosive Ende sehr massereicher Sterne. Hinzu kommen Typ-Ia-Supernovae detonierender Weißer Zwerge sowie gebündelte Gammablitze, die noch über Hunderte Lichtjahre hinweg die Ozonschichten von Planeten zersetzen können.
Schwarze Löcher und Quasare zerstören Atmosphären
Eine weitere Bedrohung geht von aktiven Galaxienkernen aus, in denen supermassive Schwarze Löcher große Mengen an Materie anziehen. Diese Quasare strahlen intensive Röntgen- und UV-Wellen ab. Über Jahrmillionen hinweg heizt diese Energie planetare Atmosphären so stark auf, dass die Gase ins All entweichen und unbewohnbare Gesteinsbrocken zurückbleiben.
In den vergangenen fünf Milliarden Jahren hat sich laut der Simulation jedoch ein mechanischer Prozess an die Spitze geschoben. Wenn sich Sterne in dichteren Gebieten zu nahe kommen, wirkt ihre Anziehungskraft wie ein Hebel auf umliegende Planetensysteme. Solche gravitativen Störungen verzerren stabile Umlaufbahnen oder katapultieren erdähnliche Welten als heimatlose Körper in den interstellaren Raum.
Limitierungen: Modelle liefern keinen Beweis für Aliens
Trotz der hohen Rechenleistung verweisen die Forscher:innen auf die Grenzen ihrer Simulation. Die räumliche Auflösung reicht nicht aus, um kleinere galaktische Strukturen wie lokale Sternhaufen detailliert zu erfassen.
Zudem basieren alle Annahmen über lebensfreundliche Bedingungen auf den Parametern der Erde. Einen Beweis dafür, dass sich unter diesen Voraussetzungen tatsächlich biologische Organismen bilden, liefert das System naturgemäß nicht. Außerdem werden natürlich bislang unbekannte Mechanismen der Lebensentstehung nicht berücksichtigt.
Die Ergebnisse verdeutlichen dennoch die statistische Begünstigung unseres Standorts. Während junge Galaxien mit hoher Sternentstehungsrate lebensfeindliche Umgebungen darstellen, bietet der Rand der Milchstraße verlässliche Verhältnisse.
Heute erfährt im Schnitt nur noch einer von tausend Sternen in der Milchstraße ein folgenschweres Zerstörungsereignis. Unser Sonnensystem profitiert von einer Galaxie, die sich in einer stabilen Ruhephase befindet.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 06.10.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Wahrscheinlich wird die Definition und Vorstellung von bewusstem Leben in 100 Jahren ganz anders aussehen als heute. Da werden sicher in den nächsten Jahren einige „erstaunliche“ Entdeckungen auf uns zukommen. ;)
Eine Simulation zeigt, was eine Simulation simuliert.
